Arthur Lupe Salazar Jr.
Grand Master
2024-2025

ARTHUR L. SALAZAR JR.
Grand Master
October 27, 2024 – October 26, 2025

ii

Brother Arthur Lupe Salazar Jr. is a past master of Irvine Valley Lodge
No. 671 in Lake Forest and was the charter master of The Thirty-Three Lodge
in Orange County. He received the Degrees of Masonry in San Francisco Lodge
No. 120 in 2004 and was honored with the Hiram Award in 2012 by Irvine Valley
Lodge No. 671.
An Orange County native, Brother Salazar is an accomplished Certified
Public Accountant having practiced tax and accountancy for over 20 years.
Most recently, he was owner and president of Salazar Accountancy Corporation.
His career in public accounting began in Palo Alto before relocating back
to Orange County in 2006. In 2020, he retired from public accounting and
accepted the full-time role of Executive Vice President and Secretary of the
California Scottish Rite Foundation. He received a Bachelor of Science degree in
Business Administration from University of California Riverside, where he was
an academic research scholar and a recipient of the A. Gary Anderson Special
Achievement Award. He later earned a Master of Business Taxation from the
University of Southern California.
Brother Salazar has acted in service and leadership to the Grand Lodge of
California for eighteen years. He’s served on several Grand Lodge committees
including Annual Communication Activities, Audit, Inspector’s Development,
and the Joint Committee on Fraternal Relations. He has served as a consultant and a member to the Executive Committee, was a member of the Let’s
Write the Future Campaign committee and served on the Strategic Planning
Group. He was an Inspector for five years and was elected Grand Treasurer in
2015 and served six terms in that role. Over that time, he served as Treasurer
of Acacia Creek Retirement Communities, California Masonic Foundation,
California Masonic Memorial Temple, Masonic Homes of California, and Nob
Hill Masonic Center.
In addition, Brother Salazar has been active in many Masonic organizations
and youth orders. He is a 33° Inspector General Honorary in the San Francisco
Scottish Rite Valley and Orange County Scottish Rite Valley where he served as
Treasurer and as Wise Master of the Chapter of Rose Croix. He was president
of the Orange County Scottish Rite Foundation. He has served as Treasurer
and Audit Committee chairman for the California Scottish Rite Foundation.

He is a member of the Orange County York Rite Bodies, El Bekal Shriners,
Royal Order of Scotland, Saint Gabriel Conclave Red Cross of Constantine,
and California College Societas Rosicruciana in Civitatibus Foederatis. He
has been an adult volunteer for the International Order of Rainbow for Girls
and DeMolay International, which bestowed upon him the Honorary Legion
of Honor and made him a Deputy Member in 2022. And he is Chairman of the
2025 Conference of Grand Masters of Masons in North America.
An engaged member of his community, Brother Salazar volunteers as treasurer of the Youth Fund of Southern California. He was previously on the school
site council for Oak Grove Elementary School, and he served as president of
the school’s foundation for six years. He has volunteered for the Red Cross
of Orange County and the American Youth Soccer Association for which he
served as a coach and referee. He and his family are members of Corpus Christi
Catholic Church. Brother Salazar is a proud husband and father. His wife of
24 years, Dr. Laura Camacho Salazar, is a physician in internal medicine. They
have three children. Ixchel is a medical student at Mayo Clinic in Minnesota.
Sofia is a nursing student at Chaminade University of Honolulu and volunteers
at the Shrine Hospital. And Amira is studying to become a genetic engineer at
UCLA. The Salazars reside in Aliso Viejo in Orange County.

ONE HUNDRED SEVENTY SIXTH
ANNUAL COMMUNICATION
Friday Afternoon, October 24, 2025
The 176th Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted
Masons of the State of California was called to order by Grand Master Arthur
L. Salazar Jr. on Friday, October 24, 2025.
Bro. Sebastian D. Marano, a member of King David’s No. 209 and son of
Assistant Grand Lecturer, Division V Christian G. Marano, called the Grand
Lodge to order.
Reception of the Past Grand Masters
The grand master welcomed the brethren and directed the grand marshal to
present the past grand masters of the Grand Lodge of California at the altar. The
grand marshal then introduced each past grand master, and the grand master and
deputy grand master personally greeted each one. The grand master asked the
brethren to join him in saluting our past grand masters by the battery of three
times three. The past grand masters were then escorted to seats reserved for them
in the auditorium. The grand master then directed the grand secretary to send to
each absent past grand master the usual letter of greeting from the grand lodge.
Roll Call
The grand secretary was asked to call the roll of grand lodge officers, past grand
masters, and past grand officers, and to ascertain if a constitutional number
were present to convene the Grand Lodge of California. The following were
present as indicated by their response to the calling of the roll:
Elected Officers

there were 780 Master Masons registered as of 12 p.m. Friday, with at least 20
percent of the lodges chartered by this Grand Lodge represented, and that
therefore a quorum was present as required for the transaction of business.
The grand secretary reported that all lodges have paid their annual per
capita assessment to Grand Lodge.

Grand Lodge Opening
The grand master then opened Grand Lodge in ancient form. The grand marshal
and the deacons retired to escort the flag of the United States of America into
the auditorium, which was followed by the Pledge of Allegiance.
Introductions
The following were asked to rise as groups for recognition:
Residents of the Masonic Homes and Acacia Creek, Diamond Jubilee Award
recipients, Golden Veteran Award recipients, Diamond Jubilee recipients, Hiram
Award recipients, worshipful masters, lodge secretaries and officers, constitutional board members, Grand Lodge committeemen, and district inspectors;
each group was greeted with a round of applause.
The grand master also recognized Grand Lodge officers visiting from other
jurisdictions.
Reception of Visiting Grand Masters
The grand master then directed the grand marshal to escort the visiting grand
masters from sister jurisdictions into the auditorium. The following were
received with private grand honors and introduced:

M\W\ Fermin Rodriguez . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . Grand Master
York Grand Lodge of Mexico

The grand master welcomed the representatives of grand masters from
other jurisdictions and directed the grand marshal to afford the guests seats
in the auditorium.
The grand master then invited Most Worshipful Fermin Rodriguez, grand
master of the York Grand Lodge of Mexico, to bring greetings on behalf of all
the visiting dignitaries. His remarks were as follows:

M\W\ Robert J. Eagle Spirit Sr. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . Grand Master
Prince Hall Grand Lodge of California
M\W\ Marc Strong . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . Grand Master
Grand Lodge of Oregon
M\W\ George Hamilton . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . Grand Master
Grand Lodge of Massachusetts
The grand master welcomed the visiting grand masters to the Annual
Communication of the Grand Lodge of California, with the fraternal wish
that they would take back to their grand lodges a full measure of brotherly
love from California. The grand master directed the grand marshal to conduct
Most Worshipful Fermin Rodriguez, grand master of the York Grand Lodge of
Mexico, to a seat in the east.
The grand master then directed the grand marshal to escort the representatives of grand masters from sister jurisdictions into the auditorium. The
following grand officers were introduced:

Brethren, have you ever wondered what it really means to inspire someone?
It’s not about great speeches or grand gestures. It’s about leaving a
spark in someone’s heart, a spark that makes them want to do better, be
better, live better.
And that spark, today, shines brightly here in the Grand Lodge of
California, because of one man and one vision.
Most Worshipful Brother Art Salazar, on behalf of all the visiting grand
masters and our respective jurisdictions, allow me to express our heartfelt
gratitude for your warmth, your vision, and your extraordinary leadership.
This year, I have had the privilege, and I would even say, the joy, of
calling you not only a brother, but a friend. When you, your wonderful wife
Laura and all your Grand Lodge officers and their families came to Mexico
in March, it wasn’t just a visit, it was a celebration of unity. I will never
forget the moment you opened the Grand Lodge of California inside our
York Grand Lodge temple in Mexico City. That was historic, emotional, and
deeply meaningful for all of us.
And when my wife, Kari, and I talk about that visit, we always say the
same thing: Art and Laura didn’t just visit Mexico, they became part of our
Masonic family.
Your theme this year, “Inspire,” is more than a word. It is a summons.
It is a call to awaken something greater within ourselves, the courage to
serve, the vision to lead, and the heart to uplift others.
You have invited the brethren of California, and all of us who stand
beside you today, to turn inspiration into action, in our lodges, in our families,
and in our communities.
You reminded us that inspiration begins with example, that leadership
is not about position, but about purpose. And, my brother, through your
kindness, your integrity, and your genuine love for this craft, you have
personified that theme.
When you spoke about true friendship, diversity and harmony, and positive awareness, those words stayed with us. You reminded us that Masonry
doesn’t live only inside our lodges, it lives in the way we treat each other,
in the way we serve our communities, and in the way we make people feel
seen and valued.
As visiting grand masters, we travel far and wide. We cross borders,
attend ceremonies, shake countless hands. But what truly matters are the
hearts we touch along the way.

California has always been a beacon, not only of light but of inclusion,
harmony, and fraternity. Brethren, Masonry has no borders. It has bridges,
built with friendship, trust, and love. The Grand Lodge of California has
built one of those bridges, strong and lasting, between our jurisdictions. From
your invitation to this Annual Communication, to every kind word and open
door, you’ve made us feel not like visitors, but like home. You have welcomed
us not as guests, but as brothers returning home.
That’s what inspiration truly looks like. It is when one person’s light
helps others find their own. So today, on behalf of all the visiting grand masters, I want to thank you and all the brethren from California for reminding
us what leadership, friendship, and love for this craft truly mean.
Art, you have inspired us, not just to lead, but to care. Not just to serve, but
to believe. And not just to wear the square and compasses, but to live by them.
May your light continue to guide this great jurisdiction, and may it keep
crossing every border, every language, every heart.
Because when we inspire each other… we become unstoppable. And
together, my brethren, together, we are stronger than ever! Thank you.

Memorial Service
The Grand Master called on the Very Rev. David M. Ferreria, grand chaplain,
to present a service of remembrance for our departed brethren. His remarks
were as follows:
Great Architect of the Universe,
We thank you for this opportunity to pause our labors and remember our brothers who have traveled to that undiscovered country from
whose bourn no traveler returns. We are all on the same rough and
rugged road and perhaps, in that way, we remain connected to them.
But our brothers have now traveled beyond our line of sight; and we
sorely miss their companionship on this journey. While they are no
longer with us, we at least have our momentos and memories of them.
But they often only serve as temporary salves for the pain of our loss.
Grief has been described in many ways. Some say it is the price we
pay for love. Others say that it is evidence that the love that caused it
was dear and valuable to us. However the best description I’ve found
is that grief is actually a form of love. Grief is love that persists. It is
bittersweet, being comprised of both happiness and sadness. It causes
our hearts to swell and ache because it is love that has nowhere to go.
The person to whom we would give that love is not present to receive
it from us.
Great Architect, we acknowledge that one of your many gifts to
us was the opportunity to meet and spend time with these men; and

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

13

to have the honor of counting them as our brothers. In gratitude, we
will not let our grief be the only means by which our beloved friends
live on. They left us with more than just memories. We have their
words, their counsel, the knowledge and bits of wisdom they imparted
upon us. We can emulate the best of who they were in our everyday
actions. We can live by the values, principles and moral precepts that
they endeavored to live up to; and we can teach them to others. We
can recount to others the acts and deeds of these men whereby they
demonstrated their dedication and commitment to their ideals. If we
decide to do that—no, if we indeed do that, my brothers—then their
influence, the essence of who they were, will live on through the rest of
our days, and perhaps, even, through the lives of generations to come.
Great Architect, we pray that you continue your care for our
brothers as they dwell in your house and ask that you bless us with
the strength to carry on their good work until we reach the end of this
road and reunite with our brothers at long last.
Amen.
The grand master thanked the grand chaplain and noted that two past grand
masters laid down their trowels and ended their earthly toils: Most Worshipful
Brother Harry Lee Maynard and Anthony Peter Wordlow.

15

The grand master called on Most Worshipful Brother Russell E. Charvonia
to deliver the eulogy for Most Worshipful Brother Maynard. His remarks were
as follows:

Eulogy
Harry Lee Maynard

Harry L. Maynard

Grand Master 1982-1983
Channel Island Lodge No. 214
November 5, 1927 – March 2, 2025

It is a rarity in Masonry for a man to be afforded the privilege of calling
his father-in-law “my brother.” This is, however, an honor I will forever cherish.
I knew absolutely nothing about Freemasonry when I started dating my
now-wife, Linda, in the late ’80s. Most Worshipful Harry would schlep—I mean
“invite”—me to various Masonic events. As I interacted with more Masons, I
became ever more impressed as to their character, and I was intrigued by this
invisible bond they seemed to share and hold so dear. It became clear to me
early on why Masonry was so important to Harry and why he received so much
spiritual fulfillment from it. I am grateful to have been able to share my Masonic
journey with such an exemplar.
It is said that a life is measured not by the dates of birth and death, but
rather how one “lived their dash”—all the days in between.
It is also fair to say that Harry lived his dash to the fullest, always striving
to improve the lives of those who came into his.
I will continue to think about Harry, the man, the Mason, the mensch, much
in the present tense instead of the past, as he is still, and shall forever remain,
an important part of all of us.
Harry Lee Maynard was born in DeWitt, Iowa on Nov. 5, 1927. He was
preceded in death by two years and one day by his wife, Carolyn. He was her
high school basketball coach, and together they moved to California where they
were married in 1952. While they were pregnant with Linda, they lost their sixyear-old son, Harry Lee Jr. due a tragic burn accident. There is no doubt this
shaped their relationship and their outlook on life. While I could never replace
their beloved son, I want to believe I helped to fill a tiny portion of the hole
that was left in Harry’s heart.
Harry was the last surviving of his five siblings, of whom he was the eldest.
He attended colleges in New York and Iowa, culminating in a bachelor of
arts degree in math, physics, and physical education from the University of
Northern Iowa. He was in the Navy V-5 aviation program which ended with
the conclusion of WWII, after which he went into teaching. He was the math,
physics, and PE teacher at Stewart High School in Iowa.
Sports were important to him, even as a man of slight stature. He played
semipro football and coached many youth teams. He was quite proud of his
nose having been broken several times on the gridiron. Harry was also an ardent
golfer and played tennis well into his 60s.
He and Carolyn moved to Ventura, California in July of 1952, where he
taught in the El Rio School District for a time. He later moved to a career in

16

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

17

finance, from which he retired as president of American Commercial Bank (now
Mechanics Bank). He made many loans on a handshake, and always trusted
people for their word. He was rarely proven wrong about a person’s character.
He and Carolyn traveled the world, touching every continent except
Antarctica. They traveled the U.S. in their Winnebago, and he and his buddies
delivered Winnebagos from Iowa to new owners in Ventura. Their stories are
legendary. Harry and Carolyn took many cruises, and they enjoyed taking family
with them, especially grandson Keith when he was a young boy.
Harry was exceptionally involved in community activities, inevitably
ending up in leadership positions. He was president of the Ventura Chamber
of Commerce, Buenaventurans, Ventura Trade Club, Ventura Civil Service
Commissioner, Redevelopment Agency, and Central Ventura Association; campaign chair for the Arnas Program Center for the Girl Scouts; a Little League
coach; founding director of the Boy’s Club; founding director and coach of
Ventura Youth Basketball Association (VYBA); a member of the American
Legion, Ventura Downtown Lions, American Bankers Association, California
Bankers Association, Ventura Farm Bureau, and he was a Ventura County Fair
board director and treasurer. He supported agriculture in Ventura County
through Future Farmers of America and the Ventura County Parks Preservation
Foundation. He served on the boards of Community Memorial Hospital and
Ivy Lawn Cemetery for several decades, literally covering his community “from
cradle to grave.” In fact, it was Harry’s idea to name the roads inside the cemetery
after current and past board members; thus there’s Maynard Way at Ivy Lawn.
Harry’s civic and business acumen is apparent. For Halloween trick or
treating, he would tape a dime to his bank president business card. I thought this
such a good idea, I dished out quarters taped to my financial planner business
card from our home eight houses up the street!
Most Worshipful Harry’s Masonic resume could fill this building. He was
raised as a Master Mason in San Buenaventura (now Channel Islands) Lodge
No. 214 in 1960. He served as master of the lodge in 1968 and became active
with Grand Lodge of California beginning in 1976. He served as assistant grand
treasurer and ascended to the role of Grand Master of Masons in California and
Hawaii in 1982–83. Harry’s theme as grand master was “Hold High the Torch
of Freemasonry.” He was the grand master who initiated Hawaii becoming its
own grand jurisdiction.
Harry was a triple valley member of the Scottish Rite and became a 33rd
degree Scottish Rite Mason in 1979, serving as the personal representative of
the sovereign grand inspector general for the Ventura valley in the ’80s and
’90s. He was in many concordant and appendant organizations in the Masonic
family, including the Al Malaikah Shrine Temple starting in 1963, serving as
orator in 1985. He was part of “Brownie’s BBQ Crew” that raised more than a
quarter million dollars for the Shrine Hospital system, along with other Masonic
charities, one New York strip steak barbecue at a time.
Most Worshipful Harry was also active in the Masonic youth orders,

including holding an honorary membership in Job’s Daughters Bethel No. 89
and No. 217, the Ventura chapter of the Order of DeMolay, and Grand Cross of
Honors with Rainbow for Girls.
Harry and Carolyn were incredibly generous, making substantial donations
to the University of Northern Iowa, where they endowed the Harry L. Maynard
Distinguished Professorship in Mathematics Secondary Education; as well as
Community Memorial Hospital, where the chapel now bears their names; and
Masonic Outreach Services. But it was also the quiet generosity to family and
friends, including Carolyn’s family, his family members in Iowa, and individuals
in Ventura who made his acquaintance and needed a leg up, that really demonstrates Harry’s consummate dedication to providing relief.
Clearly, Harry was a cornerstone of our community and a pillar of our
family. His greatest pleasure in life was time spent with family, especially Alissa
and Keith.
I think the thing he wanted most, however, was to see others succeed. He
realized that his achievements were due to his predecessors lifting him onto
his shoulders, and he was ever determined to do the same for others.
The true legacy of a person is not his worldly wealth or achievements, of
which Harry had many. Rather, it is the mark we etch in the souls of others that
really matters. It is the immeasurable acts of kindness and grace Harry extended
to others that ensured he left this physical place we call Earth in considerably
better shape that it was when he first became a part of it on Nov. 5, 1927.
Soft and safe to thee, my dear brother, be thy resting place. Bright and
glorious be thy rising from it! I thank you for allowing me to be a part of your
most incredible life journey, Dad.
Most Worshipful Harry Maynard was interred at Ivy Lawn Memorial Park in
Ventura on April 5, 2025, which was followed by a Masonic funeral at Channel
Island Lodge No. 214, which included military honors by Navy cadets.

Eulogy
Anthony Peter Wordlow

Anthony P. Wordlow

Grand Master 1997-1998
Western Star Lodge No. 2 and Union-Tehama Lodge No. 3
July 16, 1936 – June 6, 2025

On June 6 of this year, Most Worshipful Anthony P. Wordlow laid down
his working tools. Tony was born in Sheridan, Wyoming on July 16, 1936. His
family moved to Rio Linda, California when he was very young, and he grew up
in the Sacramento area. In 1956, he married his wife, Marilyn, and throughout
their long life together they were inseparable. She predeceased Tony in 2023,
and now they are together once more—a team that none of us will ever forget.
Tony served as our grand master in 1997–1998. His theme was “Freemasons
United: An Indelible Impression.” This theme was an appropriate one, because
Tony was a printer by trade. But a printer is much more than someone who puts
words to paper, and Tony was so much more. He followed in the tradition of two
famous printers in our Masonic history: Benjamin Franklin and William Preston.
Both were not only dedicated Masons but possessed a deep knowledge of the
principles of Freemasonry. Like Tony, Benjamin Franklin was grand master of his
grand lodge, the Provincial Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania, while William Preston
wrote the words which eventually became the lectures that we use in the three
degrees of Masonry to this day. Tony had a deep knowledge of what is means to be
a Mason, and his theme forcefully reminded us that you and I are someone else’s
idea of what a Mason is. The impression that we make on others will not be erased.
It is indelible. And Tony’s leadership in our fraternity was also an indelible one.
He became a Mason in Tehama Lodge No. 3 in 1959. He took his obligations on their famous “Miner’s Bible,” as all their candidates have done since
the lodge was formed. Tony was proud of the fact that his lodge was one of
the founders of our grand lodge, and both he and Marilyn had a deep sense of
California history. Tony was also active in the additional rites and degrees of
Freemasonry and served as potentate of Ben Ali Shrine at Sacramento. But it
was at the national level that he also left his mark. From 2009 to 2010 he served
as the president of the board of directors of the George Washington Masonic
National Memorial in Alexandria, Virginia.
Both Tony and Marilyn remained active in Freemasonry and in his various
Masonic activities until their declining years and health issues kept them more
and more at home. With Marilyn’s passing in 2023, Tony went into deep mourning, for their lives had truly been intertwined for so long. They leave behind
their son, Christopher Wordlow, a past master of Western Star Lodge No. 2,
another founding lodge of our grand lodge. Tony has left us, but he left us with
that “indelible impression” of what it means to be a leader in Masonry—an
example, my brothers, worthy of all imitation!

junior grand warden, moved that the grand secretary be instructed to cast a
unanimous ballot for Charles P. Cross to serve as junior grand warden for the
ensuing Grand Lodge year. The motion was seconded by the grand lecturer
and unanimously carried. Upon his return to the floor of the Grand Lodge and
upon his acceptance, he was declared unanimously elected by the grand master.
Biography of the Junior Grand Warden Recommendee
Very Worshipful Brother Charles P. Cross was raised as a Master Mason in
William Rhodes Hervey Lodge No. 767 on March 24, 1999. He affiliated with
Metropolitan Lodge No. 352 the same year. He served as master of Metropolitan
No. 352 in 2002 and 2003, and his dedication was recognized with the Hiram
Award in 2007.
Born in Baguio City, Philippines, on April 9, 1958, Brother Cross earned a
bachelor of science degree in economics from Saint Louis University in Baguio.
He has built an impressive 40-year career in banking and finance, including
nearly 20 years as controller of Atlantic, Inc., and almost a decade as chief financial officer of the Midnight Mission in Los Angeles. Since 2021, he has served as
chief financial officer of the California Scottish Rite Foundation.
Bro. Cross has been an active leader in the Grand Lodge for more than 20
years. He served as an inspector for 11 years, assistant grand lecturer for five
years, and as grand bible bearer for Most Worshipful Kenneth G. Nagel in 2010.
Currently, he is completing his fourth term as grand treasurer. His contributions
include roles on several committees, such as Ritual, Lodge Leadership, and
Strategic Planning, and he chaired the Audit Committee for two years. He has
also served as treasurer for the Acacia Creek Retirement Community, California
Masonic Foundation, California Masonic Memorial Temple, Masonic Homes
of California, and the Nob Hill Masonic Center.
Dedicated to youth, Bro. Cross has supported the Masonic youth orders
as an advisor for DeMolay International in Southern California. An honorary member of the International Supreme Council Order of DeMolay, he was
bestowed with the Grand Master’s Youth Support Award in 2011.
A 32° Scottish Rite Mason in the Valley of Orange, Bro. Cross is also a
member of Al Malaikah Shriners, Orange County York Rite bodies, the Order
of the Eastern Star, Royal Order of Scotland, and the Red Cross of Constantine.

Presentation of the Joe Jackson Award
Established in honor of Joe Jackson, a 60-year Mason, Hiram Award recipient,
and tireless servant of Joseph L. Shell Lodge No. 837 and Heartland Lodge
No. 576, this award recognizes Masons who embody his extraordinary commitment to Masonic relief and brotherly love. Joe dedicated 17 years to lodge
leadership while consistently reaching out to members, widows, and families
in need, connecting them to Masonic services, community resources, and
veterans’ programs, and serving as the catalyst for Division IX’s successful
Lodge Outreach strategic initiative. The Joe Jackson Lodge Outreach Award is
presented annually to a Mason who carries forward that same spirit through
proactive communication, consistent outreach, and an unwavering dedication
to improving the lives of those within our Masonic family.
The Joe Jackson Lodge Outreach Award recipient was Oakland No. 61.

The recipient of the award from Northern California was David E. Sokol, a past
master of Vesper No. 84.

years ago, my father, Jeremyha Lyle, stood on this very stage as the Southern
California Jurisdiction Master Councilor of DeMolay. Twenty-three years ago,
my aunt Tanya Almind stood here as Miss California Job’s Daughters. And now,

or titles, but the lasting impact we leave behind—the dedication and service
we give back to the organizations that shaped us. Legacy is the enduring gift
we offer future generations. It reflects our values, our commitments, and our
contributions. For the Masons of California, your legacy is woven not only into
the history of this nation, but into the heart of every member of Job’s Daughters.
Through your steadfast principles and generosity, you have laid a foundation
that continues to inspire. As young women in Job’s Daughters, we look up to
you. You are not just a face in the crowd—you are mentors, supporters, and role
models. In your legacy, we see a blueprint for living purposeful, service-driven
lives. Our ritual reminds us time and time again of our deep connection to the
Masonic heritage. Job’s Daughters was not formed just by one woman’s dream.
It was inspired by the centuries of work, ideals, and values carried forward
by generations of Masons. We believe that everyone has a role in building a
legacy—one of kindness, service, and leadership. As we grow and learn, we carry
the torch you’ve lit, illuminating the path for future generations. Many of you
have already made a profound impact, and it has not gone unnoticed. We see
your generosity. We feel your silent support from afar. Your legacy lives not just
in words but in the lives you have touched. I encourage all of you, whether you
know everything about Job’s Daughters or nothing at all, to reach out. There
are countless opportunities to make a difference. Sponsor a member to attend
leadership camp or our annual state convention. Even a simple conversation
can spark growth. That is how my bethel grew from one member to nine in
just a year. It wasn’t about showing up to every meeting. It was the worshipful
master of Redlands Lodge making it a point to know each member’s name. It
was the small donations collected after the members served dinner at stated

Jurisdictional Master Councilor
DeMolay International, Northern California and Hawaii
Most worshipful, grand family, and the family, friends, and members of the
Free and Accepted Masons of California, good morning. It is a great pleasure
for me to bring greetings on behalf of all the members and staff of the Northern
California DeMolay Association. I would like to quickly take the opportunity to
introduce those who I lead NorCal DeMolay alongside. Here with me today are
Deputy Master Councilor Takoda Gochenouer, Senior Councilor Ian Kirkpatrick,
and our Junior Councilor Jimmy Powell.
Inspire. Such a powerful word that stirs our motivations whenever we hear
it. A flashy word that people often like to use when giving speeches or talking
about their heroes. But what even is inspiration? Is it that slight tension we feel
in our bodies that begs us to act upon our dreams and ambitions? Is it a clear
picture of our goals with an established path for us to follow?
To inspire is to create a feeling—usually a more positive one—in any person.
Is that really all? I think there is a little more substance to it. These feelings can
be any range from a subliminal urge to choosing to completely devote yourself to
a new way of life. I believe that true inspiration requires one to fully be invested
with the desire to change or to act.
I believe that to be inspired, one must be dissatisfied. They must be dissatisfied with their situation or maybe even themselves. Whatever it is isn’t quite
providing the fulfillment they seek. But this dissatisfaction alone isn’t enough to
beget action or change in these individuals. Dissatisfaction has a little sidekick
helping along in its journey to become inspiration.
That sidekick is called hope, an optimistic state of mind which yearns for
a certain thing to happen. We sit with our dissatisfaction slowly gaining an
intimate relationship with everything we believe to be holding us back, just
waiting. Waiting for that one person to show us the hope, to give us a glimpse
of the future which we deep down always wished was possible. As some athletes
would say they just have to “see the ball go through the net once” before they
regain their confidence in their own abilities.
This leads us to the third member of our inspiring trio, confidence. The
belief in yourself that says I can do this. The understanding that your abilities
and qualities are enough to achieve your goals. This confidence doesn’t have
to be internal, either. You can be imbued with confidence from those around

33

Grand Worthy Advisor
International Order of Rainbow, California
Most Worshipful Grand Master, officers and members of the Grand Lodge,
distinguished and honored guests, and friends of California Rainbow: Hi! I’m
Aubrey, and I am so unbelievably honored to have the opportunity to speak to
you all this morning. I would like to take this time to introduce some of my
compassionate grand officers who have the opportunity to be with us today.
Inspire—one word, two syllables, seven letters, 1,000 meanings, a billion
stories. It’s a simple word, yet it holds immeasurable power. To inspire is to
breathe life into ideas, people, and movements. A teacher who lights a spark in
a student. An artist whose work stirs emotions across cultures. A leader whose
vision drives change. A stranger’s kindness that shifts someone’s entire perspective. From scientific breakthroughs to personal triumphs, every meaningful story
begins with inspiration. It’s not just motivation—it’s creation, transformation,
and connection. “Inspire” may be small in form, but in reality, it’s infinite.
The beauty of inspiration is that it’s contagious. Each of us carries the power
to inspire through the way we live, the compassion we show, and the courage we
choose every day. Sometimes it’s as simple as believing in someone, celebrating
their efforts, or giving them space to be seen and heard. Whether we mentor,
lend a helping hand, or simply show up with kindness, our actions can spark
something much greater. When we live with purpose and authenticity, we don’t

34

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

35

just find inspiration—we become it for someone else.
On July 4, 2025, the Guadalupe River in Kerr County, Texas reminded us
how quickly life can change. In less than two hours, the river surged more than
25 feet, swallowing homes, businesses, and entire communities. Among the
hardest-hit places was Camp Mystic, a beloved Christian summer camp for girls.
Cabins were torn from their foundations, two of them swept completely away.
The youngest campers, many only eight years old, never made it home. Families
searched frantically for loved ones while first responders fought to reach them
through roads that had turned into rivers. What should have been a morning of
celebration became one of the deadliest flood events in Texas history.
The devastation was almost too much to comprehend. But what happened
after the flood tells an even greater story. Texans did what Texans do best: They
came together. First responders, volunteers, and everyday people mobilized
in hours. Churches opened their doors as shelters. Neighbors cleared debris
from each other’s homes. Communities across the state sent food, clothing,
and hope. At Camp Mystic, volunteers waded through wreckage determined
to restore what was lost. What inspired this incredible outpouring wasn’t just
the scale of the tragedy. It was the belief that no one should face it alone. In
loss, in pain, in uncertainty, people found strength in one another. There was a
shared determination to rebuild not just homes, but lives. That spirit, rooted in
compassion and strength, became the driving force behind every act of kindness,
every hour volunteered, and every hand extended in help.
But here’s the truth: We shouldn’t have to wait for tragedy to be inspired.
The unity, compassion, and courage that poured out after the flood are things
we are capable of showing every single day. Inspiration doesn’t have to rise
from disaster. It can rise from a kind word, a brave choice, or a helping hand.
Imagine a world where we didn’t wait for a crisis to bring us together. Imagine
if we lived with that sense of purpose and empathy all the time, in the quiet,
ordinary moments. The flood showed us what’s possible when people unite
for something bigger than themselves. Now it’s our responsibility to carry that
spirit forward, not just in emergencies, but as a way of life.
This same spirit belongs in the Masonic family. As Masons, Rainbow Girls,
DeMolays, and Job’s Daughters, we are already connected by shared values:
service, integrity, leadership, and love for one another. But what if we lived
those values every day with the same urgency and compassion we see in times
of crisis? We are not separate branches—we are one inspired family. When
the wisdom of Masons combines with the energy and heart of youth organizations, we create something unstoppable. Together, we can build bridges across
generations, amplify each other’s voices, and lead with light and love in every
community we touch.
So I challenge us all: Let’s not wait for tragedy to inspire us. Let’s choose
inspiration daily—in our words, in our service, in the way we lift one another.
Because when we live inspired, we don’t just change moments. We change lives.
Thank you once again for letting me speak to you all today. We invite you

to come be inspired at our “Surrounded by Nature’s Grace: Stay Wild and Take
Risks, Explore with Wonder in 2026” Grand Assembly from March 28–31, 2026
in Visalia. Thank you!
Jurisdictional Master Councilor
DeMolay International,
Southern California
Most Worshipful Salazar, Masons of California, members of our Masonic
family, visitors, and friends, good morning. I am extremely grateful for the
opportunity to speak before you all here today and for all the support we have
received from the Masons of California throughout the years.
I would like for all of you to consider the acacia. Strong, beautiful, and
resilient. It pursues mutual improvement through symbiotic relationships with
those around it. In its wisdom, it sways with the energy of the storm, rather than
stubbornly allowing rigid branches to snap. It reaches wide with its roots to
enrich and stabilize the soil around it. In DeMolay, we teach youth to function
just like an acacia in their communities. We mentor our youth and improve our
order through our teachings. We work with our youth to adapt and handle rapidly
changing times. We reach wide into the community to serve our neighbors and
exemplify our cardinal virtues. These youth are the saplings we nurture, who
eventually become a force for good wherever they may go.
As much as DeMolay has to offer, the extent of our impact on youth and
their communities is determined by the harmony that is found in our Masonic
family. We have such a unique network that allow us to help each other grow
and thrive, but harmony is not guaranteed nor maintained without effort. Our
youth have faced a few roadblocks this previous term, the most alarming being
the uprooting of a chapter, whose members were thankfully taken in by a new
sponsoring lodge. Our youth dedicate time and effort to better themselves
and those around them, regardless of the challenges this world presents them
with. To them, the Masonic family is where they turn for guidance and hope,
like a traveler seeking rest and shelter under the shade of an acacia. It is for this
reason, and many others, that we should continue to show up for each other
and promote harmony. This way, we may better carry out our good works and
support the youth who are trying to make a difference.
For those of you who were present at the opening sessions, I had the honor
to stand before you as a brother Master Mason. Today, I have the responsibility
to stand before you as the Jurisdiction Master Councilor. When I speak, my
voice is not only my own, but the voice of every DeMolay there has ever been,
every DeMolay I represent today, and every DeMolay there is to come. Hear us
when we say, We need you. Not just money and spaces to meet, but your guidance. Your compassion. Your mentorship. The challenges you faced as a youth
may be different to those presented to the youth of today, but the virtues and
skills you have developed can still help them navigate the world they inherit.
Now more than ever, is the time to inspire them to do what is right, to grow as

36

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

individuals, and to become like an acacia in their communities.
Our shared virtues are our roots and foundation, the answer we must
never forget to the question of why we devote so much effort and time to our
Masonic family. When we unite around these virtues, the impact we see on our
communities is undeniable. When you invest your mentorship, we immortalize
in the hearts and minds of the youth, the virtues that ensure the perpetuity of
positive change in the world. For those of you who are already active in the
chapters, your service is priceless, and we cannot thank you enough for what
you provide for our DeMolay.
It has been an honor to speak on behalf of Southern California’s DeMolay,
and I humbly thank you all for your continued support. The future of our world
depends on the path our youth choose to take. To prepare them to walk a path
of virtue, is a choice for you to make.

George Whitmore exemplifies the highest ideals of Masonic service, inspiring the young women of Job’s Daughters to lead with kindness, creativity, and
purpose.

George Eugene Whitmore
George Whitmore has been a devoted Mason since 1995. He has twice served as
master of both Chino Valley Lodge No. 427 and Fox Coates Daylight Lodge No.
842. His leadership extended to 10 years as a district inspector and three years
as assistant grand lecturer for Division VIII. In recognition of his outstanding
service, he received the Hiram Award in 2005 and served as grand pursuivant
for the Grand Lodge of California in 2023.
George’s commitment to youth is especially evident in his long-standing
support of California Job’s Daughters. Since 2016, he has served as associate
bethel guardian for Bethel No. 262 in Victorville. At the association level, he
has served multiple terms as chaplain and was appointed Grand Outer Guard
in 2022. In 2023, he became deputy grand guardian, a role he continues to fulfill
with dedication.
Living in the high desert has not deterred George from supporting the inland
bethels—often traveling hours to assist with training and provide guidance to

his time as a guard and mentor.

George Frederick Lange
George Lange’s lifelong commitment to youth leadership began in 1968, when
he joined San Lorenzo chapter of the Order of DeMolay. He quickly rose through
the ranks, serving as deputy master councilor of Northern California DeMolay
in 1971–72. Over the decades, George has continued to guide and inspire young
people through his extraordinary service as a DeMolay advisor. He spent 20 years
as director of the Pacific Coast Leadership Conference, 20 years on the DeMolay
Convention staff—including many as director—and has served as chapter,
divisional, and Northern California Dad Advisor. Today, he continues to shape
the future of DeMolay as president of the DeMolay Foundation of California.
For his decades of exceptional dedication, George has received DeMolay’s
highest honors: the Degree of Chevalier, Cross of Honor, and Legion of Honor.
Initiated in San Leandro Lodge No. 744 in 1974, George is now a life member
of Salinas Lodge No. 204, where he chairs the Public Schools and Scholarship
committees and received the Hiram Award in 2024.
A retired educator and school principal with 35 years of service, George has
extended his passion for youth development into the broader community. He
serves as a CASA volunteer and has supported seven foster youth, including
his current case of six years. As a Kiwanian for more than 30 years, he currently
serves as a district trustee for California–Nevada–Hawaii.
George Lange is a shining example of the Masonic commitment to supporting and empowering the next generation.
George Frederick Whitten
George Whitten has been a Mason for more than 30 years, but his deepest
and most enduring impact has been through his extraordinary service to the
International Order of the Rainbow for Girls. Though he has no daughters of
his own, George has dedicated more than 25 years to the Petaluma Rainbow
Assembly, bringing boundless energy, creativity, and heart to every event, from
escape rooms to go-kart races to personalized Mickey ears at Disneyland.
For 28 years, George led the assembly’s largest fundraiser at the Marin
County Fair, managing equipment, setup, and five full days of booth operation.
His commitment extended far beyond logistics. He also contributed generously
to the assembly, securing corporate matching funds through Chevron to double
the impact of his giving.
At Grand Assembly, George organizes the food room, ensuring the girls have
the snacks and comfort they need. He pre-orders the mascot for the coming
year and surprises each girl with her own keepsake. His attention to detail and
personal care have made him a beloved figure in the Rainbow community.

INSTALLATION OF GRAND LODGE OFFICERS

Mark Edson Pressey
Mark Pressey has devoted more than 30 years to Freemasonry and nearly two
decades to supporting Masonic youth. Raised in Irvine Valley Lodge No. 671 in
1993, he has served multiple times as worshipful master of both Irvine Valley
and the Thirty-Three Lodge No. 878. His commitment to the craft is matched
by his dedication to youth leadership and development.
Mark’s journey with the youth orders began when his son joined Agate
chapter of DeMolay, inspiring him to become an advisor. When his daughter
later joined Rainbow, he also stepped in to support her assembly. Over the
years, he has held numerous leadership roles in DeMolay, including league dad,
chapter chairman, administrator, and currently serves on the advisory boards
of both Lake Forest and Agate chapters. He has been a member of the Grand
Lodge Youth Orders Committee for over a decade.
Mark’s thoughtful, behind-the-scenes approach has helped countless youth
and advisory councils navigate challenges, build collaboration, and thrive. His
dedication has been recognized with the DeMolay Cross of Honor in 2010 and
the Honorary Legion of Honor in 2017. In 2021, he was elected a deputy member
of the International Supreme Council of DeMolay.
Today, Mark serves as president of the Youth Fund of Southern California,
helping ensure chapters across the region are empowered to invest in the growth
and leadership of tomorrow’s Masonic family. His enduring commitment continues to shape the lives of young people across Southern California.

REPORT OF THE GRAND MASTER
Good afternoon, my dear brothers,
It gives me great joy to be able to see you here to celebrate our 176th Annual
Communication of the Grand Lodge of California. You have traveled far and
wide, rearranging both your work schedules and your family commitments to
fulfill your important duty as a delegate of your lodge and also to join with one
another in the incredible fellowship of the weekend. For that I wish to simply
say thank you—thank you to each of you and your significant others whose
understanding and support make all of this possible. I would also like to thank
all of the Grand Lodge officers for their dedication and support this past year;
the members of the Executive Committee, whose council and friendship have
been invaluable to me and the betterment of California Freemasonry; and my
wife and best friend, Laura, who has not only been by my side every step of the
way but is the reason I want to be a better man so that one day I may be the
man she believes me to be.
The California Masonic Code Section 404.130.F requires me to prepare a
written message setting forth all of my official acts during the year, report on
the general condition of Masonry within our jurisdiction, and recommend legislation that I deem necessary for the welfare of the craft. A full account of all my
official acts will be published in our Annual Proceedings and made available after
the completion of the independent audits of our various Grand Lodge entities.
My recommended legislation will be covered in detail shortly. I would like to
share that each Grand Master’s Decision and Grand Master’s Recommendation
originated as a means of addressing a specific pain point experienced by our
members and lodges. Please keep in mind that it is impossible to address every
need and issue at any given Annual Communication. However, I am confident
that those distinguished brothers who will in time occupy this venerable position will continue to evaluate the ever-changing needs of our brethren and work
towards the betterment of our gentle craft.
In order to report on the general condition of Masonry within our jurisdiction, I am going to share with you the details of certain events or actions,
how those impacted my perspective or knowledge of Masonry, and what those
say about who we all are as California Masons. I would like to ask you now to
please put yourself in the proper position to join me in these reflections by
clearing your mind of all the noise and chaos of everything happening outside
of these walls.

44

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

45

Within days of returning home from Annual Communication last year, still
in a state of euphoria, I received two important requests via email. One was a
request to perform an early presentation of a 75-Year Diamond Jubilee Award
for Worshipful Brother Rodger Siems, and the other was to make Bro. Domenic
Aiken a Master Mason at sight. I scheduled these to take place on Monday and
Tuesday afternoon, barely a week after my installation. On Monday afternoon,
I arrived at St. Jude Medical Center in Fullerton and was greeted in the lobby by
Worshipful Brother Siems’ daughter, Susan Holmes, and their longtime family
friend, Worshipful Brother Ralph Shelton. As they escorted me to the elevator
and on to Worshipful Siems’s room, she asked me for a favor. You see, her dad
had not yet met the official date of his 75-year anniversary as a Master Mason,
but he was determined to live long enough to receive it. With his health failing,
his family didn’t have the words to tell him that they didn’t expect him to make
it to the date, so they told him that it was necessary to make the presentation
early because it was the only date that would work. The favor was as simple as
you can imagine, so upon entering his room and finding it filled with several
generations of family and his wife of 66 years sitting in her wheelchair at his
bedside, I proceeded with the ceremony. Every few sentences or paragraphs,
he would interject with a story about Masonry or his life’s journey. I would
ask him questions, and his family were all smiles listening. Then, when he
finished the story, I would pick right up where I left off until I completed the
ceremony. Worshipful Siems passed 10 days later at the age of 95, surrounded
by his loved ones.
The following day, I received a call from Worshipful Narbeh Bagdasarian
informing me that the situation with Bro. Domenic Aiken had taken on greater
urgency. You see, Bro. Aiken, a Fellow Craft from Wisdom Lodge in Pasadena,
had been battling cancer. He had been winning his fight for a time, allowing
him to progress in his degrees but more importantly allowing him to be active
in the fellowship of his lodge. That morning. the doctors were recommending
a medically induced coma so that he could pass away peacefully, but he had
refused, stating that he needed to be awake to become a Master Mason. I asked
Worshipful Bagdasarian to call the lodge master, Worshipful Aaron Story, to
ask the brethren to assemble earlier than we had planned. I immediately left
my home and drove 90 minutes to the lodge so we could open and collect the
items we would need to take to his hospital room. From there, we headed to
Huntington Memorial Hospital in Pasadena, where we found him surrounded
by his family in his room. The family understood that we needed the room
in order to conduct the ceremony, so as they all left, his sister instructed our
grand lecturer, Very Worshipful Matt Vander Horck, and myself to each hold
one of his hands and keep rubbing his hands to keep him awake. As I was about
a paragraph into the Master Mason obligation, he became unresponsive. As
Very Worshipful and I looked at each other and began vigorously rubbing his
hands and arms and calling his name, I said a mental prayer asking God to not
let him pass without his sister by his side. After a few moments, he responded.

Very Worshipful and I looked at each other, and then I proceeded to complete
the obligation faster than I have ever said it in my entire life, declared him a
Master Mason, declared the lodge closed, and turned to the brethren to have
them open the door and bring Bro. Aiken’s family back in. As I looked into the
faces of the brethren, I was relieved I had not looked over my shoulder sooner,
because there was not a dry eye in that room. He became more alert once he
heard his sister’s voice at his side again and the brethren proceeded to provide
him with his gifts from the lodge as a new Master Mason and his family took
many photos to commemorate the occasion. Brother Aiken passed later that
evening at the age of 46 with his beloved sister by his side.
These two days at the beginning of my term focused my attention on the
importance that our experiences in lodge and with our brothers can have on
the weight that Masonry has on each of our lives. While Worshipful Siems had
a lifetime of great friendships and family engagement, our young Bro. Aiken
had only a couple of years within the craft. Yet it was clear to me that in both
instances, the brethren of their lodges practiced Masonry with joy and compassion for one another. They were with Worshipful Siems throughout his
entire life, and for Bro. Aiken they were there to the very end. This is the very
embodiment of brotherly love.
Then came the Los Angeles fires, once again putting our duty to one another
on display. As homes, businesses, and schools perished, our brothers in the
Los Angeles area began to open their lodges and homes to those in need as
a place to rest and refresh themselves. As California Masons, you organized
communities to provide relief demonstrating again how well we can all work
together. And our brethren across the world provided financial aid so that those
in need would have an opportunity to start anew. Even in the midst of having
their lives thrown into chaos, our brothers in the affected areas chose to move
forward with lodge installations and other celebrations together. They found
peace and comfort from the good food and fellowship and strength in the ties
of our obligations to one another. And as those affected brothers continue to
rebuild their homes and businesses, their lodges have grown closer than ever.
Sometimes when our lodges grow so comfortable with one another and
enjoy fellowship both at home and in the lodge, the lines of propriety can become
blurred. Such was the case for several lodges whose charters I had to suspend
when they found themselves in violation of our rules regarding the purchase of
alcohol. The investigations determined in each incident that the current master
and the brethren needed additional education on our rules and those of the
state of California. Based on the level of cooperation by all involved in these
particular lodges, I did not find it necessary to remove the master from office
and have since found the brethren of each lodge to be deserving of having the
charters returned. These instances have led us to develop new curriculum for
our lodge leaders and remind us that we all make mistakes but that it’s important
that we all learn from them together.
This year we not only rolled out new content at the retreats, we launched a

46

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

whole new format, changing the look and feel for our lodges. We no longer have
a secretaries and treasurers retreat and a masters and wardens retreat. These
have been combined into a new lodge leadership retreat, which has multiple
tracks for any officer or member in your lodge. The result was not only greater
attendance overall, but also more engagement and higher levels of energy at
each of the four locations. We also had greater attendance and engagement
from our significant others, with new social activities for their enjoyment such
as dance lessons or cabana time at the pool.
Balancing fun and work is a lesson we are shown through the symbol of
the 24-inch gauge. And there is certainly a time and place for each. We just
need to be cognizant of when and where they are. As California Masons, you all
definitely put in the work this past year achieving some incredible milestones.
In November we constituted six new lodges:

year stand as an exception. Let’s keep this momentum going.
This year we celebrated our 175th anniversary of our Grand Lodge and in
honor of that, I proclaimed the anniversary of our first meeting on April 17 to
be a day of service. The goal was to help focus attention on everything your
lodge is doing to improve your community so that together we can remind our
friends and neighbors of the important role our lodges play in building a better
world. Not only was there an incredible social media presence showcasing blood
drives, beach clean ups, service in food banks, and so much more, but you have
continued to highlight your community engagement on social media with ongoing days of service. It’s visibility like this that demonstrates our obligations are
not empty words spoken in some mysterious ceremony, but actual promises
between ourselves and our creator as well as to one another.
This much work certainly deserves to be celebrated. and that we did
throughout the year. One of the important places for fun this year has certainly
been the practice of the festive board, which brings so many people together.
There have been festive boards held in lodges small and large, in English, French,
and Spanish. And on April 19, we held not one but six festive boards throughout the state—at the San Diego Scottish Rite, the Pasadena Scottish Rite, the
Sacramento Scottish Rite, the Masonic Homes in Covina and Union City, and
of course, here in our own Grand Lodge temple. Additionally, several lodges
hosted their own festive boards simultaneously ensuring Masons throughout
California could join together on that special day.
There are a couple of reasons I truly enjoy these festive boards. The first is
the music. We come together and give it our best effort to literally sing from the
same sheet of music. It’s not always pleasing to the ear, but we keep trying with
each toast. After each attempt, there are smiles and laughter and the sharing of
memories evoked by the songs. Music is a special window into our souls, allowing
us to express feelings and recall memories we may otherwise struggle to share.
It becomes part of our collective memory and binds us all together. The other
reason I enjoy festive boards is the collection of people gathered together in
that moment. I have looked across dining rooms filled to capacity with brothers
and their significant others from all walks of life. A truly diverse collection of
people from different generations, with different countries of origin, different
languages, different hair color, skin color, and different practices of faith. But
we all come together in that moment. And in that moment, the world—our
world—is perfect: a world in harmony.
It’s these moments together with men that have become more than just
friends and Masonic brothers that reminds me—that drives me—to strive to
be a better Mason today than I was yesterday. It’s for these men that we should
all strive to ensure that the lessons taught by our gentle craft are not empty
but actual living acts of decency and civility, not just to one another but to
every person we come in contact with. It is up to each one of us to prove that
as Masons we have become better men—better than all the divisive rhetoric
that society tries to drown us in. Better than the hate that builds walls between

• Sonora No. 887

• Hermes No. 891

Since we began focusing on the development of new lodges over the last
15 years, we have chartered 42 new lodges throughout the state. And as they
say, “That’s not all!” because throughout the year, we instituted five additional
lodges:
• Oasis of Light UD
• Cicero Research UD
• Fiat Lux UD
• Danville UD
• Lautaro UD
Each lodge caters to a shared interest amongst the brethren, which increases
overall engagement.
Our candidate prospecting through social media has continued to yield
over 5,000 prospects per year over the last several years. This means that every
lodge has been a beehive of activity, welcoming prospects, building new friendships, and conferring degrees. For the 12 months ending June 30, you initiated
more than 900 new brothers into our gentle craft, conferring more than 2,200
degrees. You also reintroduced nearly 600 brothers back into the fold through
restorations. The net result of your efforts is that we experienced the first year
of positive membership growth since 1964. That’s 60 years! Let’s not let this

people instead of bridges between friends. We’re not perfect, but we can keep
trying and keep trying together.
These last 10 years you have given me as an elected Grand Lodge officer
have truly been a blessing. And this past year in particular has forever changed
my view of Masonry, the world, and our place in it. Y por eso los grandes amores
de muchos colores me gustan a mi.
I am more hopeful and excited today than I have ever been about the future
of California Masonry. I hope that over this last year I have been able to inspire
you in even the smallest way to become a better Mason, because you have and
continue to inspire me.
Thank you.
Respectfully submitted,

61

REPORT OF THE
DEPUTY GRAND MASTER
2025–2026 GRAND LODGE BUDGET

Dear masters, wardens, and esteemed members of the Grand Lodge,
Thank you for your trust in me to prepare the budget for the coming
fiscal year, November 1, 2025 through October 31, 2026. This budget reflects
our shared commitment to the future of our fraternity, building upon the per
capita proposal you adopted last year.
This year we reached an extraordinary milestone: membership growth for
the first time since 1965. This success is the result of our collective work in
prospecting, retention, and restoration, and it helps us meet the challenges of
recent years’ inflation. Our total projected revenue is just over $4.7 million. Of
that, $2.5 million—slightly more than half—comes from per capita, with the
balance from programs, services, and investments.
This budget invests in initiatives that strengthen our fraternity, including:
• Masonic Education: Programs like the International Conference on
Freemasonry, the annual symposium, and our Candidate Learning
Center
• Membership Management: iMember tools to simplify lodge administration and finances
• Financial Services: Accounting, dues collection, tax preparation, and
lodge/hall support
• Leadership Training: In-person retreats for lodge and district leaders, and the Lodge Management Certification Program
• Membership Development: Connecting prospects to lodges and
resources such as A Simple Guide to Freemasonry
• New Lodge Development: Building on the success of more than 50
new lodges established in California, we are expanding our efforts in
2026 and beyond

62

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

• Public Relations: Raising public awareness of Masonry and encouraging members to share their story

GRAND LODGE OF FREE AND ACCEPTED
MASONS OF CALIFORNIA
PROPOSED BUDGET

• New Lodge and Hall Resources: Practical tools to help officers and
hall directors succeed
We are also addressing a critical challenge: property insurance for our
halls. With carriers increasingly unwilling to cover California properties, we
are developing a captive insurance program to ensure long-term stability and
adequate coverage for our lodges and halls.
I am deeply grateful to our grand treasurer, grand secretary, finance staff,
and Finance Committee for shaping this budget, and to all of you who shared
feedback during our spring leadership retreats.
As we launch the Keystone Initiative, the multi-year plan to inspire members, strengthen lodges, and expand our community impact, I humbly ask for
your support in adopting this budget. Together, we will continue building a
vibrant and resilient fraternity.

GRAND MASTER’S
INSTALLATION SPEECH
Good morning, everyone!
I’m truly humbled to be here before you today. As I look out over all your
smiling faces, I see not just friends and brothers, but a family that has lifted
me up every step of the way.
Allow me take a moment to extend my thanks to a few more groups of
people who have made this day possible.
To all the past grand masters, thank you for your advice and counsel. Your
appointments to committees and boards over the years have prepared me for
this special duty to represent our grand lodge, and I am grateful for the trust
you have placed in me. Your legacy of compassion, past themes, and messages
remain an inspiration to us all, and I am honored to follow in your footsteps. I
hope to build upon the strong foundation you laid for us.
To all the brethren and lodges, thank you for your continued confidence and
support. Your active participation in spreading the light of Freemasonry, practicing charity, and fostering true peace and harmony in your lodges is the very
heart of our fraternity. Your confidence in me has been an incredible strength.
You’ve taught me the true meaning of brotherhood and the trust you’ve placed
in me is a responsibility I take seriously. I will strive every day to live up to the
high values and principles of our fraternity and to honor your faith in me.
I’d like to also express my excitement to our newly installed Grand Lodge
officers and inspectors. Thank you for your commitment of time, energy, and
expertise in assuming your leadership roles this year and for continually promoting our Masonic principles. I truly look forward to working alongside each
one of you.
I also want to recognize our retiring Grand Lodge officers and inspectors.
Thank you for your tireless efforts and years of service to our grand lodge and
to your respective districts. And I’d like to give a special thank you to a couple
of our retiring officers: Wor. Steve Miller, who has harmoniously served as grand
organist for over 20 years, and to Wor. Tony Cimarra, who has admirably served
as an assistant grand lecturer for nine full years. Thank you!
There are two more groups I would like to acknowledge today:
Would all the Senior DeMolays and majority members of Job’s Daughters
and Rainbow Girls who served with me during the late ’70s through the early

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

69

’80s please rise? Your love and the friendship that was developed during our time
serving together has made a lasting impact on my life, and I am truly grateful
for your being there with me then and for supporting me today!
And allow me to introduce my second family, the members of the Chinese
Acacia Club, California Lodge No. 1, and Pacific Star King No. 136. Please rise.
From the very beginning of my Masonic life, so many of you and many
brothers who have already passed on have taught me valuable lessons which
I carry with me today, and for all you, I am eternally grateful. Thank you all
being here today.
My Brothers and friends, let me now introduce my theme.
Our theme and priority for the coming year is “Peace and Harmony.” I am
looking to you to carry this message forward and for all of us to embody this
into the new year.
“Peace and Harmony” is not merely a slogan, but a call to action! Our 2050
Vision Statement, “A World in Harmony,” has guided us since 2020. Now let’s
focus on turning this aspiration into a reality.
These words are easy to say. However, it takes courage and constant daily
focus to achieve it. As Masons, we have a great opportunity to be a force for
good. When we ourselves practice peace and harmony, it radiates outward like
the sun, touching everyone in our lives, lodges and our communities.
As Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. said, “We must learn to live together as
brothers or perish together as fools.”
While not explicitly Masonic, this message resonates deeply with the principles of brotherly love, relief, and truth, which are fundamental to a harmonious
Masonic lodge and a more peaceful world.
Building on this theme, we have two integral priorities that are foundational
to our work. These are supporting and growing our youth orders, and promoting community engagement through charity and service, connecting all of our
lodges to our local communities.
By investing our time and mentoring our youth, we secure a brighter future
for our communities. DeMolay, Job’s Daughters, and Rainbow instill fundamental life skills which prepare them for the future. As Masons, we have a unique
opportunity to champion these groups, to ensure they feel connected to our
lodges and to help them flourish. We must be their mentors and their biggest
advocates.
The second priority I wish to establish for our members is a return to the
roots of our fraternity: charity and charitable giving. It’s easy to make charity an
unconscious act, but I wish to promote personal and fraternity-wide charity to
help our Masonic family, with whom we’ve obligated ourselves to help, thereby
living up to our core value of philanthropy.
While our grand lodge charities are a source of great pride and impact,
it’s also the small, daily acts of kindness that truly define us as Masons. The
quiet support of a brother in need; the community fundraiser; the anonymous
good deed are the lifeblood of our world, and they are the true measure of our

70

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

character as Masons. I believe that charity is not just a line item on a budget.
It is an active, ongoing expression of our values.
Brethren, here is what I see in the future for Masonry in California: The
future of Masonry in California is bright! Our future is not an abstract concept
or a distant dream. It is built one brother at a time, one lodge at a time, and
one act of charity at a time. It is a future in which our youth are engaged, our
members are actively enjoying the brotherhood, and our lodges are thriving
centers of peace and harmony. This bright future is the inevitable outcome of
our good and noble efforts.
My brothers and friends, I ask you to join me.
Our world today needs the principles of Masonry more than ever. I am
asking you to commit to bring peace and harmony, in a new and deeper way, into
our own lives, our lodges, and to our communities. Let’s continue to spread the
light of Freemasonry such that everyone knows that Masonry stands for good.
And by our own acts, may we continue to inspire all those around us to become
a better person, to be more service-minded, and to be charitable.
It is my hope that brotherly love, relief, and truth will always guide us in
our daily lives and actions toward others. Join me!
Together, driven by our commitment to bringing peace and harmony to
our world, there is no limit to what we can accomplish.
Thank you.
Respectfully submitted,

Garrett S. Chan, Grand Master

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

REPORT OF THE
SENIOR GRAND WARDEN
2026–2027 PER CAPITA PROPOSAL
Ara Maloyan, Senior Grand Warden
Dear masters, wardens, and esteemed members of the Grand Lodge,
As senior grand warden, it is my duty to present the per capita proposal
that will fund the Grand Lodge budget for the fiscal year beginning November
1, 2026 through October 31, 2027. This per capita will be collected next summer,
based on the number of Masons on lodge rolls as of June 30, 2026.
As our deputy grand master noted in his report, we have ended six decades
of membership decline. This remarkable turnaround reflects your dedication
to welcoming prospects, restoring brothers, and strengthening our lodges. The
thousands of men seeking out Freemasonry today remind us that our fraternity
is not only respected and relevant—but truly needed in our communities.
In preparing this budget, I relied on the best available data on membership
trends and financial indicators. The plan assumes modest membership growth,
supported by your ongoing efforts, while recognizing the reality of continued
inflation. To maintain the quality of programs and services we provide, the
proposal includes only a 2.8% increase in expenses over the prior year and
requires a $4.00 increase in per capita.
Therefore, I propose a per capita of $72.50 for Fiscal Year 2027.
With your support, this budget will allow us to continue delivering the
essential programs and services you have asked for:
• Leadership training and resources for officers, hall directors, and
members
• Communications and technology tools to support lodges
• Financial and administrative services to ease lodge operations
• Membership development and public awareness initiatives to sustain
our growth

74

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

Together, we are building a stronger fraternity—one that inspires new
members, supports our lodges, and makes a lasting difference in society. I look
forward to traveling this road with you as we continue to prosper in harmony.

REPORT OF THE
GRAND TREASURER
Most Worshipful Grand Master and brethren all,
Serving as your grand treasurer for the fourth and final term, I am pleased
to report on the financial health of our grand lodge and its related entities.
Moving forward with a “one team” culture as part of our strategic initiatives involving a synergy among the different entities, including the expertise
of our brethren who continue to volunteer their time as board and committee
members, and I am confident that our organization is prepared to address
further challenges.
The following financial highlights are based on the unaudited results for
the nine-month period through July 31, 2025 compared against the audited
results from October 31, 2024. The audited financial statements for the current
fiscal year ending October 31, 2025 will be made available with these Annual
Proceedings upon publication.
Masonic Homes of California and Acacia Creek
• Total current assets increased by $2.4 million to $25.4 million
from $23 million
• Investments increased by $40 million net of distributions to
$990.4 million from $950.4 million for the prior fiscal year
• Property and equipment decreased by $6.7 million down to
$253.4 million from $260.1 million due to depreciation
• Total liabilities decreased by $3.5 million down to $214.6 million
from $218.1 million for the prior fiscal year
• Net assets increased by $16 million through July 31, 2025 to
$1.23 billion from $1.07 billion
California Masonic Foundation:
• Investments increased by $1 million to $46.3 million from
$45.3 million for the prior fiscal year

Overall, our current master trust total as of July 31, 2025 is equivalent to
$1.097 billion, or a positive gain of $41.9 million from last year. The return on
investment for the year ending July, 31, 2025 was 3.8 percent and since the
inception of our master trust in January 1995 it remains at a healthy 7.6 percent.
While our master trust has gained a respectable size, we all must remember
that these funds are not available to simply withdraw to cover all our expense
needs of the several entities. For best practices, we are limited to drawing 4.5
percent up to 4.75 percent of the 20-quarter average of the market value portfolio for the investments of each entity to support their operations. Masonic
Homes and Acacia Creek received a 4.75 percent distribution for fiscal year
2025. What this means is that in the example of our Masonic Homes, with
a current operating budget of approximately $84.8 million each year, and an
investment distribution of approximately $43.2 million, that we have a delta of
approximately $41.6 million that needs to be made up from other sources such
as fees for certain services and each of our annual contributions in fulfillment
of our ongoing obligations to each other.
In 1992, our grand lodge created an endowment funded each year by the
budget surplus of each grand master. Since that time, the endowment fund
has grown to $2.96 million as of July 31, 2025 from $2.96 million in July 31,
2024. This allowed us to normalize our budgets and per capita assessments

Master Fund with a value of $3.8 million (from $3.2 million), and we have 41
lodges participating in the Lodge Investments Master Fund with a value of $35.3
million as of July 31, 2025.
Our Grand Lodge Financial Services team continues to assist our lodge
officers and hall association directors in planning their budgets, bank reconciliations, administer their payroll needs and tax filings, address real estate issues and
needs, reconcile their month-end investments, and provide general accounting
solutions in their day-to-day operations. We have now Grand View, the accounting software for our lodges that will be fully operational by November 2025. We
have for the first time successfully conducted a joint inspectors retreat. We will
continue to improve our leadership retreats; emphasizing impactful strategies
and providing our brethren with the tools to attend to our growing prospects in
our jurisdiction and focusing on serving our communities better. This year, for
the first time since 1964, we enjoyed positive growth, placing our fraternity in
a position to have more brethren practicing Masonry and creating meaningful
relationships, establishing life-long friendships, and showing our communities
that we are men of character.
Finally, I would like to thank Most Worshipful Salazar and all of you for
allowing me the opportunity to serve with inspiration as your grand treasurer.
I am honored working with so many devoted, caring and talented individuals.
Once again, a special thank you to my brother, colleague, and friend, Very
Worshipful Allan Casalou. My four years working with you has continuously
impacted my focus and enthusiasm in serving the jewel of our craft, our Masonic
Homes. I am ready! With the help of the almighty, I will continue to faithfully
serve our gentle craft with humility, zeal, and grace to the best of my ability.
