REPORT OF THE
GRAND SECRETARY
Membership: A Historic Milestone
Beginning Membership (July 1, 2024): 37,240
Ending Membership (June 30, 2025): 37,887
Net Gain: +647 members
Brethren, this is a historic moment. For the first time since 1965, our fraternity in California has grown. That’s 60 consecutive years of decline reversed.
Congratulations, brethren!
This remarkable achievement was not the result of luck, but of commitment, coordination, and care—your care for one another, for your lodges, and
for those seeking light in Masonry. You welcomed new members, you worked
to retain existing ones, and together we implemented strategies that made this
growth possible.
Connecting with the World
Our outreach efforts have matured into a powerful system. Through the I’m a
Mason and We Are Masons campaigns, thousands of Californians have learned
what Freemasonry means to us—told through your voices, your stories, and
your hearts.
These campaigns, amplified through paid social media, connect interested
individuals with membership advisors who reach out personally—more than
3,000 contacts this year. Over the past three years, more than 10,000 prospects
have been referred to lodges near where they live or work. Many of you have
embraced these leads and welcomed these men into your lodges.
This is outreach at its best—authentic, personal, and effective.
Restoring Brothers and Preventing Losses
Our growth story is not only about new members, it’s also about brothers
returning home.
Since 2022, our restoration program has helped reconnect nearly 1,600
brothers, and this year alone, 574 men were restored—more than double last
year’s total.

98

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

Equally important was our new suspension prevention program, launched
early this year. When a lodge records its intent to suspend someone in iMember, that information triggers an alert to our membership advisors, who then
reach out personally—calling, texting, and emailing the brother before the
suspension occurs.
This simple, coordinated step prevented more than 200 suspensions. The
result: Only 861 members were suspended, compared to 1,414 in 2022 and 1,151
in 2023. Without restoration and prevention, we would not have achieved positive growth. Together, we’ve shown that care for our membership is everyone’s
business—and it works.

Safeguarding Our Masonic Halls

Growing Lodges, Growing the Craft
While overall membership grew, the number of degrees conferred declined
slightly, following unusually high post-pandemic years in 2022–23. Yet interest
in Freemasonry remains strong. The challenge is capacity—our existing lodges
can only do so much.
That’s why new lodge development remains one of our most important
strategies. Since 2016, nearly 50 new lodges have been created. This year, we
achieved a net gain in active lodges—from 328 to 332.
Every new lodge brings fresh leadership, new energy, and unique ways to
engage members. A single lodge can only create and engage so many Masons,
but the more lodges we have, the more opportunities we create for men to
grow in the craft.
This is how we build not only numbers, but vitality.
Building Leaders for Tomorrow
Leadership is the lifeblood of Freemasonry. This year, we launched an entirely
new format for lodge leadership retreats, combining the former secretaries
and treasurers retreats with the masters and wardens retreats into one unified
program.
The results exceeded every expectation:
• More than 800 lodge officers attended—over 100 beyond our goal
• Officers reported high satisfaction, deep engagement, and genuine
optimism about the future
With distinct learning tracks for every officer, these retreats equipped
leaders with tools to lead well and the inspiration to do so joyfully. The energy
was palpable—proof that attitude drives success.
Armed with new tools and a clear plan—especially the Keystone Initiative,
which we’ll hear more about tomorrow—our leaders are ready to take California
Masonry to the next level.

99

Our fraternity’s real estate portfolio is vast and valuable. Across California,
approximately 270 Masonic halls have a combined estimated market value of
nearly $2 billion. These buildings are both assets and responsibilities.
Yet many suffer from deferred maintenance and face increasing insurance
challenges. As many Californians know, the state’s property insurance market
has been in crisis. More than a dozen major insurers have withdrawn from the
market since 2022, and premiums statewide have risen by an average of over
30 percent in the last two years.
Today, AIG is the only carrier willing to insure all of our halls—and even
they have indicated that about 60 of our buildings are at risk of losing coverage
due to their location alone.
To protect our fraternity’s assets, we are forming a captive insurance company—a form of self-insurance that allows us to assume the first $5 million
of claims. We will also secure reinsurance for any claims above that amount.
Each year, we pay roughly $3.5 million in premiums, yet historically, our
losses have been under $1 million annually. Under the new model, those premiums will be paid to a company we own. Over time, this will allow us to accumulate
reserves, reduce costs, and gain control over our insurance future.
There is some risk—there always is—but it’s manageable. And it’s the right
thing to do. We must ensure that our halls are not only insured but sustainable
for generations to come.
Alongside this insurance solution, we’ve launched a statewide building
assessment plan. Over the next three years, we’ll evaluate every Masonic hall,
provide condition reports, and deliver professional maintenance plans outlining
what should be done monthly, quarterly, and annually.
With these tools, we will preserve the legacy of our Masonic spaces and
ensure they remain centers of fellowship and community for decades ahead.
Member Services: Excellence Every Day
Our Member Services team continues to set a high bar for excellence. Over the
past year, they responded to 7,000 requests for support and information, with
93 percent resolved the same day and 100 percent within three business days.
Each request generates a satisfaction survey, and our members consistently
respond at rates higher than industry norms. Ninety percent of respondents
rated their service as “satisfied” or “very satisfied”—almost 20 points above
the national average for membership organizations.
Please join me in recognizing Pamela Ly and Jason Harding, who handle
these requests with professionalism, kindness, and care.
Communications: Telling Our Story Well
The Communications team continues to deliver professional, inspiring, and
consistent storytelling about Freemasonry.

100

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

Through weekly email updates, the monthly Leader newsletter, hundreds
of social media posts, videos, numerous websites, the annual report, and four
issues of the California Freemason magazine, our story is reaching more people
than ever.
Two of our magazine issues were honored internationally by the Content
Marketing Institute—the world’s premier organization recognizing excellence
in storytelling:

designed to make the lodge experience more engaging, more Masonic, and
more meaningful. This includes participating in a new stated meeting format
that you will help craft.
There will be three lodge leadership retreats in 2026. I encourage every
lodge to ensure its officers attend. It will be inspiring, practical, and—true to
Masonic tradition—filled with fellowship and fun.

• The Prince Hall issue won Best Nonprofit Publication
• The Heroes of Masonry issue was a finalist for Best Overall Editorial
We don’t seek awards, but these honors affirm that our message is among
the best in the world. Our communications team, led by Emily Limon and
supported by our staff and volunteers, helps ensure that the light of Masonry
shines bright.
Simplifying Lodge Operations
Administrative work should never be a barrier to leadership. For years, our
treasurers and secretaries have managed lodge finances through Sage Intacct,
a powerful but complex accounting system. Recognizing its limitations for
volunteers, we partnered with Grand View to create a more integrated and
user-friendly system within iMember.
More than 150 lodges participated in testing this year, and while transitions
of this kind are never without challenges, the benefits will be significant:
• Easier bookkeeping for non-accountants
• Better transparency and recordkeeping
• More willing and confident lodge treasurers
Thank you to all who participated in testing and feedback. Your work is
paving the way for every lodge to benefit in the year ahead.
Looking Forward: The Keystone Initiative
Tomorrow, our elected leadership will share our new strategic plan, The
Keystone Initiative—a focused effort to:
• Build Masonic leaders
• Strengthen the lodge experience
• Deepen community connection
These are the pillars that will define our future. Each directly affects the
life of every lodge, every brother, and every prospect who knocks at our door.
Our 2026 leadership retreats will take this work further. We’ll introduce
new tools for planning and conducting meetings, degrees, and events—tools

101

Gratitude and Brotherhood
There are no foreign jurisdiction requests for recognition, so I will conclude
my 18th report as your grand secretary by expressing my heartfelt gratitude:
• To the lodge secretaries and assistant secretaries, whose diligence
keeps our fraternity running smoothly
• To the inspectors and assistant grand lecturers, who not only preserve
our ritual excellence but support the administration of our lodges
• To the staff of the Grand Lodge office, who serve with professionalism
and care every day
• To Assistant Grand Secretary Jordan Yelinek, who leads the membership and lodge development efforts that help produce such great
results this year. Please join me in thanking him and his team for
helping make this year’s historic growth possible.
I also wish to recognize Worshipful Brother Charles Cross, our retiring
grand treasurer. His partnership, integrity, and friendship have been a blessing
to this fraternity. Thank you, Bro. Charles, for your distinguished service.
Finally, I offer my deepest appreciation to our grand master, Most
Worshipful Brother Art Salazar. His leadership, personality, and vision have
elevated California Masonry on the world stage. His selection as chairman of the
2025 Conference of Grand Masters of Masons in North America is a reflection
of the esteem in which he is held across our craft.
Thank you, Most Worshipful, for your service and your friendship.
Conclusion
Brethren, this year marks a turning point. We have proven that growth is possible, that unity works, and that the principles of brotherly love, relief, and truth
remain as relevant today as ever.
Our charge now is to build on this momentum—to keep our focus on the
care of our membership, the support of our leadership, the preservation of our
halls, and to truly connect with our communities. I’m looking forward to it!

Respectfully submitted,

REPORT OF THE
GRAND LECTURER
Good afternoon, brethren,
It is a profound honor to stand before you as your grand lecturer for 2025.
I want to begin by expressing my deepest gratitude for the trust and confidence
you have placed in me to serve in this office. This year has been marked by an
inspiring sense of collaboration, growth, and dedication to the quality and
relevance of our ritual work.
This year, our grand master called upon each of us to inspire—to ignite a
spirit of innovation, passion, and dedication within our fraternity and beyond.
This theme has been a constant companion for me as I visited lodges, attended
ceremonies, and worked alongside the assistant grand lecturers and inspectors.
I witnessed that call answered in lodge rooms across the state, as brethren
devoted themselves to improving the quality of our ritual and, through it, the
experience of our candidates and our communities.
We began the ritual year assisting the grand master with a very special
making of a Mason at sight for Bro. Domenic Aiken of Wisdom Lodge No. 202,
conducted bedside at Huntington Memorial Hospital. Following this moving
and memorable ceremony, it became clear that revisions were needed to update
the ritual, and the Ritual Committee acted promptly to make those changes.
Throughout the year, we performed multiple constitution ceremonies,
including six in November for Royal Street Lodge No. 890, Wayfarers Lodge,
Hermes Lodge No. 891, Sonora Lodge No. 887, California Hispanic and Latin
American Research Lodge No. 1009, and Kapayapaan at Pagkakaisa Lodge
No. 888. Additionally, we performed five institution ceremonies for Cicero
Research Lodge, Fiat Lux Lodge, Danville Lodge, Lautaro Lodge, and Laguna
Lux Lodge. During these ceremonies, it became apparent that updates were
needed to accommodate the signing of dispensations and charters, and the
Ritual Committee worked to implement those changes.
This year also included several special public ceremonies that beautifully
showcased the relevance and dignity of Masonic ritual in the communities we
serve. In March, we had the honor of opening Grand Lodge at Union-Tehama
Lodge No. 3 to celebrate their 175th anniversary. Later in the year, at the invitation of the grand master, most worshipful John E. Trauner opened Grand Lodge
at Nevada Lodge No. 13, where we joined in celebrating their 175th anniversary

122

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

as well. In October, we gathered at the Segerstrom Shelby Event Center to
open Grand Lodge and perform a cornerstone ceremony, during which, at the
invitation of the grand master, Most Worshipful Arthur H. Weiss opened Grand
Lodge and conducted the dedication ceremony; earlier in May, we performed
a cornerstone removal ceremony for San Joaquin Elementary School. Later in
September, we participated in the building rededication ceremony for Lassen
Lodge No. 149. Each of these occasions was more than a ceremony; it was an
opportunity to inspire our brethren and the public alike, to witness the timeless
values of Masonry in action, and to remind us all of the impact our ritual can
have beyond the lodge walls.
The divisions assigned to the assistant grand lecturers increased to 10
this year, accompanied by a statewide redistricting to accommodate the new
division. We said farewell to retiring assistant grand lecturers Mike Edwards,
Gary Quintrell, and Alberto Casanova, and we owe them our sincere gratitude
for their tireless dedication and service to the Grand Lodge, their inspectors,
and the lodges within their divisions. We welcomed new assistant grand lecturers Gary Sparks, Corey Leighty, Charles Dimaano, Rio Santonil, and Narbeh
Baghdisarian, who have already begun to make meaningful contributions to
our ritual programs.
This year’s inspector ritual conferences were held at Eureka Lodge No. 16
in Auburn for the north, and at Ontario Masonic Lodge No. 301 for the south.
We implemented a new format this year for the conferences: Rather than simply
exemplifying the ritual, inspectors and assistant grand lecturers demonstrated
and explained how to teach it. The performance and instruction provided by
these dedicated brethren were exemplary, and the energy and skill displayed
throughout the sessions serve to inspire all who attended.
The Ritual Committee also completed several other projects to support
the continued excellence of our ritual work. In addition to the updates made to
the Ceremony of Making a Mason at Sight/Will, the Ceremonies of Institution
and Constitution, and the Grand Lodge Installation Ceremony. We completed
the long-awaited Grand Lodge Officers’ Guide, originally initiated by Very
Worshipful Jack Rose, ensuring it is now current and distributed to the Grand
Lodge officers. Additionally, work began on revising the officers’ coach training
curriculum, with the expectation of completion before the end of next year.
Our Ritual Competition this year focused on the Masonic funeral service,
one of the most important rituals we perform, often in front of the public. This
ceremony is sometimes the first and only exposure the public will have to our
fraternity. Its proper performance requires dignity, reverence, and respect, and
the competition aimed to raise interest and improve the quality of this work.
Competitors participated in individual and team categories, and the winners
were invited to be filmed, creating tutorials accessible to all members. This
year’s division winners are:
Division I: Wor. Richard Downing, Mission Lodge No. 169
Division III: Bro. Mark Zevanove, Pleasanton Lodge No. 321

Division IV: Wor. Noel Lukas, Natoma Lodge No. 64
Division V: Bro. Shaunt Der-Grigorian, Simi Valley Lodge No. 806
Division VI: Wor. Jack Loudermill, Three Great Lights Lodge No. 323
Division VIII: Bros. Mark Echelberger, Ruben Padua, and Jonard Yanzon,

of the 2025 Ritual Competition:
The winner of the individual category is Bro. Mark Zevanove, Pleasanton
Lodge No. 321. The winners of the team category are Brothers Mark Echelberger,
Ruben Padua, and Jonard Yanzon, Widow’s Sons Lodge No. 869.
I extend my heartfelt thanks to all the brethren who participated in this
year’s competition. Your dedication and skill not only elevated the quality of our
work but also brought much-needed attention and awareness to the Masonic
funeral service, one of the most solemn and meaningful ceremonies we perform.
By focusing on this important ritual, you have helped ensure that it continues
to be conducted with the dignity and reverence our departed brethren and
their families deserve.
In conclusion, brethren, the work we perform is more than a set of words
and movements. It is the living embodiment of our values, our history, and our
shared commitment to each other and the communities we serve. The theme of
this year, Inspire, has guided us in every ritual, every ceremony, and every interaction. Let us continue to inspire one another, ensuring that our ritual remains
not only a cornerstone of our fraternity, but also a beacon for all who witness it.
Thank you for your trust, your dedication, and your support. It is a privilege
to serve you as grand lecturer.
Respectfully submitted,
Matthew Vander Horck, Grand Lecturer

GRAND CHAPLAIN’S
INSPIRATIONAL MESSAGE
Most Worshipful, brothers,
It has been a privilege to serve you as grand chaplain this year. It is with
humility that I now share some ideas with all of you, our greater Masonic family,
friends, guests, and especially the youth, joining us for our public ceremonies
this morning. I hope you will find something useful in them.
Having been raised in a Filipino American, Catholic family, it feels appropriate for me to start with something of a confession, and that is that I often
feel alone, even when I’m surrounded by people. Now, I was nerdy growing up
and so, perhaps, that feeling is just par for the course. But I suspect that more
than a few of you have felt that way before; a paradoxical feeling of loneliness
even though there are people in your life. I submit to you, friends, that this
feeling is better understood as disconnection, a sense of being detached or
separated from others. The symptoms of disconnection are many: loneliness,
apprehension, a lack of understanding between people, even hostility. For me,
and perhaps for you, it may feel like we’re living in an era of disconnection. So,
I’d like to share with you how I rebuilt my sense of connection to others and
how concepts from Freemasonry underlie that process.
First, I ground myself, to remember what I am. I don’t do anything complicated. I just take a walk. It may be a simple act, but it does so much for me,
especially when I hike. When I walk in nature, all my senses are engaged. I can
feel the ground under my feet. I see trees, plants, and flowers, each with their
own colors, shapes, and depth. Sounds from the wind to birdsong fill my ear;
and I can feel the warmth of the sun on my skin. I am literally and spiritually
grounded by the act of walking in nature. And as I observe the splendor of
nature around me, I recall a phrase in Masonry, that “numberless worlds are
around us, all framed by the same divine artist.” Everything that I can see,
touch, hear, feel, and smell in nature, each of these worlds, is the creation of
the Great Architect; and the continual cycle of their creation, breaking down,
and re-building is also the work of the Great Architect. Just as with them, my
own personal journey and growth through my lifetime is likewise the creation
of the Great Architect. I am not just an observer of nature. I am part of nature
and its blossoming through time. And likewise, my friends, that is what you are
and what your life is: You are part of God’s beautiful unfolding of the universe; you

128

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

129

are part of nature. And you matter—each and every one of you.
And because you matter, it is important for us to share, which is the second
thing I do to rebuild my sense of connection. More specifically, I share aspects of
myself with others, and I ask others to share things about themselves with me.
I know it’s hard to share. Doing so requires us to be vulnerable, and we all
have personal fears that can prevent us from putting ourselves out there. Maybe
you’re worried that you don’t have enough experience or expertise or that you’ll
say something awkward or even wrong. But just as the universe that you’re part
of is continually unfolding, you too are unfolding as a person throughout the
course of your life. You are not defined by your worst moments. You are not
defined by highest achievement. And you are not stuck with any particular version (if you will) of yourself. You are allowed to “contain multitudes” because
the creator made you human. The Greek philosopher Heraclitus expressed
this idea by saying that one “cannot step into the same river twice” because
the river and even the person stepping into it are in a constant state of change.
However, I like how Bob Dylan put it, by saying you “are constantly in a state of
becoming.” And so any time you share, you are only sharing aspects of yourself
as you are at that particular moment in time. Whether in small or large ways, you
will experience change, and we are each entitled to God’s grace as we do so.
Another common fear people have about sharing their perspective is selfdoubt. You might think that you have nothing meaningful to offer or that what
you have to say doesn’t matter, or worse, that no one cares. But each of you has
something meaningful to share and it is actually important for you to do so.
For none of us are God. If there’s anything I’m sure of, it’s that I am not
God. So, correspondingly, since I am human, I am not all-knowing. I am incapable of learning all there is to know about the universe, let alone about that
ultimate truth: the meaning of life. All I have is the sliver of knowledge I was
able to gain through my personal experiences, much of which resulted from the
happenstance of my birth. I certainly didn’t choose to be five-foot-three; and
you didn’t choose who your parents or ancestors were. I didn’t get to choose
the country I was fortunate enough to be born in; and likewise, and you didn’t
get to choose which generation you’d belong to. There are so many things about
our lives that we don’t get to choose. No one does.
What we do get to choose is how to use the talents and circumstances given
to us. What each of us has is a unique life path, with correspondingly unique
experiences and opportunities through which we learn and develop our specific
skills. As children, we all understood this: This person is great at football. This
other person knows everything about Star Wars. I know a lot about ’80s music,
and my kid can full combo any song in any rhythm game. Life is often described
as a journey. But each person’s path through life is different; and so too is the
knowledge each person gains traveling along his or her path. And none of us
know what life will throw our way or put on our path. Yet the knowledge and
wisdom that each of you gain from traveling your specific path is valuable to
others. Again, none of us are God. None of us is omniscient; and if we sincerely

want to understand the whole of life—the meaning of life—and this world the
Great Architect has gifted us, then we must rely on others to share what they’ve
learned from their life experiences; and each of you can do the same and thereby
contribute to the store of humankind’s knowledge.
As I became more comfortable sharing who I am with others, and more
welcoming of others sharing who they are with me, I realized that those acts of
sharing served to build connection in two distinct ways. First, I discovered that
even though we have different life experiences and or even divergent opinions,
we ultimately have more in common with each other than we have differences.
The things most important to us—our hopes, our dreams for our families, the
things that motivate us to get on with life—are the same. We each want to live
a life of dignity and respect, to live in peace, and to help build a better world
for future generations. That commonality speaks to the ultimate truth of our
connection: Just as I am a child of God, part of this universe created by the Great
Architect, so is each person that I meet. This truth is reflected in Freemasonry’s
understanding of brotherly love, which describes all people as being “created
by one almighty parent” and “inhabitants of the same planet” who “are to aid,
support, and protect each other.” With that truth in mind, I’ve come to believe
that our different life paths allow each of us to make unique contributions to
the collective understanding of what it means to be human, and that in sharing
our lives with each other, we each contribute to the Great Architect’s universe
in the same way that each flower, branch, stem, and leaf contributes its beauty
to the tapestry of nature.
Secondly, and perhaps more importantly, we become inspired by people
who are brave enough to share their lives, their knowledge, and their personal
convictions. When we are inspired by others, we discover those interests and
pursuits that make us engage in life wholeheartedly and thereby become connected to our communities and society at large. When I think about my own
life, I was inspired to study music because between my mother’s singing and
father’s guitar-playing, my house was always filled with music. I train in martial
arts because I’m in awe of the strength and grace of Bruce Lee in his movies.
I donate to charities for LGBTQ youth and mental health support because I
admire the courage and perseverance of my children. If you reflect on your life,
I’m sure you’ll remember the people that inspired you to pursue your interests,
your hobbies or even your profession. Similarly, whether you know it or not,
there are people who have been inspired by you: a friend who saw you make a
spectacular play in a game, a relative who was astounded by your passion for
a hobby, or even a stranger who happened to see you practice a random act of
kindness. Maybe that’s surprising to you—that you can be awe-inspiring—but
it’s not to Masons. Masons revere and study nature so that we might understand the Great Architect through his works. And you and your fellow humans
are part of nature, each of you a work of the Great Architect worthy of study,
admiration, respect, and from whom inspiration can be drawn.
We human beings are social creatures. A sense of connection to others is

130

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

important for our mental health and emotional stability. When I ground myself
to remember that I am part of the creator’s universe and share who I am with
others to discover our commonalities and find inspiration, I restore my sense
of connection. I no longer feel alone. I realize that I am part of something larger
than myself and that the rest of humanity is likewise part of that greater mystery.
Friends, our world is complicated, it is imperfect, but it is (and has always
been) composed of people of “every country, sect, and opinion.” And yet
Freemasonry is able to unite all of them together. I believe it does so by focusing
on what we have in common and building connections. When we share meals
together or just engage in small talk, we build connection through small acts
of kindness. Via our ritual, we build connection through shared experiences.
Through our charitable endeavors, we build connection by working together
for a common purpose. Life within our lodge halls and with our Masonic family
offers numerous ways to build connections among people and focus on what
we have in common. And I’ve now shared with you a couple of other ways that
I re-build my sense of connection to others. I hope you will find methods that
work for you. You already have at least one: your participation in this Masonic
family. Within this family, true friendships exist among those “who might otherwise have remained at a perpetual distance.” And, if we know how to build
those types of strong connections here, then it is possible to build them out
there too. I thank you for listening.
May the Great Architect of the Universe bless all peoples, remind us of our
connection, and bring us peace.
Amen.
Respectfully submitted,
David M. Ferreria, Grand Chaplain

MESSAGE FROM THE
GRAND ORATOR
Divine Inspiration

Most Worshipful, and to all my esteemed brethren,
It is an honor and a privilege to share this moment in time with you. I
invite each of you not just to listen but to open yourselves and engage with a
deeper exploration. Consider this an opportunity to awaken the master within.
Our grand master’s theme, Inspire, serves as a summons, a call to action,
but not just outwardly. It’s also an inward revelation. It asks us to consider
what exists deep within—the undeniable, non-negotiable, self-realized truths
of our being: divine inspiration.
Each of us in this room has journeyed from the humble role of a poor, blind
candidate to one brought from darkness into light—reforming light. Now look
at us…. With humble guidance, we petitioned the creator, asking Him to “Endue
him with a competency of thy Divine Wisdom…”
We’ve been taught to refine our minds and hearts, with the cosmic that
surrounds us, as ubiquitous as air. Like fish, immersed in water but not knowing
what water is and even questioning if it exists. We experience life through a
corporeal lens, the world as we perceive it.
And yet, this very perception can obscure the deeper truths within. When
we seek only tangible explanations, we neglect the subtle, spiritual currents that
shape our reality. It’s like attempting to alter an image on a projection screen.
It can’t be done. The image itself will not change by manipulating the screen.
We must learn to feel spiritual work, “thereby fitting our minds, as living
stones, for that spiritual building—that house not made with hands—eternal
in the heavens.”
Our corporeal and spiritual worlds don’t just coincide. They are, in essence,
the same reality, experienced from different perspectives. Imagine a magnificent
symphony. You can focus on the individual notes, the instruments, the music
sheets—that’s our corporeal world. But the very essence of the music, the
emotion, lies in the unseen vibrations you feel, the harmony, the conductor’s
vision. That’s the spiritual. The notes and the melody aren’t separate; they are

134

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

135

two aspects of one grand creation, experienced as one.
Two things can operate and coincide with one another at the same time.
Observe the hands of a clock, overlapping and operating in unison, complementing each other and never obstructing one another but rather, each is needed for
the other to accomplish its objective.
Just as our ancient symbols of balance and harmony are two distinct tools that
come together to create perfect form, so too do our physical and spiritual selves.
How do we find that balance and harmony between man and the creator,
the Great Architect of the Universe? What role has the divine orchestrated
specifically for you in this lifetime, a role you can make sense of? These questions may have challenged you through years of your life and still linger today.
For some, it may be what drew you into Freemasonry. And that question may
continue to linger even after this weekend.
Let’s consider rays of sunlight. They carry the same essence as the sun, the
source. Would you agree? So, if Genesis teaches us that man is made in God’s
image and likeness, wouldn’t that hint to something as deep as you (too), carry
the essence of the divine within you?
This awakens us to the reality that you are one with God and not separate.
Eternally present within your I, within your subconsciousness.
This divine partnership between you and God, it means your very existence
is a testament to an intelligent design within the grand scheme of things. In
other words, my brothers, you didn’t just randomly happen. You were purposely
intended. Ever thought of it that way? Give it serious consideration. It’s a profound statement to reflect on regarding your existence and why you are here.
But if belief requires evidence, then I’d ask each of you to think of the year
you were born. Now, tell yourself why you chose that year.
And you soon realize, you had no say in the matter.
Your life, leading up to this very moment, hearing these words today, is
not by chance. The Great Architect of the Universe placed you in that perfect
moment in time, that year specific to you, born in that city, that region of the
world, to those parents and surrounded by siblings and friends who would
inspire you through life experiences, academia, religious faith, your neighborhood, even joining this fraternity—all for a reason. And now, here you are.
Spiritual awareness and Hermetic law teaches us: There are no mistakes.
It’s difficult for us to argue that through our corporeal sense, without spiritual
interpretation or awareness. But it’s all by design.
“Numberless worlds are around us, all framed by the same divine artist.”
It is already written. It’s as if we’re all dancing, but no one has given thought
as to who’s playing the music.
Now, I’m not suggesting that you should live by blind faith or that your life
is so predestined there’s nothing for you to do other than wake up each day.
No. And this is not about losing free will.
The creator purposely placed you right where you need to be in this timeline,
always guiding you along your lifelong passage, providing you with opportunity

at every stage, including this brotherhood.
It is like passing a door, over and over, until the moment you finally notice
it and decide to open it and step through. But the door was always there.
You see, all that you need is before you. As we would say, “hidden in plain
sight.” The key is to notice it. And this noticing isn’t passive; it requires an active
spiritual engagement with the divine plan unfolding around you and within
you. While the grand design is set, your participation, your conscious effort,
and your alignment with this inner wisdom are crucial in order to reveal it. The
corporeal world will do nothing to bring about this experience of revelation
within you. It’s in the doing, the applying, and the conscious direction of your
creative thought that God’s plan truly comes alive through you.
As parents, we see the potential within our children even when they cannot
see it themselves. It’s a matter of time for them to develop into that being and
frame of mind. Imagine them holding themselves back and not reaching their
full potential on purpose.
The creator has the same interest in his creation as any father would have
in his children. What brings more glory, pride, and satisfaction to a father than
seeing his children doing well, to succeed, and express to the fullest their abilities and natural talents?
We are encouraged to improve the mind, giving it the most distinct idea of
any problem or proposition, as well as for enabling it to solve the same. This
request in ancient traditions is called a prayer. Ask and you shall receive.
And here is where the deeper truth resides: You are the ask, and you are
the receiver. The power to create, to manifest, to solve every problem and
paradox in your life, already resides within you—by design. This isn’t merely
positive thinking and affirmations. It’s understanding the fundamental nature
of your being.
No one else can think your thoughts for you. Only you, in the Sanctum
Sanctorum of your own mind, are the architect of that inner world. Your creativity is your freedom. Complete authenticity. To neglect it is to give away your
sovereignty; to honor it is to live as the creator intended: free, original, awake.
Thought is the architect of reality. Every invention, every structure, every
experience began as a thought. The very chair you are sitting on right now, this
building we are in, every word I speak—all were once pure thought. If this is
true for the external world, how much more paramount is it for your internal
world and the experiences you draw to yourself?
Think of this: A statue already exists inside a block of granite. The sculptor
doesn’t add to it, he reveals what was always there. The same with you. The
simplest truth you’ve ever learned—1+1=2—was not physically inserted into
your mind. The teacher didn’t open your head and put that thought inside. As
a matter of fact, everything you’ve ever learned was not placed in you from the
outside; it was revelation from what was existing already within. And if that is
true, imagine how much more still waits within us, yet to be revealed. Your life
is not a search for what is missing; it’s revealing what has always been present.

136

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

137

They’ve got you searching for cathedrals without when the temple is within.
Ancient wisdom traditions, from Kabbalah to Gnostics to esoteric teachings, whisper these same truths: Consciousness is the ultimate reality, and
your thoughts are its creative agents. When you truly grasp that the universal
mind is not separate from you, but is the very essence of your consciousness,
then divine wisdom is not something you petition for but rather something you
access and express from within.
Spiritual awareness, including our craft, is one where limitless revelation
is possible if the initiate is willing to leave their critical perspective at the door.
This is why, when we reach the limits of our understanding, when we have
exhausted all resources, when we feel there is no more we can do in this corporeal world, and when human strength and wisdom fail, we must ever remember
that “divine assistance is vouchsafed us through the medium of prayer.” Ask
and you shall receive.
And when you are finally curious enough to ask, How do we begin this inner
work of alignment? the answer is simple, my brothers: Notice what has been
with you from the beginning, since birth, something your parents never had
to teach you. Breathing. You take an average of 20,000 breaths a day, yet how
many of those are intentional or mindful? To bring awareness to your breath
is to begin the journey, for in that quiet attention, you remember and find the
light already within.
When we become still enough, we begin to hear our desires and our heart.
From this stillness, we can choose to create whatever our body or soul needs.
Listen within the silence to align with the creator.
By noticing the breath and the calm it opens, we feel how the cosmic
works, “Thereby fitting our minds as living stones.” Change within and the
world without will follow.
To create the future you desire, to manifest a life of purpose, joy, and abundance, requires a new way of thinking, brethren.
Every thought you entertain, every belief you hold, is shaping your future.
And my brothers, the future is not distant in time. By definition, the future is
time immediately following the moment of speaking, writing, or thinking. Ask
and you shall receive.
You learn that the image on the projection screen would not change,
but when we learn to change the projector, the image changes all by itself.
Manifesting all that we desire.
For too long, we’ve been told to focus on the external world. But those
who know understand the true power lies in changing the source of the projection—our inner world.
This isn’t about wishing. It’s about knowing. It’s about consciously directing
your thoughts, aligning your beliefs with your highest aspirations, and understanding that the divine inspiration you seek and salvation you desire is not
far away, external from you, above the clouds in some heaven or within some
religious edifice somewhere on this planet, asking you to pay tithes for access

disguised as a virtue.
The only thing you need to pay is attention to the very current of consciousness flowing through you, this very moment. It’s always been within you.
The truth of all that is happening is in your favor, waiting to be received. And
all that you need to begin already exists within you. Therefore; Know Thyself.
No mortal can lock a door the Almighty placed inside you. If someone sells
you a key to your own heart, remember: it opens from within.
You are not separate from the source. You are it, remembering itself.
My brothers, divine inspiration is just a thought away.
So mote it be!
Respectfully submitted,
Carlos M. Diez Jr, Grand Orator
[My brothers, this oration was not written to change your destiny—that is inevitable.
It was written to help you reach your destiny so you may experience it, sooner rather
than later.]

2025 GRAND LODGE LEGISLATION

GRAND MASTER’S DECISIONS
AND RECOMMENDATIONS
Grand Master Salazar’s Decision No. 1
Esoteric or Secret Portion of the Ritual
I have been asked to clarify the meaning of the phrase “esoteric or secret
portion” of the Ritual as referenced in the California Masonic Code (CMC).
Understanding the secrets of Freemasonry is crucial, as each of us has taken an
obligation to safeguard them. It is deemed unmasonic conduct to reduce them
to writing. To address this question, I have collaborated with the Executive
Committee, the Ritual Committee, and the Jurisprudence Committee to develop
a comprehensive answer, which is provided in the form of Grand Master’s
Decision No. 1.
Prior to 1988, the Ritual was transmitted orally, “from mouth to ear,” with
no written document containing the complete Ritual. This oral tradition was
regarded as emphasizing the experiential nature of, and safeguarding, the secrets
of Freemasonry. Recognizing the need for a standardized approach, the Grand
Lodge adopted a resolution in 1988 permitting the use of a cipher — later specifically, the Allen cipher, produced by Allen Publishing Company in Virginia and
utilized widely in the United States since at least 1907. In 1991, the Grand Lodge
adopted the version titled “King Solomon and His Travelers,” a cipher book
that includes both plain English portions and ciphered portions of the Ritual.
There is no clear delineation within the cipher that separates what is considered secret and what is not. While one might assume that anything encoded
or in cipher is automatically secret, that is not the case. For example, when an
officer is asked whether a candidate is prepared, the first response is in plain
English, while the second is in cipher—yet both are the same words. By a careful examination of the cipher, however, we can discern that portion which is
esoteric or secret. Every word in cipher is represented either by a few letters
of the word or a symbol or code for that word. Critically, however, I note that

142

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

the words, grips and tokens which we consider modes of recognition are not in
the cipher, in code or otherwise, except in one instance. While the due guards
and signs (and a token in the one instance) are referenced using a few letters
of each word in a phrase, those letters are not sufficiently descriptive of how
the sign is made for the reader to render the sign. The steps and the Points of
Fellowship are necessarily explained in more detail in the cipher, but they are
also modes of recognition, which are secret.
It is therefore my decision that the signs, words or modes of recognition
in our Ritual — which means our due guards, signs, words, grips, tokens, steps,
and the Points of Fellowship — are the “esoteric or secret portion” of the Ritual.
This interpretation aligns with our longstanding understanding of Masonic
secrets and the principle that their safeguard is fundamental to our integrity
and obligations, and any unauthorized disclosure—written or otherwise—would
compromise the very essence of Freemasonry.
If you agree with this interpretation of our law, I ask you to vote “yes” for
Grand Master’s Decision No. 1.
If you approve this decision, the following narrative will be added to the
appendix of the California Masonic Code in which the Grand Master’s interpretative decisions are recorded:

Interpretation of Section 1401.010.G.7
of the California Masonic Code.
Esoteric or Secret Portion of the Ritual
(2025 G.M. Decision No. 1)
The signs, words or modes of recognition in our Ritual — which means our due
guards, signs, words, grips, tokens, steps, and the Points of Fellowship — are the
“esoteric or secret portion of the Ritual,” the disclosure of which in any form not
approved by Grand Lodge would constitute a violation of our obligation as an
Entered Apprentice Mason to protect the secrets of Freemasonry and therefore
unmasonic conduct under Section 1401.010.G.7 of the Code.

Grand Master Salazar’s Decision No. 2
Installation of Lodge Officers
Not Included in the Ritual
Section 805.010 of our California Masonic Code requires each Lodge to
elect certain officers (the Master, Senior and Junior Wardens, Treasurer and
Secretary). It also requires each Lodge to appoint certain officers (the Chaplain,
Senior and Junior Deacons, Marshal, Senior and Junior Stewards, and Tiler).
Section 805.010 also allows each Lodge to appoint additional officers, “as the
Lodge may deem proper.”
Section 805.510 of our Code mandates that Lodge officers, whether
elected and appointed, must be “installed using the Installation Ceremony for
Constituent Lodges.” Our Grand Lodge’s Installation Ceremony, however, only
provides for the installation of those officers (listed above) that are required
by the Code to be elected or appointed. The Installation Ceremony does not
address the installation of other appointed officers “deemed proper” by the
Lodge and as permitted by Section 805.010.
How then shall a Lodge install officers that are not specifically addressed
in the Installation Ceremony? To put this question another way: how do we
harmonize Section 805.010 of the Code (that permits appointment of additional officers) with Section 805.510 (that requires officer installation via the
Installation Ceremony)?
It is my decision that it is permissible for a Lodge to install Lodge officers
that are not specifically required by the Code or named in the Installation
Ceremony. In such cases, the Installing Officer shall satisfy himself that the
installation follows as closely as reasonably practicable the spirit, principles
and ceremony of the Installation Ceremony.
This decision ensures that both Sections 805.010 and 805.510 continue to
have force and meaning without overstepping the other. If you agree with this
interpretation of our law, I ask you to vote “yes” for Grand Master’s Decision
No. 2.
If you approve this decision, the following narrative will be added to the
appendix of the California Masonic Code in which the Grand Master’s interpretative decisions are recorded:

144

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

145

Interpretation of Sections 805.010 and 805.510
of the California Masonic Code.
Installation of Officers Not Included in Ritual
(2025 G.M. Decision No. 2)
It is permissible for a Lodge to install Lodge officers that are not specifically
required by the Code or named in the Installation Ceremony. In such cases, the
Installing Officer shall satisfy himself that the installation follows as closely as
reasonably practicable the spirit, principles and ceremony of the Installation
Ceremony.

Grand Master Salazar’s Recommendation No. 1
Updates Grand Lodge Committee Membership,
Duties and Tenure
During my service as Grand Master and in other Grand Lodge leadership
roles, I have worked closely with our Grand Lodge Committees. These committees are governed by the California Masonic Code (CMC), and I have identified
several important updates to the Code to better align it with current committee
practice and purpose.
Section 406.000 of the Code requires that at least 70% of Grand Lodge
committee members be drawn from the Grand Lodge membership — defined
as current and Past Grand Officers, Masters, Wardens, and Past Masters. It also
imposes a five-year term limit for committee chairs.
Recognizing the unique functions of certain committees, the Code exempts
the following committees from these requirements: Audit, Freemason Magazine,
Compensation, Ritual, and the Executive Committee.
Clarification for Freemason Magazine Committee
Although the Freemason Magazine was converted from a constitutional board
to a committee and appropriately exempted under Section 406.000, the section
of the Code specifically addressing this committee’s assigned duties reimposed
term limits. Given the publication’s long-standing editorial stability — having
only four Editors in Chief over 70 years — this inconsistency should be corrected to reflect both historical practice and intent. I recommend amending
the section of the Code addressing the duties of Freemason Magazine to clearly
reaffirm this committee’s exemption from term limits.
Exemption for Investment Committee
Like the Audit Committee, the Investment Committee relies on the expertise
of Masons with professional financial and investment management experience. Many qualified brothers in these fields are not members of Grand Lodge.
To preserve access to this critical talent pool, I recommend the Investment
Committee be added to the list of exempted committees in Section 406.000.

146

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

Update to Finance Committee Duties
The Finance Committee is currently charged with administering all Grand
Lodge retirement plans. This responsibility was rendered obsolete in 2007
when Grand Lodge terminated its defined benefit retirement plan and, instead,
sponsored for its employees a 401(k)- plan administered by a third-party provider. I recommend removing this outdated duty from the Finance Committee’s
responsibilities.
If you adopt this recommendation, the following changes would be made
to the Code. Section 406.000 would be amended to read as marked:
§406.000. COMMITTEE MEMBERSHIP.
Members of committees shall be members of Grand Lodge or Master
Masons who are members in good standing in Constituent Lodges (other
than Research Lodges or Historic Lodges) whose special talents, in the
discretion of the Grand Master, are considered to be desirable or required
for the accomplishment of the mission of the committees. At least seventy percent of the total number of members on each committee shall be
members of Grand Lodge.
If a member has served as chairman of the committee for five consecutive years, he shall be ineligible for reappointment as chairman of that
committee until the lapse of one year. If a member has served on a committee for nine consecutive years, including service as chairman, he shall be
ineligible for reappointment to that committee until the lapse of one year.
To each committee having a membership of seven or more there shall
be appointed each year at least one brother who was not a member the
preceding year. To each committee having a membership of less than seven
there shall be appointed in alternate years at least one brother who was
not a member the preceding year.
In addition to the regular membership of all committees, the Grand
Master, under special or demanding circumstances, may appoint as a consultant to a committee any member in good standing of a Constituent Lodge
(other than Research Lodges or Historic Lodges). The Grand Master may
remove a consultant at any time. Consultants shall perform services, render
advice, and attend committee meetings, as may be directed by the Chairman
of the committees to which they are assigned, but shall have no vote.
The provisions of this section shall not apply to the Committee on
Audit, the Committee on the California Freemason, the Committee on
Compensation, the Executive Committee, the Investment Committee or
the Committee on Ritual.

Grand Master Salazar’s Recommendation No. 2
Eliminates Code Provisions Relating to
Officers Associations
Over time, provisions of the California Masonic Code (CMC) may
become obsolete or unnecessary. In such cases, it is best to eliminate these provisions so that the Code contains only the operative terms needed for the good
governance of our Fraternity. One example is Part 10 (“Officers Associations”)
of the Code and its related provisions.
Part 10 (Section 1000.000) of the Code authorizes, and sets out limitations
with respect to, the organization by Inspectors of officers associations for the
purpose of instruction in lodge affairs. Section 405.030 of the Code lists the
organization of Officers Associations as a duty of Inspectors. Today, Officers
Associations are extremely rare. Inspectors utilize other, less formal methods
to assist in their instruction in the administration of Lodges.
While I have no objection to the formation of Officers Associations, I no
longer perceive the need for the Code to mandate and regulate them. Therefore,
I propose deleting Part 10 of the Code (as well as related provisions) to streamline the Code and keep it current with modern practices. If adopted, this Code
change will not prevent an Inspector from forming an Officers Association if
he believes it will facilitate his instruction.
If you adopt this recommendation, the following changes would be made
to the Code.
Section 405.030 would be amended to read as marked:
§405.030. DUTIES.
It shall be the duty of the Inspector to:
A. Hold schools of instruction and instruct the officers of the Lodges in
the Ritual;
B. Require any Master of a Lodge in his district to convene his Lodge for
inspection, and report to the Grand Master the failure of any Master
to do so;
C. Cause to be organized within his district an Officers’ Association and to
supervise meetings of such an association for the purpose of instruction

It shall be the duty of the officers of his district to attend such meetings and failure, without due cause, of an officer to attend as required
may constitute grounds for the Inspector to withhold a certificate of
advancement where applicable or to request that the Master remove
said officer;
CD. Appoint in each Lodge within his district an Officers’ Coach, who shall
be a qualified Past Master of a Constituent Lodge, and who shall serve
at the pleasure of the Inspector. The Officers’ Coach shall assist in
teaching the Ritual to the officers of the Lodge, and assist in preparing
them to qualify for advancement;
DE. Issue certificates, where required by Masonic law, to the officers of the
Lodges when they are qualified to give the work and lectures required
of them respectively, without regard to moral or other considerations;
EF. Issue certifications to Master Masons qualified to officiate in the
Funeral Service of this Jurisdiction as provided in Section 405.050 of
this Code;
FG. Report to the Grand Master any failure of an officer to qualify within
the time required by law;
GH. Visit each Lodge in his district whenever he deems it necessary for the
faithful performance of his duties;
HI. Inspect the work and, if necessary, correct the same in accordance with
the work adopted by Grand Lodge;
IJ. Report the working condition of each Lodge in his district, as it pertains
to the Ritual, to the Grand Lecturer on or before the 30th day of June
of each year;
JK. Report the condition in all matters, other than ritual, to the Grand
Master on or before the 30th day of June of each year;
KL. Examine the books and records of each Lodge, with or without an audit
as he or the Grand Master shall determine, to determine if its manner
of transacting business conforms to Masonic law, and to report to the
Grand Master any violations of law; and
LM. Attend the Lodges of instruction as directed by the Grand Lecturer.

Grand Master Salazar’s Recommendation No. 3
Centralized Notifications for Suspensions
for Non-Payment of Dues
Over time, our Fraternity has adopted modern tools for communication and recordkeeping. As those tools evolve, so must our laws. Today, Lodge
Secretaries are required to send certified letters to delinquent members before
their suspension for non-payment of dues — a process that is costly, administratively burdensome, and often ineffective. It also creates confusion: members
of a single Lodge receive 30 days’ notice, while multiple members receive 60
days, leading to inconsistent practices and uncertainty about compliance.
This amendment replaces that system with a single, centralized process
that is fair, trackable, and clear. Lodges will initiate suspension proceedings
by notifying the appropriate office, which will begin a standardized 60-day
outreach effort using all available means to contact the member. This uniform
timeline will apply to all Masons, ensuring that each brother receives consistent
communication and an equal opportunity to respond, request relief, or speak
with his lodge before any vote is taken.
By eliminating conflicting rules, removing the certified mail requirement,
and relieving lodge officers of outdated duties, this change supports both administrative clarity and fraternal compassion. It ensures that no suspension for
non-payment of dues occurs without coordinated, documented, and good-faith
contact.
If you adopt this recommendation, the following changes would be made
to the Code. Section 804.165 would be amended to read as marked:
§804.165. SUSPENSION OR EXPULSION OF A MULTIPLE MEMBER.
A. Subject to paragraph C below, sSuspension or expulsion of a multiple
member in this Jurisdiction shall automatically suspend his membership or expel him from membership in all Constituent Lodges. The
Grand Secretary shall immediately notify every other Lodge in which
the multiple member holds membership on receiving notification of
such suspension or expulsion. Notification shall be given in like manner
in the case of the reinstatement of such member by the suspending
and expelling Lodge. Such reinstatement shall automatically restore
him to membership in every other Constituent Lodge of which he

154

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

was a member, upon payment of any dues and the performance of any
other obligations required for his restoration to membership in this
Jurisdiction, unless he has also been suspended or expelled pursuant
to the provisions of Chapter 4 of Part 14 of this Code, in which case
he must also be restored pursuant to the provisions of Article 10 of
Chapter 4 of Part 14 of this Code.
B. Suspension or expulsion of a multiple member in any other Jurisdiction
where he is a member shall automatically suspend his membership or
expel him from membership in all Constituent Lodges. If such member
is subsequently restored to membership in the suspending or expelling
Jurisdiction, he may also be restored to membership in all Constituent
Lodges of which he was a member, upon payment of any dues and the
performance of any other obligations required for his restoration to
membership in this Jurisdiction, unless he has also been suspended or
expelled pursuant to the provisions of Section 1404.810.D of this Code,
in which case he must also be restored pursuant to the provisions of
Article 10 of Chapter 4 of Part 14 of this Code.
C. Suspension of a multiple member by a Constituent Lodge for non-payment of dues shall become effective only after a sixty day prior Notice
of Intent to Suspend has been sent to every other Constituent Lodge in
which the member holds membership. During this sixty day period, the
other Lodge or Lodges may contact the member in an effort to avoid
suspension. If within the sixty day period the member fails to obtain
good standing in all Lodges involved, he may be suspended.

D. No Lodge shall suspend a Mason for non-payment of dues if the Master
or Secretary of the Lodge has knowledge that this Mason has been on
active military combat duty at any time during the preceding 36 months.
1.

Active military combat duty is defined as having been military
personnel serving in an active capacity including but not limited
to active duty personnel, reservists and National Guard personnel
in a combat zone for a named United States military conflict. A
combat zone for a named United States military conflict is any
area which the President of the United States by Executive Order
designates or has designated as an area in which U.S. Armed Forces
are or have engaged in conflict.

2.

combat duty, as defined in Section 809.370.D of this Code, at any

the Secretary of the Lodge shall immediately notify the Grand
Secretary thereof.

3.

A Mason may request his Lodge to remove a previous suspension
from his record if he was on active military combat duty, as defined
in Section 809.370.D of this Code, at any time during the 36 month
period preceding the date on which the Lodge so suspended him,
and if his Lodge then finds that he was on active military combat
duty at any time during such 36 month period, then his Lodge shall
remove such suspension from his record as if such suspension had
not occurred and the Secretary of the Lodge shall immediately
notify the Grand Secretary thereof.

4.

Once 36 months have elapsed since a Mason’s service on active
military combat duty, he may be suspended for nonpayment of dues
as provided in this section, including suspension for unpaid dues
for the period during which he was on active military combat duty.

E. A Mason shall not be expelled from Masonry for non-payment of dues.

Grand Master Salazar’s Recommendation No. 4
Updates the Duties of the Lodge Secretary
Lodge administrative practices evolve to reflect technological advancements and improved methods of recordkeeping and communication. When this
occurs, we must update the California Masonic Code (CMC) so it continues to
accurately reflect the duties and practices of Lodge officers.
In particular, the Code’s description of Lodge Secretaries’ duties needs
updating. While the role of the Lodge Secretary remains central to Lodge governance, the way those duties are fulfilled has changed significantly. Lodges
now commonly maintain digital records, transmit reports electronically, and
utilize modern platforms for financial tracking and member communication.
Many of the Code’s detailed requirements (particularly Section 805.230 of
the Code) reflect outdated practices, such as handwritten minute books and
physical deposit slips.
This recommendation updates the language of Section 805.230 to remove
obsolete requirements and allow for current and future technologies. It ensures
that Lodge Secretaries remain accountable for essential responsibilities — such
as reporting, recordkeeping, and coordination with the Grand Secretary —
without binding them to outdated practices. I also believe that the proposed
revisions will help new Lodge Secretaries better understand their duties under
the Code. I therefore recommend adoption of this change.

amended to read as marked:

Amendment to Ordinances.
5/6 affirmative vote required for adoption.

The California Masonic Code (CMC), specifically Section 1404.345,
addresses the procedures allowing an Accuser to withdraw charges of unmasonic conduct filed against a fellow brother. While this section was originally
intended to preserve procedural integrity, it has, in practice, introduced unnecessary delays and inefficiencies that burden the system, escalate conflict, and
discourage early resolution. Its scope is limited — it allows a charge to be withdrawn only after a Trial Master has been appointed, and even then, only if the
Trial Master finds no evidence in the specification that could warrant a verdict
of unmasonic conduct against the Accused.
It has come to my attention that this narrow framework does not account
for the broader range of real-world situations in which the withdrawal of charges
is not only appropriate, but also represents the best outcome for the Accuser, the
Accused, the Lodge, and the Craft as a whole. In many such cases, proceeding
with a full trial serves no productive purpose and may even deepen the disharmony that originally gave rise to the dispute.
Once charges are filed, the current system sets into motion a complex and
time-consuming process: notices must be sent, the Committee on Jurisprudence
must conduct a full review, and a willing and available Trial Master must be
located, appointed, and brought up to speed on the matter. Only then can a
charge be withdrawn — and only under the narrow conditions currently permitted. This process is burdensome and often unnecessary when reconciliation
has already occurred or can be achieved through informal resolution.
In practice, many Accusers — after engaging with Masonic leadership or
speaking with trusted brethren — come to realize that the remedy they originally
sought is either unavailable under the Code or would cause more harm than
good if the dispute proceeded to trial. The Committee on Jurisprudence may
also determine and recommend to the Grand Master that the matter is better
suited for mediation or dismissal - particularly in cases involving interpersonal
disputes, misunderstandings, or when the Accuser has failed to allege facts
meeting a threshold showing of material harm to Masonry, a Mason, or the
wife, widow, or child of a Mason. However, because no Trial Master has been
appointed in these instances, there is currently no clear mechanism to formally
withdraw the charges — even when doing so would fully resolve the matter.
Requiring all these steps to reach the point where a Trial Master can approve

164

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

withdrawal leaves both the parties and the Lodge in procedural limbo. Charges
may remain technically pending or subject to re-filing based on the same facts,
yet no formal closure is available to the parties. This ambiguity not only prolongs
conflict but also imposes unnecessary strain on the members and dedicated
volunteers who support the trial process.
To address these issues, I propose amending the Code to allow the Accuser
to withdraw charges upon written request to the Grand Master prior to the
appointment of a Trial Master and to expand the Trial Master’s ability to allow
the withdrawal of charges under Section 1404.345.
To ensure transparency and finality, the proposed amendment expands
the scope of matters to be reviewed by the Committee on Trial Review under
Section 406.075 by requiring that any withdrawal allowed by a Trial Master be
reviewed by the Committee on Trial Review and reported to the Grand Lodge at
Annual Communication, in the same manner that current Trial Master decisions
are reported and reviewed for affirmation, dismissal, modification or remand.
Importantly, this change does not diminish the seriousness with which
we treat accusations of unmasonic conduct. Rather, it reflects the exercise
of prudent judgment, discretion, and compassion — values that are central
to our Masonic tradition. It provides a clearer, more efficient, and more fraternal pathway toward resolution. It reduces the emotional and procedural
toll of unnecessary trials, conserves the time and energy of our members and
volunteers, and honors our Masonic commitment to preserving justice while
strengthening the bonds of peace and harmony within our Lodges.
Brethren, this amendment is not a departure from our principles — it
is a return to them. I urge your thoughtful consideration and support of this
measure.
If you adopt this recommendation, the following changes will be made to
the Code. Section 406.075 of the Code would be amended to read as marked:
§406.075. TRIAL REVIEW.
The Committee on Trial Review shall consist of not less than three nor
more than seven members. It shall review the trial records and the records
of trials matters held in arising out of Constituent Lodges. and It shall
examine each application for restoration after suspension or expulsion by
Grand Lodge. It shall report to Grand Lodge its recommendations as to
action to be taken.
Section 1404.345 of the Code would be amended to read as marked:
§1404.345. WITHDRAWING CHARGES.
The Accuser may submit a written request to the Grand Master for the
withdrawal of charges at any time prior to the Trial Master’s appointment.
Such request must be made in writing and state the Accuser’s reasons for

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

his request for withdrawal. If the Grand Master determines withdrawal
is appropriate, the Grand Master shall notify the Grand Secretary of his
determination and the Grand Master’s approval of such request shall be
deemed final. The Grand Secretary will notify the Accused, the Accuser, the
Master of the Accused’s Lodge, and the Inspector of the Accused’s Lodge’s
district of the withdrawn charges and direct the Accused’s Lodge(s) to
restore him to good standing, including for purposes of issuing a demit
pursuant to Sections 804.130, 804.135, and 804.160.
The Trial Master may allow a charge to be withdrawn by the Accuser at
any time after the Trial Master’s appointment if the Trial Master determines
that withdrawal is appropriate. The Accuser’s request to the Trial Master
for the withdrawal of a charge(s) must be made in writing and state the
Accuser’s reasons for his request for such withdrawal. The Trial Master may
not allow a charge to be withdrawn when he finds evidence in the specifications which may warrant a verdict of unmasonic conduct. If the Trial
Master allows a charge to be withdrawn, he shall prepare a written report
on his action and make it a part of the trial record. The Trial Master shall
provide a signed copy of the trial record to the Grand Secretary. The Grand
Secretary shall then notify the Accuser and the Accused of the action taken,
as well as the Accused’s Lodge and direct the Accused’s Lodge(s) to restore
him to good standing, including for purposes of issuing a demit pursuant
to Sections 804.130, 804.135, and 804.160. If the Accused is a member of
more than one Lodge, the copy shall be given to every Lodge of which the
Accused is a member, as shown in Grand Lodge’s records. Notwithstanding
the Accused being restored to good standing, the withdrawal and any
related actions remain subject to final review and approval by Grand Lodge
pursuant to Section 1404.910 and subject to Section 1404.950. The Trial
Master’s report of any action resulting in the withdrawal of charges shall
be deemed a “trial record” for purposes of review pursuant to Sections
1404.910 and 1404.950.

1.

The Committee shall review each trial record pertaining to a withdrawal of charges to determine whether the withdrawal was appropriate. The Committee may recommend that a withdrawn charge
may be reinstated only if the withdrawal resulted in a miscarriage of

drawn from the trial record shall be in favor of sustaining the

such recommendation.

Section 1404.950 of the Code would be amended to read as marked:

§1404.950. DOUBLE JEOPARDY.
When Grand Lodge determines that the Accused ought not to have been
convicted, and sets aside a verdict of conviction without ordering a new
trial, or determines a withdrawal of charges was appropriate, its judgment
is final, and the Accused may not be tried again on the same charge.
Upon Grand Lodge’s review and approval, a conviction or acquittal
on a charge of unmasonic conduct under this Code is a bar to a future
prosecution on the same charge in this Jurisdiction.
If so ordered by the Grand Master with the concurrence of the
Committee on Trial Review, a withdrawal of a charge of unmasonic conduct, as part of a written mediated settlement agreement signed by the Trial
Master, the Accuser(s) and the Accused, or as part of a trial record affirmed
by Grand Lodge as provided in Section 1404.910, is a bar to a future prosecution on the same charge or factual circumstances in this Jurisdiction.
Any mediated settlement agreement shall include a summary of the facts
and reasoning supporting such withdrawal. Any trial records that involve
the withdrawal of charges shall include the written statement from the
Accuser stating the reasons for the Accuser’s request for the withdrawal.

Section 407.030 of the Code would be amended to read as marked:

Updates Required Applicant Contributions
The California Masonic Code (“Code”) requires that:
• Applicants for the degrees and each applicant for affiliation whose
Demit or Certificate is from a Lodge of another Jurisdiction contribute $30 for the use and benefit of Grand Lodge and $25 for the use
and benefit of the Masonic Homes of California (unless the applicant
has paid such contribution with a former application); and
• Applicants for the degrees contribute $15 for the George Washington
Masonic National Memorial and $9 for the California Masonic
Memorial Temple (unless the applicant has paid such contribution
with a former application).
The dollar amounts of these required applicant contributions have not
been adjusted in a long time. The $25 contribution to the Masonic Homes has
not changed for nearly 100 years, and the $9 contribution to the Memorial
Temple has not changed in 70 years. The George Washington Masonic National
Memorial contribution was last changed in 2010. It is well past time to adjust
these amounts to reflect current economic reality. Between 2010 and 2024,
the U.S. dollar lost more than 30% of its value due to inflation. The buying
power of $100 in 2010 is less than $70 today. It is also time to amend the Code
so that these contributions can be more routinely adjusted to keep pace with
economic realities.
We should also take this opportunity to include in the Code the California
Masonic Foundation as a recipient of applicant contributions. Requiring applicants to contribute to the Foundation will strengthen this great charitable institution. Perhaps more importantly, a required contribution to the Foundation will
send a strong message to our applicants of the value we place on our Fraternity’s
charitable mission and activities.
Thus, I recommend that the Code be revised to state that applicants
must make contributions to Grand Lodge, the Masonic Homes, the George
Washington Masonic National Memorial, the California Masonic Memorial
