Grand Master Metroka’s Recommendation No. 6
Modifies Lodge Vote Required to Restore a Mason
Suspended for Non-Payment of Dues
A Mason suspended for non-payment of dues for two or more years may
make a request to his Lodge for restoration. Under the California Masonic Code
(“Code”), the suspended Mason shall not be restored except by a two-thirds
vote by ballot of all Lodge members present at the next Stated Meeting after his
request for restoration is presented. As a condition of his restoration, the Lodge
may require the suspended Mason to pay some portion of his outstanding dues.
I recommend that we reduce the required two-thirds vote of Lodge members to a simple majority vote. Except in very limited circumstances, our Code
sets a simple majority as the threshold for deciding Lodge matters. In matters
relating to Lodge finances, for example, a simple majority of Lodge members
carries the day. The Code’s few exceptions to the simple majority rule involve
issues of greater importance than the potential restoration of a member suspended for non-payment of dues. For example, the Code requires a unanimous
vote when balloting on an application and a two-thirds vote on changes to Lodge
Bylaws. These high thresholds are warranted as they relate to issues fundamental to the governance and character of the Lodge. Restoration of a particular
member who has failed to pay dues does not rise to this level of fundamental
or “core” importance.
The stringent two-thirds voting threshold might be justified if restoration
in all cases necessarily led to the forgiveness of all past dues. But it does not:
the Code gives Lodges the discretion to condition the suspended Mason’s
restoration on payment of a portion of his outstanding dues.
Given this discretion, it is appropriate that the will of a simple majority of
Lodge members present carries the day on this matter, as it does on so many
other matters of equal or greater importance to our Lodges.
If you adopt this recommendation, Section 809.380 of the Code would be
amended to read as marked:
§809.380. RESTORATION OF A MASON SUSPENDED FOR NONPAYMENT OF DUES.
A Mason suspended for non-payment of dues:

172

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

173

A. Shall be automatically restored if, within two years, he pays any arrearage due at the time of his suspension, together with such further dues
as would have accrued against him had he not been suspended, to the
date of his payment, unless such arrearage and dues have been remitted
by his Lodge; and
B. May make a request to his Lodge for restoration if he has not paid them
or had them remitted by his Lodge for the period of two years. The
Mason shall not be restored except by a two-thirds majority vote by
ballot of all the members present at the next Stated Meeting after the
request for restoration is presented. As a condition of his restoration,
he shall pay such amount of any arrearage due at the time of his suspension and such amount of dues as would have accrued against him had
he not been suspended, to the date of his payment, as his Lodge may
require, except such arrearage and dues that have been remitted by his
Lodge. A petition denied may be renewed at any future Stated Meeting.
The Secretary shall immediately notify the Grand Secretary of the
restoration.
Amendment to the Ordinances.
2/3 affirmative vote required for adoption.

Grand Master Metroka’s Recommendation No. 8
Clarifies Process By Which Lodges
May Use Alternative Ritual
The Ritual, including the lectures in our three degrees, is central to
our practice of Freemasonry.
Grand Lodge has adopted a version of the “American Rite” for our lodge
ritual uses. The American Rite is commonly called The York Rite. Developed
over many decades, the American Rite’s last significant formulation occurred
in the early 1800s. The American Rite is just one of several major sets of rituals
(including the York and Scottish Rites) commonly used by Masonic lodges
around the world.
The California Masonic Code (the “Code”) generally requires our Lodges
to use the American Rite as modified by our Grand Lodge. There is a long-time
exception, however. The Code allows Lodges whose “long-established ritualistic
work” departs from the Ritual adopted by Grand Lodge to perform an alternate
ritual, unless doing so has been disapproved by the Grand Master and Grand
Lecturer. As a result of this exception, several Lodges under our Jurisdiction
have practiced alternative rituals, some for over a century, and still today we
have Lodges in our Jurisdiction that perform versions of the Scottish Rite. La
Parfaite Union No. 17 has done so since the 1850s, and in 2023, La France Lodge
No. 885 was granted authority to perform a version of the Scottish Rite.
The Code does not define the term, “long-established ritualistic work.”
It also does not set out any principles by which the Grand Master and Grand
Lecturer should evaluate ritual that departs from the Ritual of this Jurisdiction.
The Code’s ambiguity and backward-looking focus has generally not been an
issue for our Fraternity. The use of alternative ritual declined in the second
half of the 20th Century in California. In the instances where Lodges sought
permission to use alternative ritual, Grand Masters and Grand Lecturers exercised their discretion under the Code reasonably and without controversy. I am
confident future Grand Masters and Grand Lecturers will do the same.
That said, the issue of alternative ritual may arise more frequently in the
future. We see the interest growing. As California continues to become more
diverse, so too does California Freemasonry. For example, a number of both
young and old lodges in California but outside our Jurisdiction use ritual from
other major rites. While they depart to some degree from our Ritual, their
practice of Freemasonry is no more or less pure, correct or wise than ours.

174

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

I believe that we should continue to allow future Grand Masters and Grand
Lecturers to exercise discretion when considering lodge requests to use alternative ritual. It would be beneficial, however, to clarify the Code’s ambiguous
language on this topic and provide guidance to our Grand Lodge officers facing
such requests.
With respect to alternative ritual, I believe that there are three key principles
upon which we can agree. First, all ritual used by our Lodges should contain
the same obligations as the Ritual adopted by Grand Lodge. It is crucial that
all of our members, regardless of their Lodge memberships, be committed to
the same obligations and personal commitments to themselves, their Lodges
and their brothers. Second, all of our Lodges should use ritual that shares the
same signs, words and modes of recognition. Third, all of our Lodges should
perform ritual that adds to, rather than detracts from, the culture, integrity
and ideals of our Fraternity. Alternative ritual that does not reflect the culture,
integrity and ideals of our Fraternity does not have a place in our Jurisdiction.
My recommendation reflects these principles by granting the Grand Master
and the Grand Lecturer the discretion to grant lodge requests to perform alternative ritual if the Grand Master and Grand Lecturer determine that the use of
the alternative ritual: (1) includes the same obligations contained in the Ritual
adopted by Grand Lodge; and (2) includes the same signs, words and modes
of recognition contained in our Ritual; and (3) is consistent with the culture,
integrity and ideals of our Fraternity.
If you adopt this recommendation, Section 402.010 of the Code would be
amended to read as marked:
§402.010. RITUAL.
All work in this Jurisdiction, including each degree conferred and all lectures, must be in conformity with the Ritual, and such must be adhered to
by all Lodges and Masons in this Jurisdiction, except as otherwise provided
in this Code. Upon request by a Constituent Lodge, the Grand Master and
Grand Lecturer may consent to a Constituent Lodge’s use of an alternative
ritual that departs from the Ritual provided that such alternative ritual (a)
includes the same obligations as those contained in the Ritual, (b) includes
the same signs, words and modes of recognition as those contained in the
Ritual, and (c) is consistent in all material respects with the culture, integrity
and ideals of our Fraternity, as determined by the Grand Master and Grand
Lecturer. The language of the obligations in the alternative ritual need not
be exactly identical to the language used in the Ritual. Unless otherwise
determined by the Grand Master and Grand Lecturer, Constituent Lodges
who have used an alternative ritual since at least January 1, 2024 that was
not disapproved by the Grand Master and Grand Lecturer may continue
their use of such alternative ritual without the affirmative consent of the
Grand Master and Grand Lecturer required by this Section. Constituent

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

175

Lodges whose long-established ritualistic work is in part a departure from
the Ritual of this Jurisdiction may continue to perform such ritual, for so
long as the same has not been disapproved by action of the Grand Master
and the Grand Lecturer. The right to perform the long-established ritualistic work of Vallee de France Lodge No. 329 has been transferred to and
assumed by La France Lodge with the requisite approval of Grand Lodge.
Amendment to the Ordinances.
2/3 affirmative vote required for adoption.

Grand Master Metroka’s Recommendation No. 11
Permits a Secretary to Serve as Master, Warden
or Secretary of Another Lodge
The California Masonic Code (“Code”) prohibits a member from serving
as the Master, Warden or Secretary of one Lodge while simultaneously serving
in any of those three positions at another Lodge.
I recommend that we continue this prohibition with one change with
respect to Lodge Secretaries. I recommend that we allow a brother serving
as a Secretary at one Lodge to also serve as a Master, Warden or Secretary
of another Lodge. This modest relaxation of the Code recognizes the many
dedicated members of our fraternity who maintain multiple affiliations. It also
recognizes and addresses the continuing need of our Lodges to identify and
select qualified candidates to fill their officer ranks. I believe that our smaller
Lodges will particularly benefit from my recommendation.
In the past, it might have been fair to suppose that a member would have
difficulty dedicating the time and energy necessary to serve as Secretary of a
Lodge while also serving as an officer of another Lodge. As a result of, among
other things, technological enhancements and the many services now provided
by Grand Lodge to our Lodge Secretaries, I have no concern in this regard now.
We all know many members who are both able and willing to competently perform the duties of Lodge Secretary while also serving as an officer of another
Lodge. We should stop denying our Lodges the opportunity to avail themselves
of these men.
I note that the Code also prohibits a member from holding more than one
office in one Lodge at the same time. I do not recommend any change to this rule.
If you adopt this recommendation, Section 805.010 of the Code would be
amended to read as marked:
§805.010. OFFICERS.
The officers of a Lodge are Master, Senior Warden, Junior Warden,
Treasurer, Secretary, Chaplain, Senior Deacon, Junior Deacon, Marshal,
Senior Steward, Junior Steward, Tiler and other officers as the Lodge may
deem proper to appoint. The Master, Senior Warden and Junior Warden,
Treasurer and Secretary shall be elected in conformity with this Code. The
other officers shall be appointed by the Master. Any Master Mason in good

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

177

standing, whether or not a member of the Lodge, may be appointed Tiler or
Organist. All other officers shall be members in good standing of the Lodge.
A member may not be Master, or Warden or Secretary, or any combination thereof, of two or more Lodges (other than Research Lodges and
Historic Lodges) at the same time. No one may hold more than one office
in a Lodge at the same time.
The title of Master applies not only to him who has been elected and
installed as Master, but to either of the Wardens while acting as Master.
Amendment to the Ordinances.
2/3 affirmative vote required for adoption.

Resolution No. 24-01
Makes Third Degree Proficiency a Prerequisite
for Nomination to the Office of Master, Senior Warden,
or Junior Warden
The proponents of this resolution seek to make the receipt of a Certificate
of Proficiency in the Candidate’s Lecture of the Master Mason Degree a prerequisite for nomination to the office of Master, Senior Warden, or Junior
Warden and remove the receipt of a Certificate of Proficiency as a condition
to an officer-elect’s installation to those offices.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

WHEREAS, that the proposed amendment consistently promotes a culture of
excellence and proficiency in Masonic ritual work, enhancing the quality and
solemnity of our ceremonies; and
WHEREAS, that this proposed requirement will also reduce the administrative burden on District Inspectors, as the process and requirement will ensure
candidates are fully prepared for their leadership roles and encourage brothers
to plan their Masonic progression; and
WHEREAS, that this proposed amendment resolution does not hinder the
progress of worthy brethren, but rather sets forth a clear path for those aspiring
to leadership roles within the Lodge; and
WHEREAS, the successful passage of this resolution would render moot the current stipulation in CMC / Chapter V, Article V Installation of Officers §805.520
(Conditions to Installation of Master-Elect), §805.530 (Conditions to Installation
of Senior Warden-Elect) and §805.540 (Conditions to Installation of Junior
Warden-Elect) which mandates the completion of Master Mason proficiency
as a condition for installation, given that this requirement would have been
fulfilled prior to election100..

WHEREAS, The Grand Lodge of Free And Accepted Masons of California
upholds the values of knowledge, proficiency, and preparedness among its
members, especially those in leadership positions within the Lodges; and

NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 805.410 of the California
Masonic Code be amended as marked:

WHEREAS, the esteemed positions of Master, Senior Warden, and Junior
Warden are critical to the effective governance and ceremonial duties of Masonic
Lodges, requiring not only dedication but also a deep understanding of Masonic
law, rituals, and traditions; and

§805.410. ELECTED OFFICERS.

WHEREAS, one of the current installation requirements for these principal
officers include the completion of the Third-Degree proficiency as stated in
Chapter V, Article V; [Installation of Lodge Officers], sections 805.520, 805.530,
and 805.540; and
WHEREAS, to further ensure that nominees for these offices are thoroughly
prepared and qualified, a proposal to amend the current California Masonic Code
/ Constitution and Ordinances is hereby submitted to require the completion
and certification of the Master Mason proficiency at the time of nomination,
which would serve to enhance the leadership quality within the Lodges and
to further ensure that nominees for these offices are thoroughly prepared and
qualified; and
WHEREAS, the requirement for proficiency at the nomination stage will ensure
candidates are well-prepared for their respective roles and duties, leading to
more effective leadership; and

The Master, Wardens, Treasurer and Secretary of each Lodge shall be
elected annually at the Stated Meeting in November each year, except
as otherwise permitted in Section 807.000 of this Code. A Certificate of
Proficiency in the Candidate’s Lecture of the Master Mason Degree shall
be a prerequisite for nomination to the office of Master, Senior Warden,
or Junior Warden. The election shall be by ballot. A majority of all votes
cast shall be necessary for an election. A blank ballot shall not constitute a
vote cast. The Lodge, by unanimous consent, may permit any designated
officer to cast the ballot for the Lodge.
If an eligible candidate fails to receive a majority of the votes cast, and
the candidate receiving a majority is ineligible, there is no election. When
a candidate for office is ineligible because he is delinquent in his dues, but
his dues are paid before a second ballot, and he receives a majority of the
votes cast a second time, he is properly elected.
All members of the Lodge in good standing shall be entitled to vote at
an election of Lodge officers.
An annual election held contrary to the provision of this section shall
be void.

Now in its 127th year, the Masonic Homes of California continued to
advance its mission of providing relief, care, and community for Masons and
their families. Building on the momentum of last year’s expansion of eligibility and service offerings, 2025 was marked by several major efforts, including
disaster relief, operational improvements, capital project advancements, and
strengthened partnerships. Through its residential and community-based services, the organization served more members than ever before while maintaining
its commitment to high-quality care and fiscal responsibility.
Distressed Worthy Brother Relief
A highlight of the past year was the work of Masonic Outreach Services, which
helped connect Masons and their families throughout the state with support
and resources in the wake of January’s fires in Altadena and Malibu. Through
MOS, the organization has provided more than $241,000 in relief since the
beginning of the year, including more than $93,000 in immediate financial
assistance to members and their families impacted by the Southern California
wildfires. However, past experience in fire relief tells us that these funds are
often accessed later—after insurance and other fire support has been depleted.
MOS expects that additional relief will be requested as the anniversary of the
fires approaches.
Community-Based Services and Partnerships
Masonic Outreach Services and the Masonic Center for Youth and Families
(MCYAF) continued to expand their reach throughout California. In 2024–25,
MOS fielded 2,695 calls to the Masonic Assistance hotline from people needing
advice, resources, and emergency funds. It ultimately supported 498 clients with
case management or financial assistance. All told, MOS provided $2,905,193 to
Masons and their families this year.
Across the state, Lodge Outreach Services conducted meetings with a cumulative attendance of 435 members and their spouses, training them to provide
support to members of their lodges and local communities. That training helps

192

Masons reach out to fellow members to provide information and aid to those
who may not be in contact with their lodges. By strengthening its partnership
with the Grand Lodge Member Services team, staff with Lodge Outreach Services
are able to help Masons return to lodge for the first time in what for many has
been several years.
Meanwhile, MCYAF worked with 750 individual clients and 60 Masonic
Homes residents over the year. After its move from San Francisco to Union
City late last year, the organization integrated itself into campus life, offering
on-site appointments and group programs that enhance residents’ emotional
wellness. New initiatives included Medicare-billable “Afternoon Tea” support
groups and the expansion of clinical internship programs through partnerships
with Pepperdine University and local graduate schools. Client satisfaction
remained high, with 100 percent of surveyed clients stating they would recommend MCYAF services.

the state. This expansion ensures that current residents can receive comprehensive skilled nursing without having to leave the supportive environment of
the Covina campus.
As a bonus, the Citrus Heights Health Center won two design awards this
year, including the International Interior Design Association Awards and the
2024 Senior Housing News Architecture and Design Awards. The center’s design
prioritizes privacy, comfort, and access to specialized services, aligning with
the Masonic Homes’ commitment to delivering high-quality care.

Occupancy and Eligibility at Our Campuses
Following the 2023 expansion of eligibilityto include all California Masons,
California Prince Hall Masons, California Grand Lodge of Iran in Exile Masons,
and their parents and parents-in-law, 2025 saw continued interest from members of these groups. Masonic Assistance fielded 86 calls from newly eligible
individuals, up from the year prior. These included requests for residential
services, financial assistance, and support through MOS.
Occupancy challenges persisted in some areas, particularly in memory care
and the Pavilion building in Union City, but overall census improved compared
with the prior year. As of June 30, 2025, capacity in our independent, assisted
living, and memory-care neighborhoods in Union City stood at 84 percent,
while Covina remains 100 percent full. In our skilled nursing neighborhoods,
capacity in Union City stood at 71 percent, while at Covina capacity stood at 59
percent. Targeted marketing, events, and sales initiatives—alongside strategic
pricing—have been implemented to address the gaps in census and to attract
both Masonic and non-Masonic residents.
One major initiative this summer and fall was an effort to apply all residents
for Medicare and Medi-Cal. This important, ongoing initiative will improve the
bottom line for the organization.
Citrus Heights Health Center
This year marked the first full year of operations for the Citrus Heights Health
Center on the Covina campus, a milestone achievement in expanding high-quality skilled nursing in Southern California. The center welcomed long-term
residents from the MOS waitlist and began admitting short-term rehabilitation
patients from the surrounding community in early April. With Medicare and
Medi-Cal billing now fully operational, the facility is positioned to serve a wider
population in the coming years, strengthening our continuum of care across

193

Capital Projects and Facilities Updates
Several significant capital projects at the Masonic Homes advanced in 2025. In
Covina, the swimming pool project reached final design development, with contractor estimates in progress and construction documents to follow. Meanwhile,
Union City began phased flooring replacement, with three units completed
each week to minimize disruption. That project is slated for completion by the
end of the year. Elevator modernization in the Lorber building also began, with
budget management closely monitored as additional repairs were identified.
Facility upgrades in Covina included roof replacement, installation of
sound-insulation panels in dining areas, and construction of a new gift shop for
residents. At Acacia Creek, collaboration with MHC continued by consolidating
the Union City sales team and the environmental-services teams to improve
efficiency and cross-training. By all accounts, this “one team” strategy is a
positive change for the Union City campus.
Marketing and Outreach
Marketing strategies in 2025 focused on increasing head count at Union City,
particularly in assisted living and memory care, through targeted digital campaigns, updated campus brochures, and a refreshed website. Events such as the
“Financial Benefits of a CCRC” seminar, the Winter Lights campus tour, the
craft beer and food-pairing event, and the Alzheimer’s Walk engaged both the
Masonic and local communities. Covina continued to benefit from targeted
email and California Freemason Magazine features.
Employee Engagement and Workforce Development
Our employee-engagement program advanced in 2025 with the release of a
comprehensive implementation guide to standardize practices across campuses.
The Employee Engagement Committees hosted activities and appreciation
events, boosting morale and cross-campus collaboration. At the same time, the
Masonic Homes Academy faced funding challenges after the loss of the Gateway
In program but secured a renewed partnership with LeadingAge California
to continue training Certified Nursing Assistants. This pipeline remains vital
to maintaining low vacancy rates in clinical positions, a challenge across the
senior-living industry.

Fundraising Success
The California Masonic Foundation achieved exceptional fundraising results in
2025, raising $10 million in total to support MHC programs and relief efforts.
These funds strengthen our ability to serve Masons and their families now and
in the future.

Masonic Homes of California – Union City

Acacia Creek Retirement Community
It has been 15 years since Acacia Creek opened. We are so proud of the outstanding community we have built over that time and look forward to a future
of continued growth and innovation. Post-pandemic, the community continues
to grow, and we look forward to being fully occupied very soon. This marks our
first full year under the leadership of CEO Terry S. Quigley, who has spearheaded
several initiatives focused on operational efficiency, strategic opportunities, and
furthering collaboration and synergy across our organization.
On balance, 2025 has been a strong year for Acacia Creek. As of July, occupancy stood at 88 percent, with 132 of 150 units filled and plans for a further five
move-ins imminent. That brings overall occupancy in line with our yearly goal.
After recording no move-ins at all in 2019 or 2020, the community saw 22 new
move-ins in 2024 and 21 so far in 2025, nearing our target of 30 move-ins by end
of year. During this time, attrition also slowed. After averaging 22 move-outs
each year from 2021 to 2023, last year saw just eight vacated apartments, and
this year only 11. The result is that our overall head count has nearly rebounded
to pre-pandemic level.
At the same time, a newly integrated sales team, now reporting to Director
of Sales Amy LaGrant, is updating and strengthening our marketing database.
This ensures that our marketing efforts are targeted and effective.
The sales team continues to keep the new-resident pipeline open. It has
done that in part by hosting monthly in-person marketing events, which over
the past quarter brought 114 prospective residents onto campus for dynamic
and informative sessions like a beer-and-food-pairing event, a “Brain Health
for Seniors” seminar, and, in September, our first-ever Alzheimer’s Walk on the
Union City campus. Altogether, we have seen an average of 60 new sales leads
per month, with underlying metrics (such as cost per lead, lead-to-application
percentage, etc.) well above industry benchmarks.
Cooperation with the Masonic Homes has been a priority under Quigley’s
leadership, evidenced by the May 2025 consolidation of the two organizations’
sales teams. That move helps align resources across the communities and
enhances our ability to deliver consistent, high-touch experiences for prospective residents and their families across all levels of care. This team is also helping

218

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

us ensure efficiency, improve customer service, and share accountability as we
work toward a more integrated service model while maintaining the unique
identities of both organizations. Campus-wide resident programs and joint
staff-recognition events also expanded this year, promoting a shared culture
of collaboration.
Sandra Simon was named executive director in October 2024, overseeing
the day-to-day operations of the community. She brings more than 25 years of
senior-living leadership experience in the Bay Area. Already, Simon has been
deeply engaged in building relationships with those on campus by participating
in all resident committees and the resident council. Together with those residents, she has created processes that foster meaningful, impactful outcomes
to enhance the overall experience at Acacia Creek. This year, she took on the
additional responsibility of overseeing operations for the Pavilion, the campus’s
28-bed assisted living residence. She is being supported in that by Mina Forsythe,
director of clinical and resident services.
Simon has set clear goals for the year, which we are well on track to meet.
That includes reviewing and updating our campus disaster plan, for which we
have engaged an outside consultant to ensure we are adopting industry best
practices. We aim to complete disaster-preparedness drills by the end of the
fiscal year. We have also adopted new workflows and training for timely and
appropriate referrals to the Masonic Center for Youth and Families for resident
mental health needs. We are grateful for the opportunity to bring these services
to residents directly on campus as they navigate life’s changes.
Another highlight of the year was the board retreat led by Quigley and her
team in April. The retreat provided valuable time for the Acacia Creek board
to connect, learn from subject-matter experts, and tour nearby senior-living
communities. These discussions inspired new ideas about the services we envision for current and future residents. We are energized by the possibilities for
innovation and continued excellence.
We look forward to another exciting year of growth in 2026.
Respectfully submitted,

California Masonic Foundation
Few years in the history of the California Masonic Foundation have so
clearly demonstrated the breadth of our mission and the depth of our fraternity’s commitment to relief, education, and community. As I conclude my
service as chairman of the board, I am proud to reflect on a year that not only
strengthened the Foundation financially but also affirmed the values that lie
at the very heart of Masonry.
This report is more than a collection of statistics and milestones. It is a
testament to how Masons across California—individually, in their lodges, and
through this Foundation—responded to urgent need, invested in the next generation, and built partnerships that will endure long after the year has ended.
Relief in Times of Crisis
Masonic relief has always been one of our most sacred duties. In early 2025,
this principle was tested when devastating wildfires swept through the Los
Angeles area, leaving some 150,000 families displaced and many of our brothers
and their loved ones in urgent need. The Foundation responded with speed
and purpose.
Within days, a special appeal was issued, and the response was overwhelming. Lodges that had already budgeted for other causes redirected resources
toward relief. Individual members sent contributions both large and small.
Several Grand Lodges outside California, including the GrandLodge of Oregon,
extended a helping hand, demonstrating the universality of Masonic charity.
As of this writing, the Foundation has raised more than $950,000 for relief
efforts—one of the largest and fastest mobilizations of fraternal philanthropy
in our history. These funds have provided housing, food, and essential care for
those most affected while also serving as a reminder to every member that when
tragedy strikes, Masons stand ready to help.
Financial Strength and Growth
The wildfire response was only one highlight of a year that saw extraordinary
support for the Foundation. Our Annual Fund has already raised more than

221

Education and Opportunity
While relief concerns the urgent, education represents the lasting. In 2025,
the Foundation continued to make good on its promise to invest in the future
through a wide range of programs for students, teachers, and families.
Raising a Reader’s 1,000-Classroom Milestone: Our long partnership
with Raising a Reader, now in its 15th year, has brought proven family literacy
programming into California’s most under-resourced communities. This year,
Raising a Reader expanded to 115 more classrooms, bringing our statewide
total to 988. This fall, we will celebrate our 1,000th classroom with a reception at Central Elementary in San Diego, the very school where we began this
journey in 2011. This milestone is not just symbolic. It represents thousands
of families who have been given the tools to read together, strengthen familial
bonds, and prepare children for lifelong success. It is a promise fulfilled from
our Let’s Write the Future campaign and a shining example of what sustained
investment can achieve.
Scholarships Transforming Lives: Our scholarships reached more students than ever before in 2025. Since 2011, we have offered in excess of $10
million in scholarships. Behind every award is a student whose path has been
altered, a family whose hope has been bolstered, and a community strengthened
through the generosity of California Masons.
Investment in Success: With more than 300 students being supported
through these scholarship funds, including nearly 100 new scholars this year,
the program is now investing more than $800,000 annually to help young
students across the state.
Masonic Youth Leadership Award: This fund supported 29 applicants
with more than $160,000 toward their college plans.
C.E. Towne Masonic Award: This scholarship, distributed in partnership
with the Prince Hall Masons of California, supported 30 applicants in 2025,
bringing all-time support to more than $1 million.

Johnny Ritchey Scholarship: Now supporting 30 students with awards

Foundation and Reality Changers of San Diego.

Leadership Beyond the Lodge

Building Awareness Through Partnership
Masonry’s influence extends beyond relief and education and into the public
square, where our values become visible to society at large. In 2025, the
Foundation made significant strides in raising awareness of Masonry and building partnerships with others in our community.
The Breaking Barriers exhibit, co-sponsored with the Padres Foundation
and the San Diego Public Library, brought the powerful history of Negro Leagues
baseball to thousands of students. This event was more than a history lesson;
it was a moment of inspiration, connecting past struggles for equality with the
opportunities we are working to create today.
Meanwhile, in Sacramento, the Green Careers Pathways program launched
with a nearly $500,000 investment from the Foundation designed to prepare
underserved youth for jobs in the clean-energy economy. Supported by CalEPIC
and local public schools, the program not only provides training but also raises
awareness about industries critical to California’s future.
Nationally, the Foundation participated in a major philanthropic panel on
early math education, positioning our fraternity as an innovator in addressing
foundational academic skills. That was backed up in March with the announcement of a three-year, $968,000 investment to improve math outcomes for
young students in Los Angeles. The initiative, which will fund a range of family
math-engagement programs and resources, will support 1,000 transitional kindergarten through second-grade students attending high-needs schools in L.A.,
and is being developed in partnership with the Center for Family Math, Raising
a Reader, PowerMyLearning, and the Partnership for Los Angeles Schools. These
moments demonstrate that the Foundation is not only a benefactor but also a
thought leader in philanthropy.
Revitalizing Masons4mitts
Now in its 17th year, Masons4Mitts remains one of the Foundation’s most visible
and beloved programs. In 2025, it underwent a thoughtful refresh: We introduced
early-season “Masons Nights at the Ballpark” events to the calendar, drawing
nearly 700 members together across four Major League cities. These gatherings
brought energy and visibility to the program at the very start of the campaign
season. We also shifted leadership from captains to ambassadors, expanding
involvement from 52 to 73 leaders statewide. This new model ensures greater
ownership and engagement from more members.
As always, the culmination of the campaign is our check presentations to
Major League Baseball partners in September—moments that shine a public
spotlight on Masonic generosity.

223

This year also saw several of our trustees take on leadership roles in the broader
community, deepening our influence and relationships. Trustees now serve on
the boards of Reality Changers of San Diego, the San Francisco Education Fund,
Operation Jump Start in Long Beach, and College Access Plan in Pasadena.
These commitments extend the Foundation’s reach and ensure that the voice
of Masonry is present in important civic conversations.
Reflections
As I write this final report as chairman of the board, I am struck by the arc
of our progress. We began 2025 facing down a natural disaster, and we end it
with historic strength. We have surpassed $10 million in annual fundraising,
reached the brink of 1,000 Raising a Reader classrooms, transformed lives
through scholarships, and made Masonry visible through public events and
partnerships.
I am proud of these accomplishments, but prouder still of the members who
made them possible. Every gift, every hour of service, every act of leadership is
a testament to the enduring strength of our craft.
It has been the privilege of my life to serve as chairman of the California
Masonic Foundation. I leave this role confident that the Foundation is stronger
than ever, guided by dedicated trustees, staff, and members, and poised for even
greater achievements through the Keystone Initiative campaign and beyond.
The work we have done together will endure, touching lives for generations to
come. For that, and for the trust you have placed in me, I am deeply grateful.

REPORT OF THE

California Masonic Memorial Temple
The past year has marked another period of meaningful progress and
continued growth for the California Masonic Memorial Temple. The CMMT
remains a vital institution, serving as both the operational hub of Freemasonry
in California and a dynamic business enterprise supporting the charitable work
of the California Masonic Foundation.
Throughout 2025, the CMMT has demonstrated strong financial performance, driven by a robust calendar of live events and expanded programming
at Freemasons’ Hall. Meanwhile, our 2030 capital plan remains firmly on track,
with several projects either completed or well underway. Just as important, the
board has embraced new opportunities to elevate CMMT’s public presence and
cultural relevance both within the fraternity and in the broader community.
As we look ahead, the foundation laid this year positions the CMMT for
even greater visibility, engagement, and long-term sustainability.
Increased Events and Economic Impact
The CMMT continues to serve as a premier destination for live entertainment in
San Francisco through its longstanding partnership with Live Nation. Following
previous approval by the San Francisco Planning Commission to increase the
number of permitted events from 79 to 91 annually, the building has seen a
meaningful rise in both attendance and event diversity. This has translated into
sustained economic and cultural impact, drawing over 250,000 visitors annually
and supporting a vibrant ecosystem of local hotels, restaurants, and businesses.
Live Nation is projected to reach 85 events by the end of 2025, including
concerts, comedy shows, and private gatherings. Notably, comedy programming
has emerged as a particularly strong performer, helping to stabilize event revenue amid shifts in the touring-music landscape.
While the pace of bookings saw some slowing early in the year, revenues
remain strong and the CMMT continues to benefit from a diverse and high-impact calendar of public-facing programming. These events not only support
our financial goals but also help reinforce the CMMT’s role as a vital civic and
cultural landmark in the heart of San Francisco.

226

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

Freemasons’ Hall

Emile Norman Arts Foundation Partnership

Now in its fifth year of operation, Freemasons’ Hall continues to thrive as one
of the most active lodge facilities in California. As of 2025, some 10 Masonic
organizations regularly meet in the space, including six lodges under the Grand
Lodge of California, three lodges under other jurisdictions, and one Royal Arch
chapter—making the hall a true center of fraternal life.
In addition to stated meetings and degree work, the hall hosted a range
of high-impact events such as the fifth-anniversary celebration of its opening,
a holiday party, and the annual Feast of Saint John the Baptist. The hall also
played host to several educational workshops and speaker events, reflecting our
commitment to both ritual excellence and community building.
The CMMT has also introduced new enhancements to the user experience
in the building, including tailored catering services and ongoing efforts to
improve the functionality and comfort of the space. Board members have regularly reported seeing the community utilize the QR codes placed throughout
the building, which guide visitors to web stories that highlight the history and
legacy of Freemasonry in California, contributing to a deeper appreciation of
the temple’s symbolic and cultural significance.
Looking ahead, the CMMT is exploring opportunities to expand public
use of Freemasons’ Hall. With its elegant design and central location, the hall
is uniquely positioned to serve as a bridge between the Masonic community
and the wider public.

In alignment with our long-term strategic priorities, the CMMT is deepening
its role as a civic and cultural landmark through an evolving partnership with
the Emile Norman Arts Foundation.
In July 2025, through the tremendous work of Allan Casalou and Andy
Cameron, the CMMT reached a significant milestone: the
Emile Norman archive was formally transferred to our care. This acquisition
reflects more than a curatorial responsibility; it marks a transformational step
in our mission to extend the Masonic values of beauty, truth, and craftsmanship
to the broader public.
Planning is now underway to establish a dedicated Emile Norman gallery
within the building. This will feature rotating displays, archival interpretation,
and public programming that will invite new audiences—particularly artists,
historians, students, and cultural tourists—to experience the building in a
new light. We envision the gallery as a dynamic bridge between Freemasonry’s
architectural legacy and San Francisco’s vibrant creative community.
By positioning the temple as a steward of California’s artistic heritage, we
are increasing its visibility and relevance beyond the fraternity. This partnership
not only enhances the public profile of the CMMT; it also reinforces its value
as a destination where art, architecture, and fraternity intersect.
The Emile Norman Arts Foundation has expressed enthusiastic support
for this collaboration, and we are grateful to the CMMT board members and
foundation leaders who have championed this vision. Together, we are shaping
a future where the CMMT is known not only for its Masonic significance, but
also as a premier cultural and educational destination in San Francisco.

Building Improvements
The CMMT continues to make significant progress on its 2030 capital plan, with
several high-impact projects advancing on time and on budget:
HVAC and Building Management System: Completed in June 2025. The
upgraded system provides improved control, energy efficiency, and cost
savings, particularly in the auditorium and exhibition hall.
Building Envelope and Façade Rehabilitation: Now 50 percent complete,
this project addresses marble restoration, stairwell repair, and lighting
improvements. Work is expected to conclude by February 2026.
Elevator Modernization: The west elevator repairs are scheduled for
completion in August 2025, with remaining elevators to follow. Full
modernization is projected by April 2026.
Terrazzo and Marble Restoration: Contracts totaling $869,000 have been
awarded for the repair and cleaning of the terrazzo flooring and marble
surfaces. Work will begin after Annual Communication.All projects are
fully funded through operations, with the Montgomery Corporation
overseeing implementation and daily facilities management.

Neighborhood Relations
The CMMT remains committed to being a responsible, visible, and valued presence on Nob Hill. The board of the temple, as one of the area’s most prominent
institutions, recognizes the importance of building trust and shared purpose
with our neighbors.
Our collaboration with the Nob Hill Liaison Group remains strong. We’ve
received no formal complaints about CMMT operations and have been recognized for our responsiveness and proactive engagement. We’ve also coordinated
with the city and other Nob Hill institutions to address unpermitted vending,
ensuring a safe and orderly public environment around the temple.
The CMMT, along with other local stakeholders, has also supported popular
neighborhood events in adjacent Huntington Park, including Movie Night in
the Park, the holiday tree-lighting celebration, and Rosé in the Park, which drew
more than 250 attendees. These programs reinforce the CMMT’s role as not
just a venue, but a neighbor, partner, and contributor to the vitality of Nob Hill.
Looking ahead, we remain focused on strengthening these relationships
through transparency, outreach, and shared investment in the success of the

Nob Hill Masonic Center
The Nob Hill Masonic Center is one of five business entities of the Grand
Lodge of California and the sole for-profit corporation among them. Profits generated through its management of the 565-stall parking garage at the California
Masonic Memorial Temple and the smaller garage across California Street at
Grace Cathedral are distributed as an annual dividend to the Grand Lodge,
thereby supporting the fraternity’s central operations and charitable initiatives. Further, rental fees paid by NHMC to the California Masonic Memorial
Temple help fund the philanthropic work of the California Masonic Foundation.
Therefore, the success of the NHMC benefits the entire organization and helps
expand the reach and impact of our collective efforts.
2025 Summary
Overall financial performance has picked up following a slow beginning to the
fiscal year, which was largely attributable to fewer events hosted by Live Nation
at the California Masonic Memorial Temple auditorium. This was largely made
up for through increases in monthly parking revenue, a bump in daily parking,
and a savings compared with projected expenses. Net income for the fiscal
year will allow NHMC to meet its projected dividend outlined in the Grand
Lodge budget.
Event Parking
As of August 29, Live Nation, which manages performances at the California
Masonic Memorial Auditorium, had scheduled 77 ticketed events for the fiscal
year, compared with 102 at the same time last year. As a result, event-parking
revenue, which emerged in 2024 as the strongest component of NHMC operations, was down compared with projections.
Monthly Parking
Partially offsetting the drops in event parking, monthly parking has improved
in FY2025, posting consecutive growth throughout the first three quarters. Q3

230

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

represented the strongest monthly parking performance in two years.
Daily Parking
Daily parking receipts continue to lag behind pre-pandemic figures: FY2024
ended at 63 percent of the total for FY2019, and so far, daily parking revenue is
still 16 percent below prepandemic levels. That said, daily parking is up markedly compared with FY2024 (including a 29 percent increase in Q1), and with
Grace Cathedral adding programming, daily parking appears to be stabilizing.
Grace Cathedral Parking
Figures were strong at Grace Cathedral, which NHMC began operating in
2023. Gross revenue is up compared with FY2024, while labor changes from
our vendor, SP+, have resulted in significant savings, as has a renegotiated lease
agreement with Grace.
Garage Enhancements
The revamp of exterior signage at the NHMC garage, intended to improve
traffic flow and increase awareness, is nearing completion. A prototype of the
lighted sign has been sent to the city for permitting review and the plan is now
with the city building department. In recent years, the board has also overseen
the installation of new license-plate recognition software and upgrades to the
parking-access and revenue-control systems, which the board is aiming to install
at Grace Cathedral in the near future. It also leased several parking spaces to
the EV-charging company Volta and continues to collaborate with Tesla to offer
EV charging and promote electric-vehicle use. Another project moving forward
is a plan to replace the garage’s fluorescent lighting, as the state of California
banned the sale of fluorescent light bulbs beginning Jan. 1, 2025.
Neighborhood Relations
Under the leadership of Grand Secretary Allan Casalou, the NHMC maintains a
strong presence within the Nob Hill Association and the Nob Hill Community
Liaison Group. These associations foster solidarity with neighboring businesses and residents and reflect our commitment to community engagement.
In 2024, Casalou concluded his two-year term as president of the Nob Hill
Association, though he remains on the board. Khalil Sweidy is still treasurer
of the association.
Looking forward, the board is optimistic that with improved business
recovery for San Francisco generally, the NHMC will continue to provide a
solid foundation on which our many other entities can build. The board extends
its thanks to Grand Master Arthur L. Salazar Jr. and the executive committee
for their support, as well as Grand Secretary Allan Casalou and Grand Lodge

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

231

staff members including Carol Hunter, Andy Cameron, and Khalil Sweidy. All
of them have been instrumental in helping us develop and meet our financial
and business-development efforts.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE
ON FINANCE
Concerning the Cost Impact of Legislation
for the 176th Annual Communication

Most Worshipful,
In accordance with California Masonic Code §406.035, the Grand Lodge
Committee on Finance has reviewed the resolutions to be considered at the
176th Annual Communication and finds the following:
The committee has reviewed Grand Master Salazar’s Decisions Nos. 1 and
2, and Recommendations Nos. 1 through 5, and finds that this legislation will
not have a financial impact on the 2025–26 Grand Lodge budget as proposed.
The committee has also reviewed carry-over legislation from 2024 and finds
that none of this legislation will have a financial impact on the 2025–26 Grand
Lodge budget as proposed. It is well to note that should carry-over legislation
item 24-04 pass, any increases in application fees contemplated therein will be
reflected in the 2026–27 Grand Lodge budget, and may be used to offset some
part of future per capita increases. The 2025–26 Grand Lodge budget currently
forecasts the application fees contemplated in this legislation at the current
historical levels.
Finally, the committee has reviewed Resolution 25-02 and 25-04 and finds
that this legislation will not have a financial impact on the 2025–26 Grand Lodge
budget as proposed.
From time to time, legislation might propose changes to the ritual or the
monitor. It has been a practice of the Grand Lodge to make the printed changes
and produce new ciphers and monitors only after the current inventory has been
depleted. Therefore, there is no additional expense caused by the adoption of
such legislation.

The Masons of California’s corporate insurance program provides
coverage for lodges including historic lodges, hall associations, the Masonic
Homes, Acacia Creek, MCYAF, the California Masonic Memorial Temple
(CMMT), and Nob Hill Masonic Center. The program includes property, general liability, umbrella liability, earthquake, D&O, employment practices liability,
professional liability and crime insurance policies, all renewed April 1, 2025. The
committee has been working toward creating a captive program which will be
part of the 2026 report.
I would like to acknowledge the positive work on this committee by Mark
Stephens for his extra work in helping create the hall building inspection program.
We continue as we ended last year’s insurance program, with another
difficult renewal. The insurance marketplace has not changed much from the

challenge of capturing an ever-evolving marketplace.

Conclusions
Our property policy is more than 50 percent of our overall total property and
casualty insurance program cost. The committee, staff and our broker are exploring the option of forming a property captive program. The goal is to control
our property insurance costs and not be subject to primary market conditions
every year. We are hoping to provide a working program early in 2026. In the
meantime, the current insurance program is robust and meets our needs to the
best of our ability to identify exposures and meet them with insurance solutions

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California

David A. Forsyth, Chairman

Executve Summary
The investment committee is charged with the prudent management
of the Grand Lodge Investment Fund (GLIF) with priority given to income
generation, capital preservation, and asset growth. The committee has adopted
a long-term target return of 6.75 percent annually.
As of the ﬁscal year ending October 31, 2025, the GLIF stands at
approximately $1.103 billion, and withdrawals by the Masonic entities during
the trailing 12 months, as reported by the Grand Lodge’s CFO, were in the
amount of $59 million.
As of October 31, 2025, the GLIF delivered a trailing 12-months annualized
return of 12.6 percent compared to the allocation index’s return of 12.9 percent
over the same period and meaningfully above the 6.75 percent long-term target
return. The double-digit return was driven by the relatively high returns of
public equity and debt. Hedge funds provided volatility stabilization during
the ﬁscal year. The private allocation within the portfolio continues to be built
out and the committee anticipates a substantial contribution to the overall
performance in the upcoming years. Absent any major shifts, the committee
continues to believe that the current long-term investment strategy has served
the portfolio well in the past and should continue to do so. In that eﬀort, the
committee and NEPC actively modiﬁed the lineup of investment managers in
the past 12 months.
Purpose
The investment committee is charged with the prudent management of GLIF.
The pool of assets invested is composed of the general and endowment funds
for the Masonic Home of California, investment funds of the California Masonic
Foundation, California Masonic Memorial Temple, and the Grand Lodge of

244

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

California. The Investment Committee’s responsibilities and activities are
governed by the CMC sections 406.045, 407.040 B and D, and the approved
Investment Policy Statement (IPS).

Investment Selection & Monitoring

Investment Objectives
The primary objectives of the Investment Committee are inculcated in the
language of the IPS: The primary objective of the funds is to provide a regular
and reliable source of ﬁnancial support to the Masonic entities or its beneﬁciaries, while preserving the purchasing power of the funds after reasonable
withdrawals are taken.
Simply put, the investment objectives that the committee is engaged in are
income generation, capital preservation, and asset growth. With that in mind,
the committee has adopted a long-term target return of 6.75 percent annualized. The 6.75 percent in total goal is comprised of 4.75 percent spending draw
and 2 percent growth (the growth component is intended for preservation of
purchase power).
Distributions
Distributions to the Masonic entities during the trailing 12 months, as reported
by the Grand Lodge’s CFO, were in the amount of $59 million. This represents
a distribution of 5.78 percent of Investment Fund balance as of the end of
Fiscal Year 2024, and 6.17 percent of the average Investment Fund balance of
the three prior ﬁscal years.

The committee is comprised of diligent ﬁnancial professionals who are astute
in portfolio construction and global economics. NEPC, LLC., serves as the
committee’s investment consultant, which provides services in the areas of
identifying investment managers, due diligence, and modeling/evaluations.
The investment committee, with the assistance of NEPC, regularly identiﬁes
and selects investment managers that have a higher probability of providing
incremental beneﬁt to the overall fund’s performance. This is accomplished
through global economic and markets analysis to identify appropriate asset
classes and allocation. Once the allocation is determined, individual managers
are selected utilizing data, research, and due diligence services provided by
NEPC. Once managers have been thoroughly vetted and consistently monitored,
if the manager’s investment style is still part of the committee’s investment
thesis, it is relatively rare that a manager get terminated, unless the committee
has adjusted the positioning of the portfolio. This philosophy is founded in the
committee’s adopted IPS, which states:
“We believe that manager turnover is very expensive and extremely
disruptive to the eﬃciency and productive operation of an investment
program. Mangers should be hired with a long-run view… We also
believe that constant and/or rapid turnover of mangers, justiﬁed solely
on the basis of relative underperformance is usually an indication of a
lack of adherence to the selection and retention process. In particular,
short-term (generally less than one year) underperformance should not
be a reason for termination, unless it is accompanied by other adverse
key retention characteristics.”
In monitoring the portfolio, the committee receives monthly performance
reports and meets quarterly. Quarterly meetings, aside from discussing outstanding business or tactical decisions, regularly involve meetings with one
or two individual investment managers, review quarterly due diligence and
performance reports from NEPC. This allows the committee to monitor the
respective performance of the managers compared to various indices representing their objective. This process provides the committee with the necessary data
to evaluate each investment manager on a timely basis, and to observe whether
they continue to achieve the objectives of their mandate.

Performance
As of October 31, 2025, GLIF delivered a trailing 12-months annualized return

period. For the ﬁve-year period ending October 31, 2025, GLIF returned an

9.3 percent. The one- and ﬁve-year return numbers encompasses a period of
meaningful volatility stemming from what has been labeled by some as the
AI bubble, global trade friction, uncertainty surrounding monetary policy—
central banks’ interest rates decisions and changing ﬁscal policy—and federal
government spending. Looking forward into 2026, it is expected that inﬂation
remains stubbornly above the target rate of 2 percent, uncertainty relating to
the federal reserve’s interest rate decisions will continue, concerns regarding
the equities market’s frothy evaluations will fuel volatility, and the midterm
elections will create further uncertainties as it relates to global trade policies. it
is appropriate that these factors should be viewed with a level of consciousness
by the investment community.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE
ON JURISPRUDENCE

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California,
The Committee on Jurisprudence serves as the legal adviser to the grand
master and the legal adviser to the Grand Lodge when in session. The committee
reviews proposed resolutions and recommendations to be considered at the
next Annual Communication and prepares any necessary legislation to carry
out the intent of the proponents. At the Annual Communication, it comments
on the legality of the grand master’s decisions and dispensations and on the
legal effect of the proposed recommendations and resolutions. After the Annual
Communication, it prepares the changes to the California Masonic Code to reflect
the legislation which was adopted.
In the committee’s view, those of Grand Master Salazar’s decisions and
dispensations coming to its attention were legal and within his discretion.
The committee will separately report on Grand Master Salazar’s Decision
No. 1. In the committee’s view, the legislation posted by the grand secretary
to the Grand Lodge website on August 25 of this year is sufficient to carry out
the intent of the proponents, and the legislation contained in Grand Master
Salazar’s recommendations which he will present in his message are sufficient
to carry out his intent. We believe that each piece of this legislation has the
legal effect set forth in it.
In presenting the legislation for your consideration, we make no recommendations as to the action to be taken with it. While the committee has written the
title and introductory explanation for each resolution before you and assisted
the proponents in drafting the Code changes required to effect their intent, the
proponents’ arguments in their whereas clauses are their own. The committee
does not assist in drafting the whereas clauses and makes no comments on them.
The legislation posted by the grand secretary to the Grand Lodge website
on August 25 of this year and the legislation contained in Grand Master Salazar’s
recommendations require no separate motion because they are automatically
before this Annual Communication. The presiding officer will announce the vote
required for the passage of each item before discussion begins. Any legislation
which does not amend the California Masonic Code or the ritual requires a simple
majority only for adoption. Any amendment to the California Masonic Code or

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

249

the ritual must be adopted by a five-sixths affirmative vote. If the amendment
receives a simple majority but less than a five-sixths affirmative vote, it carries
over to the next Annual Communication when only a two-thirds affirmative
vote is required for adoption.
In addition to the foregoing responsibilities, the committee reviews all
charges and specifications of unmasonic conduct, strikes out those portions
which are not supported by a clear and precise specification of unmasonic conduct and revises those portions which are incorrect, ambiguous, or insufficient.
The committee may dismiss charges if all the facts set forth in the specifications,
even if true, would not warrant a verdict of unmasonic conduct. As part of its
review, the committee provides the parties with every essential factual element
which must be proven at trial for the accused to be found guilty of each charge.
Since the last Annual Communication, the committee commented on 15 sets
of charges and specifications.
If a Mason under the disciplinary jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge has
pleaded guilty or nolo contendere (or no contest) to, or has been convicted
of, a crime of moral turpitude by a federal or state court, he shall be deemed
automatically expelled from all the rights and privileges of Masonry without
any further action of his lodge or the Grand Lodge. The committee reviews a
certified copy of the record of conviction to determine whether there has been
an automatic expulsion. Since the last Annual Communication, the committee
has reviewed four federal or state court records to evaluate whether there has
been an automatic expulsion of the Mason involved in the proceeding. These
matters are summarized in the attached exhibit.
No person shall hold or be eligible for membership in any constituent lodge
who has pleaded guilty or nolo contendere to, or has been convicted of, a crime
involving a violation of the moral law unless, for the reason that he did not
commit the offense, he either has been pardoned or had his judgment of conviction vacated or reversed. All applicants are subject to background checks to
determine compliance with this rule. The grand secretary reviews all background
checks received and evaluates whether an applicant is ineligibility for the degrees
because of a federal or state court record disclosed in his background check.
The committee assists in this process as requested. The committee provides
the grand secretary assistance in reviewing any federal or state court records
to evaluate whether an applicant is eligible for the degrees.
We thank the grand master for the opportunity which he has given us to
serve this year.
Respectfully submitted,
David M. Ferreria, Chair
David L. Brandon, Vice Chair

EXHIBIT
Automatic Expulsions
October 26, 2024 to October 26, 2025
Case No. 3086 (Carlson)
In Case No. 3086, the member pled no contest to violations of California Penal
Code Sections 313.1 and 664 (the “crime”). Cal. Pen. Code Section 313.1 provides
that “[e]very person who, with knowledge that a person is a minor, or who fails
to exercise reasonable care in ascertaining the true age of a minor, knowingly
sells, rents, distributes, sends, causes to be sent, exhibits, or offers to distribute
or exhibit by any means… any harmful matter to the minor shall be punished
as specified in Section 313.4.” “Harmful matter” is defined under Cal. Pen. Code
Section 313 as “matter, taken as a whole, which to the average person, applying
contemporary statewide standards, appeals to the prurient interest, and is
matter which, taken as a whole, depicts or describes in a patently offensive
way sexual conduct and which, taken as a whole, lacks serious literary, artistic,
political, or scientific value for minors.” Cal. Pen. Code Section 664 provides that
“[e]very person who attempts to commit any crime, but fails, or is prevented or
intercepted in its perpetration, shall be punished where no provision is made
by law for the punishment of those attempts.”
Under Section 100.075 of the California Masonic Code and 2009 Grand
Master’s Decision No. 2, lewdness involves moral turpitude. Under Section
100.075 of the California Masonic Code and 2009 Grand Master’s Decision No.
2, an attempt to commit an act involving lewdness also involves moral turpitude. In the committee’s opinion, the conduct described in California Penal
Code Section 313.1 and 664 involves lewdness and an attempt to commit an act
involving lewdness. Therefore, based on the court record and the foregoing
analysis, it is the judgment of a majority of the members of the Committee on
Jurisprudence that the member pled no contest to a crime of moral turpitude
before a federal/state court. Accordingly, the member was automatically expelled
from all the rights and privileges of Masonry pursuant to Section 1404.820 of
the California Masonic Code. His expulsion from Masonry was effective on July
16, 2024, the date he entered his plea of no contest.

252

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

Trial No. 3097 (Carter)
In Trial No. 3097, the member pled guilty to a violation of California Penal
Code Section 647(A) (the “crime”). This section provides that “every person
who commits any of the following acts is guilty of… a misdemeanor… (A) An
individual who solicits anyone to engage in or who engages in lewd or dissolute
conduct in a public place or in a place open to the public or exposed to public
view.” Under Section 100.075 of the California Masonic Code and 2009 Grand
Master’s Decision No. 2, lewdness involves moral turpitude. In the committee’s
opinion, the conduct described in California Penal Code Section 647(A) involves
lewdness. Therefore, based on the court records and the foregoing analysis, it is
the judgment of a majority of the members of the Committee on Jurisprudence
that the member pled guilty to a crime of moral turpitude before a state court.
Accordingly, the member was automatically expelled from all the rights and
privileges of Masonry pursuant to Section 1404.820 of the California Masonic
Code. His expulsion from Masonry was effective on June 21, 2004, the date he
entered his plea of guilty.
Trial No. 3096 (Hardberger)
In Trial No. 3096, the member pled guilty to a violation of California Penal Code
Section 452(c) (the “crime”). This section provides that “[a] person is guilty
of unlawfully causing a fire when they recklessly set fire to, burn, or cause to
be burned any structure, forest land, or property… causing a fire of a structure
or forest land is a felony punishable by imprisonment in the state prison for 16
months, two or three years, or by imprisonment in the county jail for not more
than six months, or by a fine, or by both such imprisonment and fine.” Under
Section 100.075 of the California Masonic Code and 2009 Grand Master’s Decision
No. 2, arson involves moral turpitude. In the committee’s opinion, the conduct
described in California Penal Code Section 452(c) involves arson. Therefore,
based on the court record and the foregoing analysis, it is the judgment of a
majority of the members of the Committee on Jurisprudence that the member
pled guilty to a crime of moral turpitude before a state court. Accordingly, the
member was automatically expelled from all the rights and privileges of Masonry
pursuant to Section 1404.820 of the California Masonic Code.
His expulsion from Masonry was effective on September 17, 2020, the date
he entered his plea of guilty.
Trial No. 3095 (McKinney)
In Trial No. 3095, the member pled guilty/no contest to a violation of California
Penal Code Section 245(a)(1) (the “crime”). This section provides that “[A]
ny person who commits an assault upon the person of another with a deadly
weapon or instrument other than a firearm shall be punished by imprisonment in the state prison for two, three, or four years, or in a county jail for not
exceeding one year, or by a fine not exceeding ten thousand dollars ($10,000),

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

253

or by both the fine and imprisonment.” Under Section 100.075 of the California
Masonic Code and 2009 Grand Master’s Decision No. 2, assault with a dangerous
or deadly weapon involves moral turpitude. In the committee’s opinion, the
conduct described in California Penal Code Section 245(a)(1)) involves assault
with a dangerous or deadly weapon. Therefore, based on the court record and
the foregoing analysis, it is the judgment of a majority of the members of the
Committee on Jurisprudence that the member pled guilty/no contest to a
crime of moral turpitude before a state court. Accordingly, the member was
automatically expelled from all the rights and privileges of Masonry pursuant
to Section 1404.820 of the California Masonic Code.
His expulsion from Masonry was effective on August 26, 2024, the date he
entered his plea of guilty/no contest.
Report of the Committee on Jurisprudence
on Grand Master Salazar’s Decision No. 1
In Decision No. 1, the Grand Master answers the question, What are the secrets
of Freemasonry, the disclosure of which in any form not approved by Grand
Lodge would constitute a violation of our obligation as an Entered Apprentice
Mason and therefore unmasonic conduct under Section 1401.010.G.7 of the code?
In much of the English-speaking Masonic world outside of the United
States, this question was answered many decades ago. For many, the secrets of
Freemasonry are limited to the modes of recognition which our grand master has
decided are the due guards, signs, words, grips, tokens, steps, and the points of
fellowship in our California ritual. We believe that the grand master’s decision
is consistent with the Emulation Ritual of the United Grand Lodge of England
and other rituals known to us in the English-speaking Masonic world outside
of the United States.
This issue was actually addressed, although not then clearly reported, when
in 1990 Grand Lodge approved use of and Grand Lodge began to sell what we
now know as the California cipher. At that time, the Grand Lodge Committee
on Policy and General Purposes recommended a “NO” vote on the adoption
of the California cipher. It reported that some might see its use as a violation
of their obligation. We can assume that Grand Lodge would never order us
to do anything which is unlawful. Therefore, we can conclude that use of the
California cipher does not violate our obligation. We note that the only part of
our ritual in the California cipher not written in plain English or in cipher are
the modes of recognition. Therefore, by adoption of the California cipher in
1990, Grand Lodge effectively limited the secrets of Freemasonry to the modes
of recognition which in our California ritual are the due guards, signs, words,
grips, tokens, steps and the points of fellowship. Grand Master Salazar’s Decision
No. 1 simply confirms an action we have already taken.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE
ON LEGISLATIVE ANALYSIS
Grand Master’s Decisions
Decision No. 1
By his Grand Master’s Decision No. 1, Most Worshipful Arthur L. Salazar
Jr. clarifies the definition of the phrase “esoteric or secret portion” of the ritual.
His decision is consistent with Masonic law.
During debate regarding Grand Master Metroka’s Recommendation No. 7 at
our last Annual Communication, it became apparent that there was confusion
as to what, exactly, the “esoteric or secret” portion of the ritual is. When it was
not adopted, a definition was needed, and this decision provides that definition.
In 1988, the Grand Lodge adopted a resolution permitting the use of a
cipher, which, by its nature, is intended to make the contents thereof legible
or intelligible to its users. As such, that which is enciphered is, by definition,
not “secret,” being legible and intelligible to Masons who fall within the phrase
“any person under the canopy of heaven.” Notably, the signs, words, and modes
of recognition are not set forth either plainly or in cipher, as they are secrets.
All acts or actions that are in material breach of Masonic obligations remain
unmasonic conduct under Section 1401.010(G)(7) of the California Masonic
Code. This decision applies only to the meaning of the phrase “esoteric or secret
parts” of the ritual.
Most Worshipful Salazar’s decision acknowledges these facts and, for the
first time, provides a bright line definition of the phrase “esoteric or secret
portion” of the ritual, and resolving once and for all the question of what,
exactly, it means.
Decision No. 2
This decision would clarify that it is permissible for a lodge to install officers
who are not named in our ritual, but are “deemed proper by the lodge,” as
codified in California Masonic Code Section 805.010. Section 805.510 requires
that “Lodge officers shall be installed using the Installation Ceremony for
Constituent Lodges.” The question has arisen as how to install officers who
are locally created at individual lodges while maintaining harmony with the

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

text of the Installation Ceremony.
This decision does not decide the verbiage of how to install such other officers
“deemed proper by the lodge,” when in the ceremony to install such officers, or
provide any verbiage for the installation of such other officers. This decision does
not create a blanket requirement to install such other officers. The decision only
clarifies that the installing officer shall satisfy himself that that the Installation
Ceremony is followed as closely as reasonably practicable and in the spirit of the
Installation Ceremony when installing the officers who are “deemed proper.”

Grand Master’s Recommendations
Recommendation No. 1
The California Masonic Code Section 406.000 entitled “Committee Membership”
states in part that at least 70 percent of the total number of members on each
committee shall be members of the Grand Lodge. Members of the Grand Lodge
have been defined to include past elected grand officers, masters, wardens, and
past masters of constituent lodges.
This section also limits the term of committee members to nine consecutive
years, and committee chairs to five consecutive years. This recommendation
will exempt the Finance Committee and the Insurance Committee from those
term limits.
The provisions of this section do not apply to the Audit Committee, the
Committee on the California Freemason, the Compensation Committee, the
Executive Committee, or the Committee on Ritual.
Grand Master Salazar’s Recommendation No. 1 would add the Investment
Committee to the list of exempt committees listed in CMC Section 406.000
based on his finding that this committee requires the expertise of those who
may not be members of the Grand Lodge, but who have expertise in financial
and investment matters.
This recommendation would also amend the CMC Section 406.020 regarding the Committee on the California Freemason to remove the portion of this
code that limits the editor-in-chief or associate editor to a nine-year consecutive
term. Grand Master Salazar’s recommendation points out that in the last 70
years, there have only been four editors-in-chief.
Finally, this recommendation would remove CMC Section 406.035.(a)
regarding the Finance Committee. Subsection (a) authorizes in part the
Financial Committee to administer all retirement plans on behalf of the Grand
Lodge of California. It is a fact that this section is now obsolete as the Grand
Lodge no longer administers any retirement plans. A 401k plan is administered
by a third party.
It is up to this voting body to accept or reject these proposed changes to
our Masonic code.

This recommendation seeks to amend the California Masonic Code to eliminate
