Recommendation No. 3
This recommendation would modify the California Masonic Code to create a
centralized system to notify members of their possible suspension for non-payment of dues. In doing so, it would also modify several rules pertaining to the
suspension of Masons for non-payment of dues.
Lodge secretaries would no longer be required to send suspension notices to
a Mason via certified mail. Instead, a secretary would send a notice to the grand
secretary of the lodge’s intent to suspend a Mason using a method prescribed
by the grand secretary. The grand secretary would then make good faith efforts
to contact the Mason using the information sources reasonably available to
Grand Lodge. The grand secretary would be required to inform the lodge of the
results of such efforts. If the Mason does not pay his dues within 60 days after
the secretary sends the notice to the grand secretary, then the Mason may be
declared suspended by the master. This recommendation does not require that
the Mason be suspended after the 60-day period expires. However, if the lodge
does not suspend the Mason within six months after having sent is notice to
the grand secretary, then the lodge is not permitted to suspend the Mason until
its secretary sends another notice to the grand secretary and another 60-day
period (during which the grand secretary would again attempt to contact the
Mason) has passed. This notice procedure would continue until the Mason is
actually declared suspended by the master in accordance with the new rules.
This procedure would be applicable to Masons who belong to multiple lodges
as well as Masons who belong to only one lodge.
While these rules would limit when a Mason may be declared suspended,
they would potentially afford multiple opportunities for a Mason to be contacted
regarding his possible suspension and for a Mason to be suspended only within
a reasonable time frame following the most recent attempts to contact him.
This recommendation would also give each lodge the option to authorize
the grand secretary to remit the dues of its Masons on the lodge’s behalf. A
lodge would only be able to do so by passing a revocable standing resolution
granting such authority to the grand secretary.

Recommendation No. 4
This recommendation proposes to modernize the duties of the lodge secretary
as defined in the California Masonic Code Section 805.230.
Over time, lodge administrative practices have evolved to incorporate
technological advancements, improve communication tools, and provide more
efficient methods of record-keeping. To ensure that the CMC remains accurate,
practical, and reflective of current operations, it is necessary to revise sections
that no longer align with how lodges function today.
The position of lodge secretary remains one of the most vital offices within
the lodge, serving as the administrative cornerstone for its governance, communication, and historical continuity. The lodge secretary responsible for maintaining accurate records, managing correspondence, and ensuring compliance
with the reporting and procedural requirements of the Grand Lodge.
However, while the core responsibilities of the secretary have not changed,
the tools and processes by which those duties are carried out have transformed
significantly.
Most lodges now use digital systems to manage membership records, track
finances, submit reports, and communicate with both lodge members and the
Grand Lodge. Traditional practices such as handwritten minute books, manual
ledgers, and physical deposit slips are increasingly obsolete. Yet, portions of
the CMC continue to reference these outdated methods, creating unnecessary
confusion and administrative inefficiencies for lodge secretaries.
This recommendation updates the language of Section 805.230 to remove
obsolete and overly prescriptive requirements, replacing them with flexible,
technology-neutral language. The revised section preserves the intent and
accountability of the secretary’s office—ensuring that critical responsibilities
such as accurate record-keeping, timely reporting, and coordination with the
grand secretary remain firmly in place—while allowing each lodge to employ
current and future technologies to fulfill those duties.
Adopting this change will:
1.

Align the CMC with contemporary administrative practices used by
lodges across California.

2.

Provide greater clarity and consistency for current and future lodge
secretaries.

3.

Reduce administrative burdens caused by outdated procedural
requirements.

4.

Ensure the CMC remains adaptable to future technological
advancements.

261

Recommendation No. 5
The Grand Master’s recommendation No. 5 will modify the California Masonic
Code to allow for the withdrawal of properly filed Masonic charges before a
trial master is appointed and to expand the ability of a trial master to allow the
withdrawal of charges once he is appointed.
Currently, the CMC does not allow properly filed charges to be withdrawn
until a trial master is appointed, reviews the charges, and then, only if he finds no evidence
in the specifications that could warrant a finding of guilt, can he allow the charges to be
withdrawn. The CMC restricts the withdrawal of properly filed charges to ensure
that Masonic misconduct is not ignored because of undue influence such as
threats, intimidation, social pressure, or the standing of the accused. Our fraternity’s high moral values demand that members conduct themselves with do
order and propriety. If any member is guilty of Masonic misconduct, they need
to be held accountable. Failing to hold a member accountable for unmasonic
conduct is a violation of our Masonic values and diminishes what it means to
be a California Freemason.
The Grand Master’s recommendation acknowledges the need to protect the
integrity of our Masonic justice system. The proposed addition of a petition to
the grand master to withdraw charges by the accuser and the additional latitude
of a trial master to do the same, requires a written justification that is consistent
with our Masonic values and standards. Both processes are subject to the review
and approval of the Grand Lodge at the next Annual Communication. Grand
Lodge, by a vote in open session, can overturn the withdrawal of charges, just like
it can overturn the verdicts of all trials. If Grand Lodge overturns a withdrawal
of charges, then a trial master will be appointed, and charges will go forward to
trial as prescribed in the CMC as if the charges had not been withdrawn.
This recommendation creates two opportunities to allow Masonic charges
to be withdrawn that do not exist today. It provides for oversight of those
decisions and gives the voting members of Grand Lodge the final say in the
process. It is up to you to decide if this addition to our Masonic justice system
is warranted.
If this recommendation is adopted, it will take effect at the close of the
Annual Communication in which is approved.

CARRYOVER LEGISLATION
Carryover Recommendation No. 4
This recommendation would modify the California Masonic Code to allow for
budget-based modifications to the fees constituent lodges pay per application,
the amounts each candidate must donate to Masonic causes and charities, and
adds the California Masonic Foundation as one of the charities.
Since the formation of Grand Lodge, every lodge has paid a fee to Grand
Lodge for each member. The method of determining the fee and the amount
has changed over the years. Currently, CMC Section 407.030 sets the fee at
$30 per new candidate. Since the amount is specified in the CMC it can only be
changed by modifying the code, which requires a 5/6 vote.
Since the inception of the Masonic Homes, we have collected donations
from each applicant. The amount has been set at $25 for more than a hundred
years without change. In today’s dollars that would be approximately $460.
When the membership decided to build this beautiful California Memorial
Masonic Temple in memory of our brothers who served and lost their lives in the
defense of our nation, donations were collected from every member and from
each applicant. The fee for applicants is set at $9 and has not changed in more
than 70 years. In today’s dollars that would be approximately $98. When the
George Washington Memorial was proposed, our grand lodge voted to support it
and a donation to it by each candidate was added to the CMC, which is currently
set at $15. All three of these amounts are specified in the CMC, therefore each
of them can only be changed by modifying the code, which requires a 5/6 vote.
When the California Masonic Foundation was formed in 1969, it was funded
by the sale of the Masonic clubhouses on two University of California campuses. There was no assessment of members nor was the code modified to
add a donation from each new candidate. Grand Master Metroka asserts that
the outstanding work of the Foundation in our various communities should
be included in the charitable contributions of our applicants. Therefore, he
proposes to amend the code to include a contribution from each applicant for
the foundation, the amount to be determined during the preparation of the
Grand Lodge budget.
Grand Master Metroka’s recommendation will remove the specific dollar
amount of the application fee, donations to the Masonic causes and charities,
and replace it with the following language: “The contribution amount shall be
established from time to time with the adoption of the Grand Lodge budget.”

This is the same process used to establish the fee for background checks on

The current contributions to the Masonic Homes, California Masonic

Carryover Recommendation No. 6
This recommendation would change the voting threshold required for a lodge to
restore a Mason who is not eligible for automatic restoration for non-payment
of dues from a two-thirds vote to a simple majority vote. This recommendation
does not change any other rule applicable to such a restoration. A supermajority threshold for a vote, such as the current two-thirds threshold, can serve to
ensure there is broad consensus for the matter subject to the vote. However, a
simple majority threshold for a vote can prevent a minority group from gaining
a de facto veto power; and as noted by the Grand Master Metroka, a simple
majority vote is the threshold used for deciding most lodge matters.
It is up this Grand Lodge to decide whether reducing this voting threshold
for restoration from a 2/3 supermajority vote to a simple majority will benefit
our lodges and their members.
Carryover Recommendation No. 8
This recommendation would provide guidelines for the grand master and grand
lecturer to use in the exercise of their discretion in authorizing constituent
lodges to use alternative ritual.
It is well settled that the grand lecturer is the custodian of our ritual and
that the grand master is not only our presiding officer but also the guardian of
our Masonic tradition, culture, and ritual. The grand master, and only the grand
master, is charged with the interpretation of our Masonic law.
The grand master and grand lecturer already have the authority, under
California Masonic Code Section 402.010, to authorize any constituent lodge to
utilize an alternative ritual, such as La Parfaite Union No. 17, which has practiced a version of the Scottish Rite ritual since the 1850s, and La France Lodge
No. 885, which was granted authority to perform a version of the Scottish Rite
ritual in 2023.

264

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

This recommendation seeks to provide clarity and guidance for the benefit
of our Grand Lodge leadership as to the criteria they should consider when
determining whether to exercise that authority in a given instance, as follows:
(1) the alternative ritual includes the same obligations contained in the ritual
adopted by Grand Lodge; (2) that the alternative ritual includes the same signs,
words, and modes of recognition contained in our ritual; and (3) that the alternative ritual is “consistent with the culture, integrity and ideals of our fraternity.”
This recommendation would not enhance or increase the ability of the
grand master and grand lecturer to approve the use of alternative ritual beyond
the authority already granted to them in our code. Rather, the recommendation
proposes that this authority be tempered and shaped, and provides context
for consideration of when and how best to exercise their existing authority. It
provides for standards and principles to be included in CMC Section 402.010
instead of relying on the existing ambiguous language.
This recommendation does not require them to approve a lodge’s request
simply because the alternative ritual contains the same obligations, signs,
words, and modes of recognition in our ritual. Rather, it requires the additional
condition that the alternative ritual is consistent with the “culture, integrity,
and ideals of our fraternity.”
It is for this grand lodge to decide whether the recommendation to establish standards and principles and to provide clarity would be a benefit to our
Fraternity by giving the grand master and grand lecturer guidelines by which
they may better exercise their existing authority.

Carryover Recommendation No. 11
This recommendation will modify the California Masonic Code to allow a brother
to be secretary in more than one of the lodges of which he is a member. Currently,
CMC Section 805.010 only allows a master, a senior warden, a junior warden,
and a secretary to hold one of those offices in only one lodge.
It has a been a long-standing practice of the Grand Lodge of California to
prohibit a member from being a master, warden or secretary in more than one
lodge to prevent a potential conflict of interest and to maintain the autonomy
of each individual lodge. In 2009, Resolution 09-07 proposed to make the same
change and was not adopted.
In 2023, Resolution 23-02 was proposed to allow a secretary to hold the
office in more than one lodge with no change to the prohibition of the master
and wardens also serving as a secretary in another lodge. This resolution was
not adopted.
The CMC provides for an assistant secretary to assist the secretary and/or
to teach a brother how to perform the duties of a secretary. The CMC allows a
secretary to be an assistant secretary in another lodge if they are a member of
it. This allows a brother to be trained by an experienced secretary when one is
not available to serve in that lodge.

Carryover Resolution 24-01
This resolution would amend the California Masonic Code sections 805.520,
805.530, and 805.540 to make the receipt of a certificate of proficiency in the
candidate’s lecture of the Master Mason degree a prerequisite to nomination
for the offices of master, senior warden, and junior warden, and remove the
receipt of the certificate of proficiency as a condition to a pillar officer-elect’s
installation.
Adoption of this resolution would mandate that every Master Mason who
seeks a pillar office is proficient in the third degree candidates lecture prior to
nomination.
Lodges with large pools of ritualistic talent may not have difficulty meeting
the proposed requirement. Rural lodges with small memberships may have
difficulty meeting the proposed requirements.
The proponents point to this resolution raising the bar of leadership in a
lodge by requiring Master Masons in possession a certificate of proficiency in the
candidate’s lecture of the Master Mason degree be the only candidates eligible
for nomination. However, no research points to ritual ability and leadership
ability being the same thing. Strong administrative leaders with middling ritual
ability might be precluded in the short-term from advancement to pillar offices.
Adoption of this resolution may create a quandary for constituent lodges
in the short term. If a lodge has identified a brother for advancement in any
of the three offices heretofore listed who is not in possession of the certificate
of proficiency in the candidate’s lecture of the Master Mason degree, and was
planning on having that requirement completed after election but prior to installation, that brother would become ineligible for election at the CMC required
November election immediately following the Annual Communication at which
this resolution may be adopted. This could create a condition where a lodge
would then need to postpone election for that office or maintain a vacancy in
a pillar office until a qualified candidate presents himself.
It is up to the voting members of this grand lodge to determine whether
this change is a benefit, or a burden to our constituent lodges.

RESOLUTIONS FOR 2025
Resolution 25-02
This resolution seeks to amend the California Masonic Code to allow the Cicero
Research Lodge UD to hold a single stated meeting annually. Cicero Research
Lodge iscomprised of only Master Masons who have served as grand orator of
the Grand Lodge of California.
Part 8 of the CMC, Chapter 14, Paragraph K governs stated meeting frequency for research lodges: “Their stated meetings shall be held at least once
quarterly.”
The proponents seek to change the CMC to reflect Cicero Research Lodge’s
desire to hold only one stated meeting annually at a date, time and place selected

to attend their meeting.

Resolution 25-04
This resolution seeks to modify California Masonic Code to change the titles of
certain officers in the Grand Lodge and constituent lodges. The grand organist
and the assistant grand organist would be renamed the grand musician and
the assistant grand musician. In constituent lodges the organist would then
become the musician.
In Freemasonry, music is more than just decoration—it symbolizes harmony, balance, and the unity of creation. The organist’s role represents the
“harmony of the lodge,” mirroring the harmony that should exist among its
members. Just as the organ’s pipes produce different tones that blend beautifully, so too should Masons of differing backgrounds work together in unity.
The title reminds members that music and harmony are tools for moral and
spiritual refinement.
Learning to play the organ was once very common not only in Masonry
but also in religious services. The title “organist” is traditional and has been
kept in use even though learning or playing the organ is less common and has
become almost obsolete. Other musical instruments like the piano, keyboard,
guitar, violin, bagpipes, and even singing are more commonly learned and used.
The organist in a Masonic lodge provides music during meetings and ceremonies, setting the mood and supporting the dignity and harmony of the

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

267

proceedings. They play at openings and closings of the lodge, accompany processions, installations, and degree ceremonies and they provide music during
moments of reflection or prayer.
An organist is a very specific kind of musician whose primary role is to
play the organ. Musician is a broader term that can include anyone involved
in music-making or providing music—for example vocalists, those able to play
musical instruments, or even those skillful in creating music by any means
including electronically. In short, every organist is a musician but not every
musician is an organist.
This resolution only seeks to change the title of organist. It doesn’t preclude
a musician from playing an organ. It provides the lodge musician, no matter what
instrument he plays, the ability to provide music to accompany stated meetings, degrees, ceremonies and Masonic events. While it changes the tradition
of having an officer named grand organist or lodge organist, recent practices
promulgated by grand lecturers state that “any music available, whether it’s
playing the organ or not, is good.” It brings the title of the office in line with
actually what’s been practiced in individual constituent lodges. We have precedents set at the level of Grand Lodge where we have had music played during
processions and installations using other musical instruments like bagpipes and
even mariachi bands which use guitars, violins, trumpets, and other instruments.
This resolution does not change the language used in the Installation
Ceremonies or the officers’ jewels. If adopted, further action would be required
to align the Installation Ceremonies with the intent of this resolution. It focuses
on the representation or emblem of music and supports all our talented musical
brethren who are capable of sharing their gifts within their lodges.
It is up to the voting members of this grand lodge to determine whether
this change in name and title will help in maintaining a musical tradition within
our craft.

AS TO THE FIRST RESOLUTION,

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE
ON TRIAL REVIEW

Most Worshipful and brethren,
It has been an honor to serve once again as chairman of the Grand Lodge
Committee on Trial Review. I extend my sincere thanks to Vice Chairman
Geoff Holbrook and committee members Freddie Davis, Todd Williams, and
Charles Harris, for their dedicated service throughout the year. I would also
like to express appreciation to the trial masters, whose time and knowledge
of the California Masonic Code were essential to our work and review process.
Their service continues to support the fair and efficient resolution of Masonic
disputes brought before this committee.
The Committee on Trial Review ensures proper oversight of all Masonic
disciplinary matters referred to the Grand Lodge by the Committee on
Jurisprudence for adjudication. Our role is to ensure fair and impartial resolutions in accordance with the California Masonic Code.
We remind all Masons that charges of unmasonic conduct must meet the
threshold standard of proof, and each element of the specification of charges
must be proven by the preponderance of the evidence demonstrating that the
accused more likely than not committed the act or acts prescribed in the charges
in order to be found guilty. In many instances, early intervention or wise counsel
may resolve misunderstanding before charges are necessary. This report and
subsequent recommendations hereby made by this committee provides some
demonstration of how early intervention has shown to be beneficial to our craft
and the involved Masons.
During the 2024–2025 Masonic year, 12 cases of alleged unmasonic conduct
were assigned to trial masters whose decisions have been reviewed. Additionally,
two requests for restoration to good standing in California Freemasonry were
considered.
Our committee conducted a thorough analysis of the records for all completed cases and, with a majority recommendation from the committee, we
submit the following four resolutions for approval by this grand lodge. The first
resolution are three cases resolved through mediation or settlement agreements.
The second resolution ratifies six cases wherein the accused was found not
guilty. The third resolution ratifies three matters finding the accused guilty, and

We present the following three cases that were resolved through mediation,
settlement agreement, or otherwise dismissed by the appointed trial master:
• In Case No. 3013, the accused was charged with possession of prohibited plain-text esoteric Masonic materials. The inspector confiscated
the materials and filed charges against the accused. During the trial
process, the accused submitted letters citing a terminal cancer diagnosis, an inability to present a defense, expressed remorse, and requited
to demit from Freemasonry. The accuser, recognizing the accused’s
terminal medical circumstances and lack of intent to return to active
membership, petitioned the trial master to allow withdrawal of the
charges. The trial master accepted the accused’s request to withdrawal
the charges and dismissed the case without prejudice.
• In Case No. 2975, the accused was charged with repeated use of
defamatory or threatening language toward lodge members, including
the master, to which he pled not guilty. Following a pre-trial mediation
facilitated by the trial master, the parties reach a mutually agreeable
settlement, and the trial master dismissed the case.
• In Case No. 3012, the accused was charged with breach of fiduciary
duty and failure to use reasonable care related to financial discrepancies identified during a 2021 audit conducted following his term as
lodge master to which he pled not guilty. During pre-trial proceedings,
it became evident that key records and witness testimony from 2021
was no longer available or non-existent. Unable to meet the burden
of proof, the accusers consented to dismissal of the charges. The trial
master dismissed the case without prejudice, preserving the right to
refile should new evidence arise.
As to the first resolution and having completed our review of these matters,
the Committee on Trial Review therefore submits the following resolution:
“THAT, IN THE MATTERS OF CASE NUMBERS 3013, 2975, AND 3012,
PROCEDURES AND DECISIONS OF THE TRIAL MASTERS BE HEREBY
AFFIRMED AS PRESENTED.”
AS TO THE SECOND RESOLUTION,
We present the following six cases that resulted in the appointed trial master
finding the accused not guilty, and dismissing the charge, or charges, accordingly:
• In Case No. 3071, the accused was charged with fabrication of a lodge

270

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

dues card and for seeking a refund for dues not recorded as paid. The
accused plead not guilty, and a full trial was held. Upon the review of
witness testimony and evidence, the trial master concluded this was
more likely a result of poor record keeping by the lodge and found the
accused not guilty, dismissing the charges.
• In Case No. 3077, the accused was charged with breach of fiduciary
duties, engaging in related falsehoods, larceny, use of defamatory language, and injuring a brother in his good name while serving as junior
warden of his lodge. The alleged charges stemmed from allegations of
inappropriate management of the junior warden funds entrusted to his
care. The trial master properly served the accused and the accused failed
to initially respond or submit a plea within the required 30 days of the
trial master’s service of charges. The trial master therefore proceeded
with an investigation given the accused’s default. Upon later submission of justification for the accused’s default and delay in responding
to the trial master’s summons due to personal circumstances, the trial
master permitted the accused to present information to be considered
in rendering a decision. In assessing all of the evidence, the trial master
found the accuser had not met the burden of proof, found the accused
not guilty and dismissed the charges.
• In Case No. 3081, the accused was charged with engaging in falsehood
for allegedly misrepresenting himself as a licensed contractor and in
performing remodeling work for a hall association renovation project.
The accused pled not guilty and the matter proceeded to trial before a
trial master with commissioners. After reviewing evidence and hearing
testimony, the trial master and commissioners concluded the accused
had acted in good faith and the charges stemmed from budgetary misunderstandings, not intentional deception or acts of the accused. The
accused was found not guilty and the charges dismissed.
• In Case No. 3082, the accused was charged with hazing or the intentional infliction of physical or mental harm upon a candidate, bringing a firearm onto lodge property, and disobeying a master’s directive
to discontinue bringing the firearm. The firearms-related charge was
resolved through pre-trail settlement agreement wherein the accused
agreed to not bring firearms on lodge property and to demit from
the lodge. The remaining charges proceeded to trial. The trial master
determined that the physical contact during a degree was not intentional and did not rise to the level of unmasonic conduct based on
there being no injuries resulting, that the accuser himself admitted he
did not believe the acts to be intentional, and both parties admission
that the incident was a result of overzealousness during a degree ceremony. Subsequently, the trial master found that without evidence of
intent or injury, the accuser did not sufficiently prove facts showing it

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

271

was more likely than not that the accused committed the unmasonic
conduct. The trial master therefore found the accused not guilty and
dismissed the remaining charges.
• In Case No. 3063 and 3078, both cases involved related circumstances
of two accused Masons from the same lodge which were combined into
one trial presided over by a trial master and two commissioners. Both
of the accused, one while holding officer positions in the lodge (including master) and the other while holding positions on the hall association (including president), were accused of engaging in a course of
conduct that included reducing rent owed for a lodge-owned property
to below fair market value, failing to properly prepare or preserve meeting minutes, maintaining disorganized financial records, and authorizing payments without proper documentation. One of the two accused
was also charged with a third specification of making false statements
to secure a reduction in rent due to personal financial hardship.
Both pled not guilty, and the matter proceeded to trial. The trial master
and commissioners concluded that the accuser failed to meet the burden
of proof necessary to establish the elements outlined in the specifications and that the evidence presented was insufficient to substantiate the alleged misconduct. It was generally acknowledged that both
accused were involved in paying reduced rent, but they offered plausible explanations during testimony that was not effectively rebutted by
the accuser. Evidence presented concerning lodge and hall association
recordkeeping was inconclusive. The trial master noted that while it
is apparent the lodge and hall association are experiencing significant
issues, the trial did not yield sufficient evidence to support the allegations set forth in the specifications. Both accused Masons were found
not guilty, and the trial master dismissed the matter.
As to our second resolution and having completed our review of these
matters, the Committee on Trial Review therefore submits and moves for the
adoption of the following resolution:
“THAT, IN THE MATTERS OF CASE NUMBERS 3071, 3077, 3081, 3082,
3063, AND 3078, THE PROCEDURES, FINDINGS AND DECISIONS OF
THE TRIAL MASTERS, BE HEREBY AFFIRMED AS PRESENTED.”
AS TO THE THIRD RESOLUTION,
We present the following three cases that were investigated by or heard before
a trial master, finding the accused guilty, and setting a penalty accordingly:
• In Case No. 3056, the accused was charged with breach of fiduciary
duty, failure to exercise undivided loyalty, and embezzlement while

272

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

serving as treasurer of both the lodge and hall association related to
financial misconduct and approving improper below market lease
agreements. The accused also allegedly failed to maintain financial
records and authorized payments to personal accounts without substantiation and participated in conflict-of-interest transactions.
After being properly served, the accused failed to respond with a plea,
resulting in a default, and the trial master proceeded with an investigation. The investigation and related materials showed the accused
failed to develop proper financial reports, such as balance sheets,
budget reports, or keep accurate records of expenses to verify expenditures, and various other record keeping and transactional issues. The
charges also alleged the accused issued and endorsed checks directing
lodge funds to a personal account without substantiation for the transactions and breached his officer duties by entering into a conflict of
interest lodge transaction by permitting another brother to enter into
a similar arrangement to the determinant of the lodge.
After interviewing witnesses and reviewing evidence, the trial master
determined the accused was not guilty of embezzlement, but the trial
master found him guilty of his breach of fiduciary duty and failure to
exercise his duty of undivided loyalty. The trial master affixed the penalty of suspension for an indefinite period.
• In Case No. 3065, the accused was charged with repeated acts of inflicting physical and emotional harm and hazing on Masons and candidates
over an eight-year period, including physically handling blindfolded
candidates inappropriately during degree ceremonies. Due to the serious nature of the allegations, the grand master temporarily suspended
the member from his rights and privileges of Masonry pending results
of the trial. The accused pled not guilty, and the matter proceeded to
trial. At trial, the trial master found sufficient evidence showing the
accused assaulted multiple blindfolded candidates in the preparation
room prior to degrees, including grabbing, twisting, and pulling them by
their nipples, slapping one candidate on the chest, and striking another
on the back of his head. The trial master found the accused guilty of all
charges and set the penalty at expulsion.
• In Case No. 3085, the accused was charged with battery on a candidate
and use of abusive language. After being properly served, the accused
failed to respond within the required 30-day timeframe and defaulted.
The trial master proceeded with an investigation given the accused
default. After reviewing evidence and interviewing witnesses, the trial
master determined that the accused, while intoxicated and attending a public installation of officers Masonic event in November 2024,
engaged in inappropriate and aggressive behavior toward a prospective

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

273

candidate, resulting in the accused being removed from the lodge
property. All witnesses interviewed by the trial master stated that the
prospective candidate shared that he felt intentionally bullied by the
accused, as well as publicly demeaned and humiliated. This included
unwelcome physical contact, verbal humiliation, and a later confrontation that escalated to physical altercations with other Masons and use
of threatening language. The trial master noted aggravating factors that
occurred but were not charged, including a disregard by the accused for
the sanctity of ballot secrecy, electioneering, the lack of remorse, and
that the incident involved forcible inappropriate physical conduct with
a prospect. The trial master found the accused guilty on both charges,
and the penalty of expulsion from Freemasonry was imposed.
As to the third resolution and having completed our review of these matters,
the Committee on Trial Review therefore submits and moves for the adoption
of the following resolution:
“THAT, IN THE MATTERS OF CASE NUMBERS 3056, 3065, AND 3085
THE PROCEDURES, FINDINGS AND PENALTY AFFIXIED BY THE TRIAL
MASTER, IF ANY, BE HEREBY AFFIRMED AS PRESENTED.”
AS TO THE FOURTH AND FINAL RESOLUTION,
We present the following two reviewed petitions for restoration to good standing
in Freemasonry received during this Masonic year and analyzed these requests
applying the criteria set forth in the 2009 Grand Master’s Decision No. 3, which
establishes more than 22 considerations to be evaluated of such requests prior
to making a recommendation to Grand Lodge. The Guidelines for Restoration
outlines items that an individual should meet prior to be considered for restoration back into Freemasonry, including the seriousness of the nature of the
conduct giving rise to the suspension or expulsion, the passage of time between
the conduct and the request, and other evidence showing the individual is
worthy of consideration for membership.
• In the matter of William Gaede and Case No. 3069, William Gaede
was found guilty of embezzling $2,350 from his lodge and expelled
from Freemasonry last year, in 2024. Mr. Gaede pled no contest to the
embezzlement, which constitutes conduct involving moral turpitude
as defined in the California Masonic Code. Mr. Gaede submitted written
statements to the trial master offering an explanation, citing financial
hardship, expressing remorse, and his intent to eventually repay the
lodge, while admitting to embezzling lodge funds for his own use. The
trial master determined that the elements and violation of embezzlement had occurred, the accused admitted his guilt, and the trial master
set the penalty at expulsion.

274

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

Mr. Gaede’s prior home lodge, Drytown Lodge No. 174, submitted, for
our consideration, lodge meeting minutes of a vote that occurred on
April 2, 2025, in support of Mr. Gaede being restored to Freemasonry;
with seven votes in the affirmative and zero votes against the motion.
The Committee on Trial Review interviewed brothers of Drytown
Lodge, the original accuser, and spoke with Mr. Gaede directly to
assist in our assessment of whether Mr. Gaede had met the threshold described in the 2009 Grand Master’s Decision No. 3 governing requests for restoration. The committee determined that in this
instance, while Mr. Gaede has shown remorse and the lodge brethren
rallied around Mr. Gaede in his support, which included them helping repay the embezzled funds, your Committee on Trial Review vote
unanimously to recommend denial of Mr. Gaede’s request for restoration to good standing in Freemasonry. In our deliberation, it became
evident that Mr. Gaede is on a good path for reentry into Freemasonry,
but with only one year’s time elapsing since this serious misconduct
and his expulsion, the request does not meet the threshold nor is it
equitable to other individuals expelled for similar violations to consider altering a penalty of expulsion to a simple one year suspension.
Therefore, your Committee on Trial Review recommends Mr. Gaede’s
request for restoration be denied at this time.
• In the matter of Xavier Gozon and Case No. 3027, in 2024, Xavier
Gozon was found guilty at trial for maintaining membership in an irregular or unrecognized Masonic organization called Travelers Tambayan,
in violation of the requirements of our Masonic code and in violation
of his duty to obey the proper order of several grand masters to discontinue such prohibited conduct. The trial master found the accused
guilty of maintaining the unrecognized Masonic organizational membership and guilty of violating different grand masters’ orders and set
the penalty at expulsion.
In consideration of his request for restoration, the case materials and the
materials submitted by Mr. Gozon have been considered in determining whether
the request met the guidelines set forth in the 2009 Grand Masters Decision
No. 3 governing requests for restoration. In our deliberations, the committee
determined Mr. Gozon demonstrated a lack of remorse for a serious pattern
of violations of our Masonic code, and that he has not demonstrated behaviors
consistent with the considerations outlined in 2009 Grand Master’s Decision
No. 3, including the short one-year period from the date of his expulsion, and
the serious breach of our craft’s mandates to follow the proper orders of the
grand master. Altering the penalty from expulsion to punishment equivalent
to only a one-year suspension would not be equitable to other individuals who
have been expelled for similar violations. Therefore, your Committee on Trial
Review recommends not authorizing Mr. Gozon’s restoration request.

As to the fourth and final resolution and having completed our review of
these petitions for restoration to good standing in California Freemasonry, the
Committee on Trial Review therefore submits and moves for the adoption of
the following resolution:
“THAT, IN THE MATTERS OF CASE NUMBERS 3069 and 3027, THE
REQUESTS FOR RESTORATION TO GOOD STANDING BE DENIED
AND THE COMMITTEE’S FINDINGS AND RECOMMENDATIONS BE
HEREBY AFFIRMED AS PRESENTED.”

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE
ON YOUTH ORDERS

To Most Worshipful Grand Master Arthur L. Salazar Jr. and the members of the
Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of California,
This committee is charged with fostering positive fraternal relations
between the youth orders we support and the grand and constituted lodges
of California.
This committee has continued an open dialogue between the youth orders
through our committee members, district inspectors, and those advisors working with the individual youth orders. Contact with many of the adult leaders
is difficult as each organization has its own agenda. For example, trying to
reach the individuals in charge of making the recommendations for the Grand
Master’s Youth Support Award took several emails and phone calls and constant
reminders as deadline dates arrived and passed. After three deadline extensions,
I finally received all the recommendations. Despite this, the recommendations
were sent to the Grand Lodge a week before the grand secretary’s deadline.
It was our goal to encourage the Masons of this grand jurisdiction to visit
and support their local youth groups and assist in any way possible. However,
several of our constituted lodges who housed youth orders in their halls were less
than accommodating. The committee came across complaints about excessive
rental fees, sudden changes in scheduled events, such as meetings and installations being cancelled at the last minute for more lucrative hall rentals, and
being blamed for damaged lodge property even when the group was not present.
In one case, it was written into a rental contract with a DeMolay chapter that
the youth perform lodge membership recruiting duties to satisfy fulfillment of
the contract. Other complaints involved calling district inspectors to intervene
with lodges and remind the lodge of their duty to support our youth. Sadly,
there are lodges that treat their youth groups as if they are personal property.
They groups are regarded as “second class renters.” I have a copy of one such
contract and it is totally in conflict with our grand lodge’s ideals and morals
surrounding the support of our beloved youth orders. In cases such as these,
the only remedy is to move the group from that toxic environment and relocate
them to a more appreciative lodge setting, which has been done. Unfortunately,
it is a stark reality there are some lodges and hall associations that do not work

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

277

well with youth groups for a variety of reasons, usually for attitude, financial
reasons, or building scheduling conflicts. There are also opinions that the youth
group “works” for the sponsoring body, rather the than the other way around.
The committee also participated in several Zoom meetings for the purpose
of planning and assisting with the annual Masonic Tri-Youth Field Day held on
September 14, 2025. By advertising the event to local lodges, the committee was
able to secure some funding to offset the costs of the event.
The committee was also tasked with creating a “virtual youth program”
to benefit all three youth orders. This was a bit difficult because we needed to
define what “virtual” meant in relation to how we would proceed. We looked
into Spectrum advertising, hoping they would be able to create content and
advertise the youth groups in local markets. Spectrum is a nationwide cable
and Internet provider that can reach local as well as mass audiences. We then
realized that we should have a broader reach around California if we are to
expand chapters, assemblies, and bethels in more rural areas. The cost became
astronomical and therefore was not a feasible option.
We next approached iHeart Media, a conglomerate of radio stations
nationwide, to inquire about statewide advertising but again found it to be
cost-prohibitive.
In June of this year, an attempt was made by Northern California Jurisdiction
to hold a virtual DeMolay informational meeting. The idea was to invite DeMolay
members and non-members to participate. The idea was to treat non-members
as DeMolays until they could join a nearby chapter. If there was a large enough
attendance of non-members that were located too far from an operating chapter,
then attempts would be made to open a chapter at or near the closest lodge
in that geographical area. One of the problems is that we must still reach that
non-member to participate. Another was the fact that this meeting was for area
DeMolays only and did not include any other youth groups. This idea, though
well intentioned, fell short of the goal to include all the youth orders and was
therefore deemed infeasible.
We are of the opinion that to complete the task of a virtual youth program,
the makeup of the Committee on Youth Orders might include appointments
of brethren skilled in the techniques of mass marketing and media. Appointees
could include brothers who have a degree and are working in the marketing
and advertising fields, brothers who work in the film and television industries
who can produce such virtual content, or brothers who are experts in YouTube
content and Internet influencers as well as podcast specialists. This collaborative effort could release insightful, meaningful content and target distribution
at minimal costs and efforts, all benefiting the Grand Lodge of California and
our precious Masonic youth orders.
As indicated earlier, the committee was pleased to recommend the names
of the following brothers to receive the Grand Master’s Youth Service Award
for the year 2025. They are as follows:

278

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

279

Worshipful Brother George E. Whitmore, a past master of Fox-Coates
Daylight Lodge No. 842, receiving the award for his service to Job’s
Daughters International, California.
Brother George F. Lange, a member of Salinas Lodge No. 204, receiving
the award for his service to DeMolay International, Northern California
Jurisdiction.
Worshipful Brother George F. Witten, a past master of PetalumaHamilton Lodge No. 180 for his service to the International Order of the
Rainbow for Girls, California.
Worshipful Brother Mark E. Pressey, a past master of Irvine Lodge
No. 671 for his service to DeMolay International, Southern California
Jurisdiction.
Each of these recipients has demonstrated outstanding commitment and
service to our youth orders and was honored during the public ceremonies at
our 2025 Annual Communication.
The members of the committee are most appreciative of the confidence of
Most Worshipful Salazar and the entire Executive Committee. We thank them
for the privilege of service to the Grand Lodge and our masonic youth orders.
I trust that the 2026 committee will flourish and bring an even greater bond
between our Masonic youth orders and the Grand Lodge of California.
Respectfully submitted,

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE
ON THE CALIFORNIA FREEMASON MAGAZINE

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California,
The 2025 publishing cycle marked a year of creative expansion and renewed
historical focus for the California Freemason magazine. Each issue carried its
own character and purpose, and together they offered a varied and thoughtful
portrait of the fraternity’s work and traditions during this milestone period in
our history.
The spring issue focused on the 175th anniversary of our grand lodge and
tied directly into the celebrations happening throughout the state. Rather than
simply looking back, the issue highlighted key moments that brought us to this
milestone and shared stories from members and lodges that have carried our
fraternity forward. It was designed to give readers a grounded sense of how
far we’ve come and to recognize the many people and efforts that have shaped
California Masonry over the past 175 years.
The summer issue shifted to a different kind of examination, turning its
attention to the aspects of our craft that rely on performance. From the structure of our ritual to the theatricality present in many lodge traditions, the issue
invited readers to consider the skills, preparation, and expressive elements
that contribute to the experience of Masonic work. It offered perspectives
from members whose interest in theater, music, and public speaking connect
naturally with their Masonic practice.
For the fall issue, produced in conjunction with Annual Communication in
San Francisco, the magazine adopted a more exploratory approach. This edition highlighted the city’s central place in the story of Masonry in California. A
detailed fold-out map of Masonic points of interest provided members with the
opportunity to step beyond the printed page and encounter the city’s Masonic
landmarks directly. This element proved to be a popular companion during the
Annual Communication weekend and reflected the magazine’s ongoing interest
in blending print with hands-on engagement.
Our magazine also received notable recognition this year through the
Content Marketing Awards, marking the first time our publication was entered
into that program. The Prince Hall issue from 2024 earned top honors in the
nonprofit publication category and was also named a finalist for a special-topic

280

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

issue. In addition, the Heroes of Masonry issue received recognition for editorial excellence. These acknowledgments, drawn from a broad field of entries
representing many industries and organizations, speak to the consistent quality
of the magazine’s writing and design.
The committee is grateful for the dedicated efforts of the communications
staff who carry this work forward throughout the year. Their steady coordination,
editorial planning, design work, and production management make it possible
for the magazine to remain timely and relevant. Appreciation is also extended to
the contributors, photographers, designers, and editors whose work appears in
these pages, and to the many members who continue to support the magazine
through their engagement and feedback.
Respectfully submitted,
Standing Committee
Russell E. Hennings, Chairman, Editor-in-Chief
Arthur L. Salazar Jr., Grand Master
Allan L. Casalou, Grand Secretary
Ian E. Laurelin
Dago Rodriguez, PM
Emanuel A. Rose, PM

LODGES WITH DISPENSATIONS OR CHARTERS
PREDATING THE FORMATION OF
THE GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA
1

California
California No. 13 charter issued November 9, 1848 by the Grand Lodge of District
of Columbia.

2

Western Star
Western Star No. 98 charter issued May 10, 1848 by the Grand Lodge of Missouri.

3

Tehama
Connecticut No. 75/76 charter issued January 31, 1849 by the Grand Lodge of
Connecticut.

4

Berryman
New Jersey U.D. dispensation issued March 1, 1849 by the Grand Lodge of New
Jersey.

5

Benicia
Benicia U.D. dispensation issued June 5, 1849 by the Grand Lodge of Louisiana.

7

Davy Crockett
Davey Crocket U.D. dispensation issued in 1849 by the Grand Lodge of Louisiana.

9

Marysville
Lavely U.D. dispensation issued in March 1849 by the Grand Lodge of Illinois.

13

Nevada
La Fayette Lodge No. 29 charter issued April 17, 1850 by the Grand Lodge of
Wisconsin.

MUTUAL RECOGNITION WITH
FOREIGN GRAND LODGES 2025-2026
The Grand Lodge of California enjoys mutual recognition with grand
lodges in the United States and around the world. This includes some, but not
all, of the foreign grand lodges in the 2024 Acacia Book, as well as a number of
foreign grand lodges that are not listed therein.
For clarity, the foreign grand lodges that are recognized by the Grand Lodge
of California are listed below alphabetically by country. For those that are published in the 2025 Acacia Book, the corresponding page number is provided in
parentheses. Recognized grand lodges that are not published in the 2025 Acacia
Book are marked with an asterisk (*). The mutual recognition between our Grand
Lodge and those listed all include the right to intervisitation.
In some cases, the Grand Lodge of California has extended an offer of recognition to a number of grand lodges where mutual recognition does not yet exist.
Those are found at end of this list.
The Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge of California is responsible for all
correspondence with these grand lodges and the lodges under their jurisdiction.
Please contact this office for assistance.

To the Board of Trustees
The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted
Masons of the State of California
Opinion
We have audited the accompanying consolidated financial statements of The Most Worshipful Grand
Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California (the ''Organization''), which comprise the
consolidated statement of financial position as of October 31, 2025, and the related consolidated
statements of activities, functional expenses, and cash flows for the year then ended and the related notes
to the consolidated financial statements.
In our opinion, the consolidated financial statements referred to above present fairly, in all material
respects, the financial position of The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the
State of California as of October 31, 2025, and the changes in their net assets and their cash flows for the
year then ended in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of
America.
Basis for Opinion

Schedule of Fraternal Expenses (Unaudited)

34

We conducted our audit in accordance with auditing standards generally accepted in the United States of
America. Our responsibilities under those standards are further described in the Auditor's Responsibilities
for the Audit of the Financial Statements section of our report. We are required to be independent of The
Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California and to meet our
other ethical responsibilities in accordance with the relevant ethical requirements relating to our audit.
We believe that the audit evidence we have obtained is sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for
our audit opinion.

Schedule of Program Appropriations (Unaudited)

Responsibilities of Management for the Financial Statements

Schedule of General and Administrative Expenses (Unaudited)

36

Management is responsible for the preparation and fair presentation of these consolidated financial
statements in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America,
and for the design, implementation, and maintenance of internal control relevant to the preparation and
fair presentation of consolidated financial statements that are free from material misstatement, whether
due to fraud or error.

Other Information

In preparing the consolidated financial statements, management is required to evaluate whether there are
conditions or events, considered in the aggregate, that raise substantial doubt about The Most Worshipful
Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California's ability to continue as a going
concern within one year after the date that the consolidated financial statements are available to be issued.

Auditor's Responsibilities for the Audit of the Financial Statements
Our objectives are to obtain reasonable assurance about whether the consolidated financial statements as a
whole are free from material misstatement, whether due to fraud or error, and to issue an auditor's report
that includes our opinion. Reasonable assurance is a high level of assurance but is not absolute assurance
and therefore is not a guarantee that an audit conducted in accordance with generally accepted auditing
standards will always detect a material misstatement when it exists. The risk of not detecting a material
misstatement resulting from fraud is higher than for one resulting from error, as fraud may involve
collusion, forgery, intentional omissions, misrepresentations, or the override of internal control.
Misstatements, including omissions, are considered material if there is a substantial likelihood that,
individually or in the aggregate, they would influence the judgment made by a reasonable user based on
the consolidated financial statements.
In performing an audit in accordance with generally accepted auditing standards, we:


Exercise professional judgment and maintain professional skepticism throughout the audit.



Identify and assess the risks of material misstatement of the consolidated financial statements,
whether due to fraud or error, and design and perform audit procedures responsive to those risks.
Such procedures include examining, on a test basis, evidence regarding the amounts and disclosures
in the consolidated financial statements.



Obtain an understanding of internal control relevant to the audit in order to design audit procedures
that are appropriate in the circumstances, but not for the purpose of expressing an opinion on the
effectiveness of The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of
California's internal control. Accordingly, no such opinion is expressed.



Evaluate the appropriateness of accounting policies used and the reasonableness of significant
accounting estimates made by management, as well as evaluate the overall presentation of the
consolidated financial statements.



Conclude whether, in our judgment, there are conditions or events, considered in the aggregate, that
raise substantial doubt about The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the
State of California's ability to continue as a going concern for a reasonable period of time.

Supplementary Information
Our audit was conducted for the purpose of forming an opinion on the consolidated financial statements
as a whole. The information on pages 29 - 32 is presented for purposes of additional analysis and is not a
required part of the consolidated financial statements. Such information is the responsibility of
management and was derived from and relates directly to the underlying accounting and other records
used to prepare the consolidated financial statements. The information has been subjected to the auditing
procedures applied in the audit of the consolidated financial statements and certain additional procedures,
including comparing and reconciling such information directly to the underlying accounting and other
records used to prepare the consolidated financial statements or to the consolidated financial statements
themselves, and other additional procedures in accordance with auditing standards generally accepted in
the United States of America. In our opinion, the information is fairly stated in all material respects in
relation to the consolidated financial statements as a whole.

HISTORY AND ORGANIZATION
The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California (the
"Grand Lodge") is a nonprofit, unincorporated fraternal organization governed by a constitution
and ordinances setting forth its jurisdiction and authority. The jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge
includes all lodges and Masons within the state of California, and members of lodges of
California, wherever residing.
The Grand Lodge provides general and administrative services to its related entities: The Masonic
Homes of California (the "Masonic Homes") and its subsidiary Acacia Creek, a Senior Living
Retirement Community in Union City (Acacia Creek Union City); the California Masonic
Memorial Temple (the "Temple"); and the California Masonic Foundation (the "Foundation")
(collectively, the "Masonic Entities"). These services are reimbursed by the related entities.
The California Masonic Code (Code) sets forth the effects and process of a lodge dissolution
upon the surrender of its charter. The members of the chartered lodges of the Sublime Benicia
Lodge No. 5, Plumas Lodge No. 60 voted to surrender their respective charters to the Grand
Lodge.
The Grand Lodge accepted the surrender of these lodges' charters and directed that these lodges
be dissolved in accordance with the Code. At the 2024 Annual Communication, the charter of
Sierra Lodge No. 788 was revoked, and no assets were transferred to Grand Lodge for the year
ended October 31, 2025.
Upon the surrender of a lodge charter, Grand Lodge assumes the position of the lodge and
becomes the sole member of the lodge's Hall Association. As a result of the lodges' dissolution
named above, the Grand Lodge became the sole member of the following Hall Associations:


The Benicia Masonic Temple Association (Benicia Hall) on October 11, 2014;



Plumas Hall Association (Plumas Hall) on October 10, 2015.



Sierra Masonic Center Association on October 27, 2024

The financial statements of these "Hall Associations" are included in the consolidated financial
statements of the Grand Lodge.
Nob Hill
On February 15, 2007, the Temple transferred the auditorium and garage operation to a new
entity, Nob Hill Masonic Center, Inc. ("Nob Hill"), an entity for this purpose. Nob Hill is a
subsidiary of the Grand Lodge.
On October 30, 2008, the Temple transferred operations of the auditorium from Nob Hill to Live
Nation, not an affiliate.

SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES

2.

427

SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES (continued)

Principles of consolidation

Use of estimates

The consolidated financial statements include accounts of the Grand Lodge, Nob Hill, and the
Hall Associations (collectively, the "Organization"). All significant intercompany accounts and
transactions have been eliminated.

The preparation of consolidated financial statements in conformity with accounting principles
generally accepted in the United States of America requires management to make estimates and
assumptions. These estimates and assumptions affect the reported amounts of assets and
liabilities, disclosure of contingent assets and liabilities at the date of the consolidated financial
statements, and the reported amounts of revenues and expenses during the reporting period.
Actual results could differ from those estimates.

Comparative information
The consolidated financial statements include certain prior-year summarized comparative
information in total but not by net asset class. Such information does not include sufficient detail
to constitute a presentation in conformity with accounting principles generally accepted in the
United States of America. Accordingly, such information should be read in conjunction with the
Organization's consolidated financial statements for the year ended October 31, 2024, from which
the summarized information was derived.
Net assets classifications
The accompanying consolidated financial statements have been prepared in accordance with the
standards set forth in Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB) Accounting Standards
Codification (ASC) 958-605 Revenue Recognition, ASC 958-205 Presentation of Financial
Statements, and the guidelines set forth in the industry audit and accounting guide Not-for-Profit
Entities issued by the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants. Under these guidelines,
contributions of cash and other assets are classified as one of the following two categories:


Net assets without donor restrictions - Net assets without donor restrictions represent
resources that are not subject to donor-imposed stipulations and are available to support all
activities of the Grand Lodge, including the Grand Lodge Endowment Fund (the
"Endowment Fund").
The Endowment Fund was established at the Grand Lodge's October 1993, Annual
Communication. If, in any fiscal year, there was an excess of support and revenues over
expenses, as defined by the Grand Lodge Executive Committee, the excess shall be added to
the Endowment Fund. For the years ended October 31, 2025 and 2024, there was no excess
of support and revenues over expenses.



Net assets with donor restrictions - Net assets with donor restrictions represent contributions
that are limited in use in accordance with donor-imposed stipulations. These stipulations may
expire with time and/or may be satisfied by the actions of the Grand Lodge according to the
intention of the donor. Upon satisfaction of such stipulations, the associated net assets are
released from net assets with donor restrictions and reported as net assets without donor
restrictions.

10

Fair value of financial instruments
The carrying amounts reported in the accompanying consolidated statements of financial position
for cash and cash equivalents, accounts receivable, accounts payable and accrued liabilities, and
due from/due to related entities, approximate fair value due to their short-term nature. Discussion
on the fair value of financial instruments is included in Note 3.
Fair value process
The Organization determines fair value measurement policies and procedures for assets and
liabilities under the supervision of the Investment Committee. These policies and procedures are
reassessed annually to determine if the current valuation techniques are still appropriate. A
variety of qualitative factors are used to subjectively determine the most appropriate valuation
methodologies. Methodologies are consistent with market, income, and cost approaches.
Unobservable inputs used in fair value measurements are evaluated and adjusted on an annual
basis, or as necessary based on current market conditions and other third-party information. In
determining the reasonableness of the methodology, Grand Lodge evaluates a variety of factors
including a review of existing agreements, economic conditions, industry, and market
developments. Certain unobservable inputs are assessed through review of contract terms while
others are substantiated utilizing available market data including, but not limited to, market
comparable, qualified opinions, and discount rates.
Cash and cash equivalents
Cash and cash equivalents consist of highly liquid investments with original maturities of three
months or less at the time of purchase, with the exception of cash and cash equivalents held as
investments.
Prepaid expenses
Prepaid expenses consist primarily of prepaid insurance coverage, IT applications advance
subscription fees and other events-related advance payments.

Investments

Leases (continued)

Investments in fixed income and equity securities are stated at estimated fair values based on
quoted market prices. Investments received through gifts are recorded at estimated fair values at
the date of donation. The fair value of alternative investments is recorded at the investment
manager's Net Asset Value (NAV), as the managers have the greatest insight into the investments
of their funds and the related industry and have the appropriate expertise to determine the NAV.
The Grand Lodge assesses the NAV and takes into consideration events such as suspended
redemptions, restructuring, secondary sales, and investor defaults to determine if an adjustment is
necessary. Additionally, asset holdings are reviewed within the investment manager's audited
financial statements, as are interim financial statements and fund manager communications, for
the purposes of assessing valuation. Unrealized gains or losses that result from market
fluctuations are recorded in the period in which such fluctuations occur. Realized gains or losses
resulting from sales or maturities of securities are calculated on a cost basis.

The Organization also elected to combine lease and nonlease components and to keep leases with
an initial term of twelve months or less off the consolidated statements of financial position and
recognize the associated lease payments in the consolidated statements of activities and changes
in net assets on a straight-line basis over the lease term. The Organization has elected to not
recognize operating lease ROU assets and operating lease liabilities for leases with a
noncancellable lease term of twelve months or less and management has determined that the
expected term of the existing month-to-month leases are not reasonably certain to extend past
twelve months and therefore not recognized as operating lease ROU assets and operating lease
liabilities.

Property and equipment
Property and equipment, including leasehold improvements, greater than $1,000 are recorded at
cost and are depreciated using the straight-line method over estimated useful lives of 3 to 25
years.
The Grand Lodge periodically evaluates the carrying value of its long-lived assets for
impairment. The evaluations address the estimated recoverability of the assets' carrying value,
which is principally determined based on projected undiscounted cash flows generated by the
underlying tangible assets. When the carrying value of an asset exceeds its estimated
recoverability, a write-down is recorded. No impairment was recorded during the years ended
October 31, 2025 and 2024.
Other assets
Other assets consist primarily of a collection of jewelry used in lodge ceremonies.
Leases
In the ordinary course of business, the Organization enters a variety of lease arrangements,
including operating and finance leases. Transactions give rise to leases when the Organization
receives substantially all the economic benefits from and has the ability to direct the use of
specified property and equipment. The Organization determines if an arrangement is a lease at
inception. As of October 31, 2025 and 2024, there are no operating lease right-of-use ("ROU")
assets and operating lease liabilities in the Organization's consolidated statements of financial
position. Finance leases are included in property and equipment and loan payable.

fiscal year. These amounts are recognized as revenue in the following fiscal year, which is the

Revenue recognition (continued)

Concentration of credit risk

The Organization records certain revenue from contracts with customers in accordance with ASC
Topic 606. Under ASC Topic 606, the Organization must identify the contract with a customer,
identify the performance obligations in the contract, determine the transaction price, allocate the
transaction price to the performance obligations in the contract, and recognize revenue when (or
as) the Organization satisfies a performance obligation. Significant revenue has not been
recognized in the current reporting period that results from performance obligations satisfied in
previous periods.

Financial instruments potentially subjecting the Grand Lodge to concentrations of credit risk
consist primarily of bank demand deposits in excess of Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
(FDIC) insurance thresholds, cash held in money market accounts in excess of the amounts
insured by the U.S. Treasury insurance for money market funds, and various debt and equity
investments in excess of Securities Investor Protection Corporation (SIPC) insurance. Demand
deposits are placed with a local financial institution, and management has not experienced any
loss related to these demand deposits in the past. If any of the financial institutions with whom
the Grand Lodge does business were to be placed into receivership with the FDIC, the Grand
Lodge may be unable to access the cash they have on deposit with such institutions. If the Grand
Lodge was unable to access its cash and cash equivalents as needed, the Grand Lodge's financial
position and ability to operate its business could be adversely affected. The Grand Lodge has not
experienced any losses in such accounts, and management believes it is not exposed to any
significant credit risk on cash and investments. Investment securities are exposed to various risks,
such as interest rate, market, and credit risk. It is at least reasonably possible, given the level of
risk associated with investment securities, that changes in the near term could materially affect
the amount reported in the consolidated statements. The risk associated with the investments is
mitigated through diversification.

Certain sources of revenue are derived from interest and dividends earned on investment
securities and other financial instruments that are not within the scope of ASC Topic 606.
Revenue from contracts with customers in the scope of ASC Topic 606 is recognized in
noninterest income. Sources of revenue from contracts with customers that are in the scope of
ASC Topic 606 include the following:


Lodge per capita fees - Grand Lodge earns per capita dues revenue from member lodges
for services rendered. Per capita fees are charged to member lodge annually and are
recognized as revenue ratably as the performance obligation is satisfied. The performance
obligation is met over the period to which the services relate.



Garage revenues - Nob Hill earns garage revenue from customers for services rendered
as the contract transaction occurs. Garage revenue is charged to customers as they enter
the location and is recognized as the performance obligation is satisfied. The performance
obligation is met when services are provided.

ASC 820, Fair Value Measurements and Disclosures, defines fair value as the price that would
be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market
participants at the measurement date. ASC 820 also establishes a fair value hierarchy that requires
an entity to maximize the use of observable inputs and minimize the use of unobservable inputs
when measuring fair value. The standard describes three levels of inputs that may be used to
measure fair value:
Level 1 - Quoted prices in active markets for identical assets or liabilities.
Level 2 - Observable inputs other than Level 1 prices, such as quoted prices for similar assets or
liabilities; quoted prices in markets that are not active; or other inputs that are observable or can
be corroborated by observable market data for substantially the full term of the assets or
liabilities.
Level 3 - Unobservable inputs that are supported by little or no market activity and that are
significant to the fair value of the assets or liabilities.

3.

Following is a description of the valuation methodology used for instruments measured at fair
value on a recurring basis and recognized in the accompanying consolidated financial statements,
as well as the general classification of such instruments pursuant to the valuation hierarchy:
Investments - Where quoted market prices are available in an active market, securities are
classified within Level 1 of the valuation hierarchy. Level 1 securities include exchange traded
equities. If quoted market prices are not available, then fair values are estimated by using
pricing models, quoted prices of securities with identical characteristics, or discounted cash
flows. In certain cases, where Level 1 or Level 2 inputs are not available, securities are
classified within Level 3 of the hierarchy and include certain real estate investments, and other
less liquid securities using investment appropriate models like the income approach for real
estate investments.

Foreign stocks
These are funds invested primarily in common stocks of international issuers. This includes both
large and small-cap issuers as well as opportunistic exposure to issuers in the emerging markets.
Domestic equity
These common trust funds are invested and reinvested primarily in a portfolio of equity securities
with the objective of approximating as closely as practicable the capitalization weighted total rate
of return of the entire United States market for publicly traded equity securities. The criterion for
selection of investments is the Dow Jones U.S. Total Stock Market Index.
Foreign equity
This category represents investments in global equity fund. The objectives are to invest primarily
in long-only portfolio of global equities and to invest only in 'exceptional' companies that have
that rare ability to grow the real value of their profits and cash flows over long periods of time.
The investments are spread across global markets.

20

437

INVESTMENTS (continued)
Alternative investments
Global Macro - The fund's objective is capital appreciation. Its principal activity is trading in
the international currency, financial, commodities, and securities markets. The fund has a
broad mandate to trade in all exchange and over-the-counter markets, and to trade in
derivative products and other instruments.
Credit Long/Short - The investment objective of the fund, the Intermediate fund, and the
Master fund is to achieve long-term capital appreciation, on a favorable risk-adjusted basis, by
applying a flexible and opportunistic approach to investing which involves evaluating the
current attractiveness of various asset classes, including bank loans, bonds, equities,
speculative investments, and cash equivalents, and investing its assets accordingly.
EM Macro - The fund will generally focus on seeking an enhanced risk adjusted return
through capital appreciation within a macro investment framework, investing primarily in
global macro-opportunities with a focus on emerging markets securities and related
derivatives, across the complete universe of FX, rates, credit, and equity as well as
commodities. The fund expects to utilize discretionary macro processes, systematic macro
processes and special situation macro processes and aims to deliver returns that are agnostic to
the business cycle of emerging markets.
Structured Credit - The fund seeks to achieve high absolute returns with low volatility and
low correlation to traditional fixed income and equity markets by investing in credit
investments across credit sectors and throughout an issuer's capital structure with a primary
focus on structured credit, which includes secured and structured commercial, consumer and
corporate assets. The fund may also pursue direct lending opportunities, including joint
ventures with third parties and debt and/or equity investments in newly formed lending
companies. Further, the fund may use a variety of instruments to manage credit spread
duration, interest rate duration and market volatility.
Real Estate - This is an investment in an actively managed core portfolio of equity real estate
that seeks to provide attractive returns while limiting downside risk and has both relative and
real return objectives. Its relative performance objective is to outperform the NFI-ODCE index
over any given three-to-five-year period. The fund's real return performance objective is to
achieve at least a 5% real rate of return (i.e., inflation-adjusted return), before advisory fees,
over any given three-to-five-year period.
Special Opportunities - This is an investment in a multi-strategy event driven hedge fund. The
fund invests opportunistically throughout capital structures and targets catalysts in a variety of
event equity and event credit strategies. The fund will invest across a number of sectors but
has historically held a bias and preference towards companies in the gaming, lodging, leisure
and real estate sectors. Underlying strategies include distressed debt, relative value, event
driven equity, value equity and leveraged loans. Investments are predominantly made with
small and mid-cap U.S. based companies, and historically the fund's exposure has been 8590% U.S.-based. Structured credit, municipal debt, and sovereign debt are generally avoided.
